title: Tokens & Typography
text: Themvora's token system goes far beyond colors: typography (font family, font size, line height), spacing, radius, shadows, border widths, z-index and breakpoints are all semantic theme tokens. Live interactive demos per token group, how tokens map to CSS variables (--theme-color-*, --theme-typography-*, --theme-spacing-*, --theme-radius-*, --theme-shadow-*, --theme-border-width-*), and defining every group in one defineTheme call.

title: Zero Flash
text: How Themvora prevents a flash of the wrong theme on reload and SSR. The problem (flash of incorrect theme), the full pipeline (persist → resolve → generate → render → blocking bootstrap → paint → hydrate), the core primitives (createThemeBootstrapScript, buildThemeCssMap, darkModeCSSTemplate), and per-framework integration for React, Next.js, Vue/Nuxt, SvelteKit, Solid, Angular, Astro, Remix and Web Components.

title: generateShades(baseColor, count, baseIndex): string[]
text: generateShades(baseColor, count, baseIndex): string[] Generates a `count`-step tonal scale from a single base color. The base color sits exactly at `baseIndex`; lighter steps blend towards white and darker steps towards black. Non-hex colors are repeated unchanged. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `baseColor` | `string` | — | | `count` | `number` | — | | `baseIndex` | `number` | — | **Returns** `string[]` ---

title: hexToRgb(color): RGB | null
text: hexToRgb(color): RGB | null Parses a hex color string into an RGB triplet. Accepts `#rgb` (3-digit) and `#rrggbb` (6-digit) forms. A leading `#` is required; any other input returns `null`. **See also:** `rgbToHex` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `color` | `string` | The hex color string to parse. | **Returns** `RGB | null` — The parsed triplet, or `null` when the input is not a valid hex color. ---

title: mixColors(a, b, t): string
text: mixColors(a, b, t): string Mixes two hex colors by interpolating their RGB channels. When either input is not a valid hex color, the closer input (`t < 0.5` picks `a`, otherwise `b`) is returned unchanged. **See also:** `mixHex` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `a` | `string` | The starting hex color (`t = 0`). | | `b` | `string` | The ending hex color (`t = 1`). | | `t` | `number` | The interpolation factor, typically `0`–`1`. | **Returns** `string` — The mixed color as a `#rrggbb` hex string. ---

title: mixHex(a, b, t): RGB
text: mixHex(a, b, t): RGB Linearly interpolates between two RGB triplets. Each channel is computed as `a + (b - a) * t` and clamped to `0`–`255`. **See also:** `mixColors` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `a` | `RGB` | The starting triplet (`t = 0`). | | `b` | `RGB` | The ending triplet (`t = 1`). | | `t` | `number` | The interpolation factor, typically `0`–`1`. | **Returns** `RGB` — The interpolated triplet. ---

title: readBreakpoints(tokens, fallback): Record<string, string>

When no breakpoints resolve, `fallback` is returned unchanged. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `tokens` | `ThemeTokens \| undefined` | The theme's resolved tokens, or `undefined`. | | `fallback` | `Record<string, string>` | The map returned when no breakpoints resolve. Defaults to `{}`. | **Returns** `Record<string, string>` — A map of breakpoint name to value. ---

Accepts nested paths (`primary.main`) and matches camelCase / kebab-case variants so both `primaryForeground` and `primary-foreground` token keys work. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `theme` | `AdapterResolvedTheme` | — | | `key` | `string` | — | | `fallback` | `string` (optional) | — | **Returns** `string | undefined` ---

title: readFontFamily(tokens, fallback, preferred?): string
text: readFontFamily(tokens, fallback, preferred?): string Resolves a font family from the theme's `typography.fontFamilies` tokens. When `preferred` is given and resolves to a string it wins; otherwise the first of `sans`, `body`, `ui`, `heading` that resolves is used, then the first family in the group, and finally `fallback`. **See also:** `readToken` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `tokens` | `ThemeTokens \| undefined` | The theme's resolved tokens, or `undefined`. | | `fallback` | `string` | The value returned when no family resolves. Defaults to `"system-ui, sans-serif"`. | | `preferred` | `string` (optional) | An optional family key to prefer over the built-in order. | **Returns** `string` — A resolved font family string. ---

title: buildThemeCSSMap(themes): ThemeCSSMap
text: buildThemeCSSMap(themes): ThemeCSSMap Builds a ThemeCSSMap of flattened CSS variables from a list of themes. Selects the light and dark themes of the first theme family and flattens their tokens into CSS variables. Falls back to the first light/dark theme, or the first theme, when a mode is not present. **See also:** `createBlockingScriptContent` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `themes` | `readonly ThemeDefinition<string>[]` | The theme definitions to build the map from. | **Returns** `ThemeCSSMap` — A ThemeCSSMap with light and dark CSS variables. ---

title: createAngularPersistence(): ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter
text: createAngularPersistence(): ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter Creates an Angular-aware theme selection persistence adapter. May be called from an Angular injection context. The adapter reads and writes the theme selection (mode and theme family) to `localStorage` in the browser and to `TransferState` on the server, so the selection survives server-side rendering and is hydrated on the client. It also subscribes to cross-tab `storage` events. **See also:** `provideTheme` **Returns** `ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter` — A `ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter` bound to the current platform. ---

title: createBlockingScriptContent<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(themes, savedSelection?, options): string
text: createBlockingScriptContent<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(themes, savedSelection?, options): string Generates the blocking bootstrap HTML (a critical CSS `<style>` and a blocking `<script>`) that applies the theme before first paint. The script sets the theme mode and family attributes and toggles the `dark` class. The critical `<style>` carries the CSS variables: a plain `:root` rule when the resolved mode is concrete, or — when it is `"system"` — a `prefers-color-scheme` block per scheme, so an OS-dark visitor is correct with no JavaScript at all. The saved selection (from persistence) is honored when provided. **See also:** `buildThemeCSSMap`, `BlockingScriptOptions` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `themes` | `readonly T[]` | The theme definitions to emit CSS variables for. | | `savedSelection` | `{ family: string; mode: ThemeMode } \| null` (optional) | The persisted mode and theme family, if any. | | `options` | `BlockingScriptOptions<T>` | Fallback mode/family inputs. Must match the client runtime's `initialMode`/`defaultTheme` so the two resolve the same theme. | **Returns** `string` — An HTML string containing the critical style and blocking script. ---

title: injectEffectiveThemeMode(): Signal<"light" | "dark">
text: injectEffectiveThemeMode(): Signal<"light" | "dark"> Injects the mode actually **applied** — `"light"` or `"dark"`, never `"system"` — as a read-only signal. The narrow form of injectTheme: use it in a component that only displays the current appearance, so it re-renders for an OS change or a sunrise/sunset transition and not for anything else. May be called from an Angular injection context. **See also:** `injectTheme`, `ThemeState.resolvedMode` **Returns** `Signal<"light" | "dark">` — A read-only `Signal<"light" | "dark">`. ```ts const mode = injectEffectiveThemeMode(); // template: {{ mode() }} ``` ---

title: injectGeneratedTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): Signal<T>
text: injectGeneratedTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): Signal<T> Injects the theme produced by `generateTheme()` and registered with the provider, as a read-only signal. Resolves the registered theme that carries the generator's origin marker (`meta.generation.kind === "generated"`); shipped presets never qualify. When both halves of one `generateTheme()` call are registered, the signal tracks the theme the active selection resolves to, and unsubscribes automatically when the injector is destroyed. May be called from an Angular injection context. Throws `ThemeError` with code `TV_GENERATION_THEME_NOT_FOUND` when the provider holds no generated theme, and `TV_GENERATION_THEME_AMBIGUOUS` when several are registered and the active selection does not identify one. Re-resolves on every settled change to the registry, store, or selection; if the generated theme is later removed, the same error is raised at the next reactive read rather than a stale theme being returned. **See also:** `injectTheme` **Returns** `Signal<T>` — A read-only `Signal<T>` holding the registered generated theme. ```ts const generated = injectGeneratedTheme(); effect(() => console.log(generated().name)); ``` ---

title: AntdStyleRegistry(namedParameters): Element
text: AntdStyleRegistry(namedParameters): Element Serialises Ant Design's CSS-in-JS cache into the server HTML.

title: Why this is needed
text: Why this is needed Ant Design does not ship a stylesheet — every rule lives in a cssinjs cache that only exists at runtime. Without serialising it, the server HTML carries the markup but none of the styling, and the first frame after a reload is unstyled: no card surfaces, native form controls, stacked text.

title: Why the layer matters
text: Why the layer matters See SSR_LAYER. The short version: this block must never outrank the live cache, or theme switching silently stops working for every component whose colours come from antd tokens. **Returns** `Element` ```ts // app/layout.tsx import { AntdStyleRegistry } from "@themvora/antd/next"; <ThemeProvider> <AntdStyleRegistry>{children}</AntdStyleRegistry> </ThemeProvider> ``` ---

title: buildAntdConfig(theme): ThemeConfig
text: buildAntdConfig(theme): ThemeConfig Builds an Ant Design `ThemeConfig` from a resolved Themvora theme.

title: What this maps, and why
text: What this maps, and why Ant Design's design tokens are *derived*: it runs an algorithm over a handful of seeds (`colorPrimary`, `colorBgBase`, `colorTextBase`, …) and computes every alias from them. Two consequences shape this adapter: - The algorithm itself is mode-specific. `defaultAlgorithm` computes a light palette; `darkAlgorithm` computes a dark one. Running the light algorithm over a dark Themvora theme is what made dark integrations look washed out — every derived surface was still the light one. The algorithm is therefore selected from the resolved theme's mode, not fixed. - Semantic roles must be seeded from the *matching* Themvora token. Ant Design's `colorWarning` was being seeded from `accent` and `colorSuccess` from `muted`, so warning and success rendered in unrelated colours. The neutral roles are seeded from Themvora's own neutrals — `background` for the page, `card` for containers, `popover` for elevated surfaces, `muted` for hover/selected fills, `mutedForeground` for secondary text — so cards, inputs and overlays stay visually distinct instead of collapsing onto one surface. **See also:** `AntdThemeProvider` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `theme` | `AdapterResolvedTheme` | The resolved theme to map from. | **Returns** `ThemeConfig` — An Ant Design `ThemeConfig` object. ---

title: ThemeProviderClient<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(props): null
text: ThemeProviderClient<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(props): null Client island component that installs the theme runtime on the browser. It publishes it as the app-wide runtime (see getGlobalRuntime), wires the cookie persistence adapter, and mirrors the selection back to cookies so the server resolves the same state on the next request. **See also:** `getGlobalRuntime`, `createAstroThemePersistence`, `useThemeRuntime`, `ThemeScope`, `createBlockingScript` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `props` | `ThemeProviderClientProps<T>` | The island props (see ThemeProviderClientProps). | **Returns** `null` — `null` — this component only sets up the runtime and side effects. This is an island component: it renders nothing and only runs on the client. Mount it inside the server-rendered provider (e.g. `provider.astro`) so the SSR-resolved `initial` state is available. **One runtime per document.** If a runtime is already installed — by `getThemeController()` behind `<ThemeToggle />`, or by another island — this component adopts it rather than creating a second one, and leaves its destruction to the owner. That is what lets a page mix native Astro controls and React islands without two runtimes racing to write `<html>`. On a server-rendered page the island's *own* markup must come from the same registry the document used. `provider.astro` publishes the configuration on `globalThis` for exactly that reason; without it the island's server render falls back to the built-in themes while its hydrated render uses the real ones, and React reports a text mismatch (error #418) and re-renders the island. ```ts --- import { ThemeProviderClient } from "@themvora/astro/client"; --- <ThemeProviderClient client:load initial={initial} /> ``` No theme props are needed: the registry, the default theme and the initial mode/family all come from the `theme.config.ts` the integration transported. Pass `initial` only when the page resolved the selection on the server with `getInitialThemeState()`. ``` ---

title: ThemeReadout(props): Element
text: ThemeReadout(props): Element Renders a theme-derived value that the **server cannot know**, without the post-hydration settle — and without the caller having to remember the contract that makes it work. **See also:** `ThemeReadoutKind`, `ThemeReadoutProps` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `props` | `ThemeReadoutProps` | The readout props (see ThemeReadoutProps). | **Returns** `Element` — A `<span>` carrying the bootstrap-readout contract. For `mode: "system"` the server renders a fallback it cannot verify (it cannot read `prefers-color-scheme`). The pre-paint bootstrap resolves the real value and patches this element's text before the first paint, so the readout is correct from frame one instead of correcting itself after hydration. Two attributes make that work, and this component is the reason callers do not have to know about them: - `data-tv-readout` marks the node as bootstrap-owned, so the end-of-body patch script (see `createThemeReadoutScript`) writes the resolved value into it. - `suppressHydrationWarning` tells React that this text node is intentionally divergent: React renders its own (server) value, sees the DOM already differs, and neither warns nor rewrites it. Its post-hydration render then produces the live value — the same value the script wrote — so nothing moves. Drop either one and the settle comes back: without the marker nothing patches the text, and without the suppression React rewrites the server's fallback over the patched value and then corrects it again. It degrades safely. If the bootstrap is not present (for example `injectBootstrap: false` with no replacement) the patch script returns immediately, the server-rendered fallback stays on screen, and no exception is thrown — so this is progressive enhancement, not a hard runtime dependency. A value that is not one of the four semantic kinds — a resolved CSS variable, say — is not covered here. Use the raw contract for that: `data-tv-readout="var:--theme-color-primary"` plus `suppressHydrationWarning` on the element that renders the value. **This is the only supported way to display a theme value in a React island.** `useTheme()` and its siblings read through `useSyncExternalStore`, so during hydration they return `runtime.initial` — the resolution the *server* produced, which cannot know the persisted selection or `prefers-color-scheme`. Rendering that as text paints a value the document does not have and corrects it once hydration commits; the visitor sees the same line change from one theme name to another for a frame or three. Values from those hooks are for behaviour — comparing, deriving, deciding — and a displayed one belongs in a readout. ```ts Active theme <ThemeReadout kind="theme" fallback="—" /> ``` ---

title: ThemeScope(props): Element
text:
ThemeScope(props): Element Applies a local theme to a subtree, overriding the app-wide selection. **See also:** `ThemeProviderClient`, `ThemeScopeProps` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `props` | `ThemeScopeProps` | The scope props (see ThemeScopeProps). | **Returns** `Element` — A `
` wrapping the scoped content. The scope is a nested override: it does not change the app-wide selection, only the CSS variables on its own element. The binding is destroyed when the scope unmounts. The variables are resolved **during render**, not in an effect, so they are present in the server-rendered markup. That distinction is what makes the scope flash-free: an effect-only scope emits a bare `
` on the server, so its content paints with the *global* theme on the first frame and is repainted with the scoped one after hydration — a visible colour change on everything inside. Resolving during render puts the same variables in the server HTML and in the client's first render, so hydration confirms them and there is nothing to correct. The effect below then only has to handle later changes (`theme`, `transition`) and the cross-fade between them. ```ts

This content uses the brand-dark theme.

 ``` ---

title: useGeneratedTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): T
text: useGeneratedTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): T Returns the theme produced by `generateTheme()` and registered with the provider. Client-only; re-renders when the resolved generated theme changes. Resolves the registered theme that carries the generator's origin marker (`meta.generation.kind === "generated"`); shipped presets never qualify. When both halves of one `generateTheme()` call are registered, the theme the active selection resolves to is returned. Throws `ThemeError` with code `TV_GENERATION_THEME_NOT_FOUND` when the provider holds no generated theme, and `TV_GENERATION_THEME_AMBIGUOUS` when several are registered and the active selection does not identify one. Re-resolves on every settled change to the registry, store, or selection; if the generated theme is later removed, the same error is raised at the next render rather than a stale theme being returned. **See also:** `useThemeValue` **Returns** `T` — The registered generated theme. ---

title: useTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): { family: string; mode: ThemeMode; setFamily: type(nextFamily: string): void; setMode: type(nextMode: ThemeMode): void; theme: T; toggleTheme: type(): void }
text: useTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): { family: string; mode: ThemeMode; setFamily: type(nextFamily: string): void; setMode: type(nextMode: ThemeMode): void; theme: T; toggleTheme: type(): void } Returns the current theme, mode, family, and stable setters. Client-only; re-renders when any of the reactive values change. **See also:** `useThemeRuntime`, `useThemeValue`, `useThemeMode`, `useThemeFamily` **Returns** `{ family: string; mode: ThemeMode; setFamily: __type(nextFamily: string): void; setMode: __type(nextMode: ThemeMode): void; theme: T; toggleTheme: __type(): void }` — An object with `theme`, `mode`, `family`, `setMode`, `setFamily` and `toggleTheme`. **These values are for behaviour, not for display.** `theme`, `mode` and `family` are read through `useSyncExternalStore`, so while the island hydrates they hold `runtime.initial` — the resolution the *server* produced, which cannot know the persisted selection or `prefers-color-scheme`. Rendering one of them as text paints a value the document does not have, and corrects it once hydration commits: the line visibly changes from one theme name to another a few frames in. Use `ThemeReadout` for anything on screen. It is owned by the pre-paint bootstrap contract, so it agrees with `<html>` from the first frame — for these same three values. Compare, derive and decide with them; render with a readout. ```ts const { theme, mode, setMode, toggleTheme } = useTheme(); ``` ---

title: useThemeSchedule(): ThemeSchedule | null
text: useThemeSchedule(): ThemeSchedule | null Reactive sunrise/sunset schedule controller. Returns `null` when the runtime was created without the `scheduled` option. ```tsx const schedule = useThemeSchedule(); schedule?.enable(); schedule?.disable(); schedule?.set({ timeZone: "Asia/Kathmandu" }); ``` **See also:** `useThemeRuntime` **Returns** `ThemeSchedule | null` The returned controller is a **reactive view**: its state reads (`state`, `enabled`, `active`, `status`, `sunrise`, `sunset`, …) come from the subscription below, not from the live controller. That distinction is what makes it safe to render during SSR. The schedule is resolved per visitor (timezone auto-detection) and recomputes on a timer, so sunrise/sunset differ between the server render and hydration. The subscription hydrates from EMPTY_THEME_SCHEDULE_STATE — the same snapshot the server rendered — and only adopts the live state after mount, so hydration matches. Returning the raw controller instead (which is what this hook used to do, discarding the subscription it had just created) handed consumers the *live* value during the hydration render: React saw a mismatch against the server HTML and re-rendered the whole island. Consumers must therefore read state through this return value — never through a controller they obtained some other way, which has no server snapshot. ---

text: ThemeProviderClientProps<T extends ThemeDefinition> Props for the Astro `ThemeProviderClient` island component. Describes the SSR-resolved initial state and the theme registry the client runtime is created with. **See also:** `ThemeProviderClient` | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `adapters` (optional) | `ThemeAdapter<T>[]` | DOM adapters (component-library bridges) to install. | | `broadcast` (optional) | `ThemeSelectionBroadcastAdapter \| null` | Cross-tab broadcast adapter. Omitted → a `BroadcastChannel` on `"theme-selection"`; `null` disables cross-tab sync. | | `cssVariables` (optional) | `false \| CSSVariablesOptions` | CSS custom property binding. Defaults to `{}` (write `--theme-*` on `<html>`). Pass `false` to disable. | | `defaultTheme` (optional) | `ThemeIdentifier<T>` | Fallback theme when no selection is persisted. Accepts a supplied theme **name** (`"cocoa-light"`) or a **family** (`"cocoa"`); a family resolves to the variant for the mode in effect. | | `dom` (optional) | `false \| DOMBindingOptions` | DOM attribute binding. Defaults to `{}` (bind `data-theme` on `<html>`). Pass `false` to disable. | | `initial` (optional) | `InitialThemeResolution<T>` | The SSR-resolved initial theme state (from `getInitialThemeState`). When provided it wins on first paint, so hydration matches exactly. Omit it on prerendered/static pages (no request available) — the island then reads the persisted selection from storage on the client instead. | | `initialFamily` (optional) | `ThemeIdentifier<T>` | Family used when nothing is persisted. Optional for the same reason as ThemeProviderClientProps.initialMode — the transported configuration already carries it. A variant name is accepted and normalised to its family; its mode applies only when `initialMode` is absent. | | `initialMode` (optional) | `ThemeMode` | Mode used when nothing is persisted. | | `plugins` (optional) | `ThemePlugin<T>[]` | Theme plugins to install at runtime creation. | | `scheduled` (optional) | `false \| ScheduledThemeOptions<T>` | Sunrise/sunset scheduling. Enables `useThemeSchedule()`; without it that hook returns `null`. `autoDetectLocation` resolves coordinates from the browser, and `timeZone` overrides the detected one. | | `themeOverride` (optional) | `ThemeOverride<ThemeIdentifier<T>>` | An explicit theme override applied over any persisted selection. Applied once per value and never written to persistence. Pass the same value to the integration's `provider.astro` / `createBlockingScript` for a flash-free override — the island alone can only correct it after mount. | | `themes` (optional) | `readonly T[]` | The theme registry the client runtime resolves against. | | `transition` (optional) | `boolean \| ThemeTransitionOptions` | Animate theme changes. Omit it to use the `transition` declared in `theme.config.ts` (the transported configuration); `true` uses the defaults, `{ enabled, duration, easing }` tunes it, and `false` disables it for this island. The transition itself is applied by the DOM/CSS bindings, so it also needs `dom`/`cssVariables` to be left at their defaults (they are). | ---

title: ThemeReadoutKind
text: ThemeReadoutKind Which bootstrap-owned value a ThemeReadout displays. **See also:** `ThemeReadout` `"theme" | "label" | "mode" | "family"` These are exactly the text kinds `data-tv-readout` defines — the same set the pre-paint bootstrap and the controller resolve (see `readoutValue` in `dom.ts`), plus the raw `var:<custom-property>` form, which this component does not wrap. `"label"` was missing for one release while the contract, the bootstrap and the controller all supported it. A React app that wanted the human label therefore had to hand-write `data-tv-readout="label"` *and* `suppressHydrationWarning` — precisely the pair this component exists so that nobody has to know — and the obvious workaround, rendering `useTheme().theme` as text, is the one that fluctuates on load. A component that wraps "the contract" has to cover it whole, or callers route around it and rediscover the bug it was written for. ---

title: Related docs
text: Related docs - [Families & Modes](/core-concepts) — A selection is a family (which palette) plus a mode (light/dark/system); every framework exposes the same read/write surface for it. - [Theme Discovery & Overrides](/advanced-features) — A provider exposes exactly the themes it was given — grouped by family, with variants and resolved tokens — and accepts an explicit one-shot themeOverride that outranks a saved selection. - [Runtime](/architecture) — One runtime per app owns the store, selection, registry, history, lifecycle and adapters; every framework binding is a thin view over it. - [ThemeScope](/scoped-theme) — Apply a different family/mode (or a local theme definition) to a subtree, with scoped CSS variables and pre-paint support. - [Theme generation](/theme-studio) — Generate a complete, accessible light/dark theme pair from a single seed color, ready to drop into the runtime. - [Astro](/framework-guides/astro) — the framework integration

title: @themvora/astro/runtime
text: @themvora/astro/runtime Browser entry for the Themvora Astro integration (`@themvora/astro/runtime`). This is the **framework-neutral client API**, and it is the entry a `<script>` in a `.astro` file should import. It ships the global runtime controller — `getThemeController()` / `createThemeController()` — plus the low-level shared-runtime accessors, and it imports no client framework. > Generated from `packages/astro/src` by `apps/docs/scripts/generate-api-reference.mjs`. title: Functions

title: createThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeController<T>
text: createThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeController<T> Creates a controller over a **new** runtime and installs it as the app-wide runtime. **See also:** `getThemeController`, `ThemeController` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `ThemeControllerOptions<T>` | Overrides for the transported application configuration (see ThemeControllerOptions). | **Returns** `ThemeController<T>` — A new controller owning a new runtime. Prefer getThemeController in application code: this function replaces any runtime already installed, so two calls give two runtimes racing to write `<html>`. ```ts import { createThemeController } from "@themvora/astro"; const theme = createThemeController({ themes: myTestThemes }); theme.setMode("dark"); ``` ---

title: getGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T> | null
text: getGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T> | null Returns the app-wide global runtime, or `null` when none has been installed yet (e.g. before `ThemeProviderClient` mounts). **See also:** `setGlobalRuntime` **Returns** `ThemeRuntime<T> | null` — The installed runtime, or `null`. ---

title: getThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeController<T>
text: getThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeController<T> The app-wide ThemeController, created on first call. **See also:** `ThemeController`, `createThemeController`, `getGlobalRuntime` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `ThemeControllerOptions<T>` | Overrides, honoured only on the call that creates the controller (see ThemeControllerOptions). | **Returns** `ThemeController<T>` — The shared controller. **One runtime per document.** The provider, `<ThemeToggle />`, a hand-written `<script>` and a React island all end up here, and the first caller wins: every later call returns the same controller rather than building a second runtime that would fight the first over `<html>`. That is what lets a page go from `<Provider>` to `<ThemeToggle />` with no per-page `initialMode` / `initialFamily` and no React island. If a runtime is already installed — a React island created one — this adopts it instead of replacing it, so the two surfaces share one runtime and one state. Browser-only. It reads the transported configuration, the persisted selection and `prefers-color-scheme`, none of which exist on a server — call it from a `<script>`, never from Astro frontmatter. ```ts <button id="theme-toggle">Toggle theme</button> <script> import { getThemeController } from "@themvora/astro"; const theme = getThemeController(); document .querySelector("#theme-toggle") ?.addEventListener("click", () => theme.toggleTheme()); </script> ``` ---

title: installThemeBindings(): void
text: installThemeBindings(): void Installs the delegated DOM bindings for the Themvora contracts. **See also:** `THEME_SELECTION_ATTRIBUTE`, `THEME_TOGGLE_ATTRIBUTE` **Returns** `void` Two contracts, one listener each, registered once per document: | Contract | Event | Effect | | -------- | ----- | ------ | | `[data-tv-toggle]` | `click` | `toggleTheme()` | | `[data-tv-select]` | `change` | `setFamily()` / `setMode()` from `value` | The `change` listener is the input half of `[data-tv-select]`; the output half — writing the live selection back into the element — lives in `syncSelectionControls`, and `[data-tv-pressed]` (a segmented control's `aria-pressed`) is mirrored by `syncPressedControls` on the same change. A page that renders `<ThemeToggle />` and a segmented control therefore needs no script of its own, and the two controls cannot disagree. **Delegated, not per-element.** This is the fix for the interaction bug, not a style preference. Astro bundles a component's `<script>` once per page, so a component that rendered the select cannot know how many instances the page has — `getElementById` binds one of them. And Astro's module scripts never re-execute across `<ClientRouter />` navigations, so a page you navigate back to keeps the listeners its *first* visit registered and no others. A `document`-level listener has neither problem: it is registered once and matches whatever the DOM contains at the moment the event fires. **Lazy.** Nothing here creates a runtime. The controller is resolved on the first interaction, so a page that renders a control but is never used ships the script and pays nothing else — the runtime, its persistence adapter and its cross-tab channel are still created on demand. Safe to call more than once, and safe to call on the server (a no-op). ```ts <select data-tv-select="family"> <option value="mint">mint</option> <option value="cocoa">cocoa</option> </select> <script> import { installThemeBindings } from "@themvora/astro/runtime"; installThemeBindings(); </script> ``` ---

title: requireGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T>
text: requireGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T> Returns the app-wide global runtime, throwing when none has been installed. **See also:** `getGlobalRuntime`, `setGlobalRuntime` **Returns** `ThemeRuntime<T>` — The installed runtime. ---

title: setGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(runtime): void
text: setGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(runtime): void Installs the given runtime as the app-wide global runtime and, in the browser, publishes it where the rest of Themvora looks for it. **See also:** `getGlobalRuntime` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `runtime` | `ThemeRuntime<T>` | The theme runtime to install globally. | **Returns** `void` Three publications, all of them the same runtime: 1. the module-level `globalRuntime` — what this package's hooks read; 2. `window.__themvoraRuntime` — the documented escape hatch; 3. `document.documentElement.__themvoraRuntime` plus a `theme-ready` event — which is how `@themvora/web`'s custom elements (`<themvora-scrollbar>`, `<themvora-inspector>`, `<themvora-toggle>`, …) find a runtime. They resolve it by walking **DOM ancestors** for that property, and they only fall back to waiting for `theme-ready`, which until now was dispatched solely by `<themvora-provider>`. Without these two lines an Astro app that installs its runtime from a React island had no way to use the framework-neutral elements at all — the runtime existed, but nothing in the element tree could see it. ---

title: ThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition>
text: ThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition> A framework-neutral controller over the app-wide Themvora runtime. **See also:** `getThemeController`, `createThemeController` | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | readonly `runtime` | `ThemeRuntime<T>` | The underlying runtime, for anything the controller does not wrap. | | `destroy` | `void` | — | | `getFamily` | `string` | — | | `getMode` | `ThemeMode` | — | | `getResolvedMode` | `"light" \| "dark"` | — | | `getTheme` | `T` | — | | `setFamily` | `void` | — | | `setMode` | `void` | — | | `subscribe` | `__type(): void` | — | | `toggleTheme` | `void` | — | This is **not** a React hook, and not a hook of any kind: it is a plain object with getters and setters, valid in any browser context — an Astro `<script>`, a custom element, an event handler, a devtools console. Nothing here re-renders; ThemeController.subscribe is how a caller observes change. It exists so Astro does not have to borrow React's shape. A `.astro` file has no reactive component runtime, so `useTheme()` — a React hook, valid only inside a React island — is the wrong abstraction there. The Astro-idiomatic spelling is: ```ts const theme = getThemeController(); theme.toggleTheme(); ``` The React hook keeps its own shape, for React islands: ```tsx const { theme, mode, toggleTheme } = useTheme(); ``` ---

title: THEMEPRESSEDVALUEATTRIBUTE
text: THEMEPRESSEDVALUEATTRIBUTE The option a THEME_PRESSED_ATTRIBUTE element represents, compared against the live mode selection (`"light"` / `"dark"` / `"system"`) or the live family selection. `"data-tv-value"` ---

title: THEMEREADOUTATTRIBUTE
text: THEMEREADOUTATTRIBUTE Opts an element into the **bootstrap readout** contract: its text is owned by Themvora. **See also:** `THEME_TOGGLE_ATTRIBUTE` `"data-tv-readout"` ---

title: THEMESELECTIONATTRIBUTE
text: THEMESELECTIONATTRIBUTE Opts a `<select>` into the **selection-control** contract: `data-tv-select="family"` or `data-tv-select="mode"`. **See also:** `THEME_TOGGLE_ATTRIBUTE`, `THEME_READOUT_ATTRIBUTE` `"data-tv-select"` ---

title: THEMETOGGLEATTRIBUTE
text: THEMETOGGLEATTRIBUTE Marks an element as a Themvora theme toggle. **See also:** `THEME_READOUT_ATTRIBUTE` `"data-tv-toggle"` ---

title: @themvora/astro
text: @themvora/astro Themvora Astro integration. This entry point is **framework-neutral**: it ships the Astro integration (`themvora`), the zero-flash server helpers (`createBlockingScript`, `buildThemeCssMap`, `darkModeCSSTemplate`, `systemModeCSSTemplate`, `computeFingerprint`, `getInitialThemeState`), the Astro-specific `ThemePersistence`, the browser-side `getThemeController()` / `createThemeController()` API, the shared-runtime accessors, and the framework-neutral `ThemvoraScrollbar` / `ThemvoraInspector` re-exports from `@themvora/web`. None of it imports React. The React island (`ThemeProviderClient`), the React hooks, and the React `ThemeScope` live behind the opt-in `@themvora/astro/client` subpath, which is the only entry that depends on React. > Generated from `packages/astro/src` by `apps/docs/scripts/generate-api-reference.mjs`. Do not edit by hand — run `pnpm --filter @themvora/docs api:generate`.

title: buildThemeCssMap<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(themes, options?): Record<string, Record<string, string>>
text: buildThemeCssMap<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(themes, options?): Record<string, Record<string, string>> Build a lookup map of theme keys to flat CSS variables. Each theme is registered twice: - under its own `name` (e.g. `"sunrise-light"`) - under a `family:mode` key (e.g. `"sunrise:light"`) so that a persisted family + effective mode can be resolved without knowing theme names. **See also:** `createThemeBootstrapScript` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `themes` | `readonly T[]` | — | | `options` | `BuildThemeCssMapOptions` (optional) | — | **Returns** `Record<string, Record<string, string>>` ---

title: computeFingerprint(themes, defaultTheme?): string
text: computeFingerprint(themes, defaultTheme?): string Fingerprints a theme registry so a persisted selection from an older build — different themes, or a different `defaultTheme` — is ignored rather than applied against themes it was never valid for. **See also:** `ThemeBootstrapCookieSource`, `buildBootstrapPlan` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `themes` | `readonly ThemeDefinition<string>[]` | The theme registry to fingerprint. | | `defaultTheme` | `string` (optional) | The fallback theme name. Included in the fingerprint, so changing it invalidates previously persisted selections. | **Returns** `string` — A stable fingerprint string, or `""` when `themes` is empty. The result is written to the `theme-fingerprint` cookie and compared on the next request, so it is part of the **stable cookie contract** documented in `VERSIONING.md` — changing the format invalidates every visitor's persisted selection on their next visit. It lives here, in core, because four SSR integrations (Next, Nuxt, Astro, Remix) previously each carried a byte-identical private copy. Any edit to one of them would have silently broken cross-framework persistence with nothing to catch it. ---

title: createAstroThemePersistence(themes?, defaultTheme?): ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter | null
text: createAstroThemePersistence(themes?, defaultTheme?): ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter | null Creates the client-side persistence adapter for Astro. Mirrors the theme selection to `localStorage` (cross-tab sync, offline) AND to the theme cookies (`theme-family` / `theme-mode` / `theme-fingerprint`) so the server resolves the exact same state on the next request. Reads from both: `localStorage` first, then the cookies. Reading the cookies as well is what keeps the client runtime in agreement with the pre-paint bootstrap script, which only ever sees cookies — a read path that ignored them made the runtime overwrite an already-correct first paint. **See also:** `ThemeProviderClient` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `themes` | `readonly ThemeDefinition<string>[]` (optional) | The theme registry used to compute the config fingerprint. | | `defaultTheme` | `string` (optional) | Fallback theme name used in the fingerprint. | **Returns** `ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter | null` — A persistence adapter, or `null` when running outside the browser. Returns `null` during SSR (no `window`). The cookie contract matches the other SSR integrations (`@themvora/next`, `@themvora/nuxt`, `@themvora/remix`). **Blocked storage degrades, it does not throw.** `window.localStorage` can throw on access and `setItem` throws when the quota is full; both are treated as "this browser cannot remember the selection". The cookie mirror is written either way, so the server still resolves the same theme on the next request. ---

title: createBlockingScript(fingerprint, themeCssMap, options): string
text: createBlockingScript(fingerprint, themeCssMap, options): string Builds the blocking, inline bootstrap script that applies the persisted theme before first paint (zero-flash). The script reads the theme cookies, rejects them when the config fingerprint is stale, resolves the effective mode (`"system"` against `prefers-color-scheme`), and writes the CSS variables plus the full DOM contract the client runtime applies — `data-theme`, `data-theme-family`, `data-theme-mode`, the `dark` class and `color-scheme` — onto `document.documentElement`. Hydration therefore confirms the server-rendered theme instead of correcting it. It is deliberately tiny and synchronous: no runtime, no listeners, no storage access beyond cookies, and no framework dependency. **See also:** `buildThemeCssMap`, `buildThemeBootstrapPayload`, `darkModeCSSTemplate` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `fingerprint` | `string` | The config fingerprint used to reject stale cookies. | | `themeCssMap` | `Record<string, Record<string, string>>` | A map of theme keys to CSS variable records (see buildThemeCssMap). | | `options` | `BlockingScriptOptions` | The fallback selection and theme lookup (see BlockingScriptOptions). Omit it only when the caller resolves the fallback itself. | **Returns** `string` — The inline script string to emit in the document `<head>`. Pass `options` so a visitor with no valid cookies is resolved against the same fallback the runtime uses. Without it the script still corrects the mode marker and uses the first matching `family:mode` entry it finds, but it cannot guarantee it agrees with the client runtime. ---

title: createThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeController<T>
text: createThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeController<T> Creates a controller over a **new** runtime and installs it as the app-wide runtime. **See also:** `getThemeController`, `ThemeController` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `ThemeControllerOptions<T>` | Overrides for the transported application configuration (see ThemeControllerOptions). | **Returns** `ThemeController<T>` — A new controller owning a new runtime. Prefer getThemeController in application code: this function replaces any runtime already installed, so two calls give two runtimes racing to write `<html>`. ```ts import { createThemeController } from "@themvora/astro"; const theme = createThemeController({ themes: myTestThemes }); theme.setMode("dark"); ``` ---

title: darkModeCSSTemplate(variables): string
text: darkModeCSSTemplate(variables): string Generate a `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` CSS block carrying the given variables. **See also:** `systemModeCSSTemplate` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `variables` | `Record<string, string>` | The CSS variables to emit under the dark media query. | **Returns** `string` — A `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` block targeting `:root`, escaped so it cannot terminate a `<style>` element (`</` becomes `</`, which CSS parses identically). This is a **pre-script** fallback only, and it cannot beat an inline `style` on the same element: inline declarations outrank every stylesheet rule regardless of specificity. So it is only safe when nothing inlines the light variables — do not pair it with a server render that writes them onto `<html>`, or an OS-dark visitor keeps the light ones and this block is inert. When the resolved mode is `"system"`, use systemModeCSSTemplate instead: it emits both schemes and expects no inline variables. ---

title: getGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T> | null
text: getGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T> | null Returns the app-wide global runtime, or `null` when none has been installed yet (e.g. before `ThemeProviderClient` mounts). **See also:** `setGlobalRuntime` **Returns** `ThemeRuntime<T> | null` — The installed runtime, or `null`. ---

title: getInitialThemeState<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(request, options): Promise<InitialThemeResolution<T>>
text: getInitialThemeState<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(request, options): Promise<InitialThemeResolution<T>> Resolves the initial theme state server-side from the incoming request's theme cookies, so the server-rendered HTML is already themed and a client island can hydrate against the exact same state (zero-flash). Framework-neutral: only reads the standard `theme-mode` / `theme-family` cookies, the optional `Sec-CH-Prefers-Color-Scheme` client hint, and the theme registry, so it works from any Astro server context (`Astro.request`) without pulling in a client framework runtime. **See also:** `- `provider.astro` - `ThemeProviderClient`` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `request` | `Request` | The incoming request (e.g. `Astro.request`). | | `options` | `GetInitialThemeStateOptions<T>` | The theme registry, fallback selection, and optional system-preference read (see GetInitialThemeStateOptions). | **Returns** `Promise<InitialThemeResolution<T>>` — The resolved initial theme state. Pair this with `provider.astro` (which paints the themed `<html>` on the server) and pass the result to the opt-in React island (`@themvora/astro/client`) as its `initial` prop so hydration matches. ```ts --- import { getInitialThemeState } from "@themvora/astro"; import { getBuiltInThemes } from "@themvora/core"; const initial = await getInitialThemeState(Astro.request, { themes: getBuiltInThemes(), defaultTheme: "mint-light", mode: "system", systemPreference: true, }); --- ``` ---

title: getThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeController<T>
text: getThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeController<T> The app-wide ThemeController, created on first call. **See also:** `ThemeController`, `createThemeController`, `getGlobalRuntime` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `ThemeControllerOptions<T>` | Overrides, honoured only on the call that creates the controller (see ThemeControllerOptions). | **Returns** `ThemeController<T>` — The shared controller. **One runtime per document.** The provider, `<ThemeToggle />`, a hand-written `<script>` and a React island all end up here, and the first caller wins: every later call returns the same controller rather than building a second runtime that would fight the first over `<html>`. That is what lets a page go from `<Provider>` to `<ThemeToggle />` with no per-page `initialMode` / `initialFamily` and no React island. If a runtime is already installed — a React island created one — this adopts it instead of replacing it, so the two surfaces share one runtime and one state. Browser-only. It reads the transported configuration, the persisted selection and `prefers-color-scheme`, none of which exist on a server — call it from a `<script>`, never from Astro frontmatter. ```ts <button id="theme-toggle">Toggle theme</button> <script> import { getThemeController } from "@themvora/astro"; const theme = getThemeController(); document .querySelector("#theme-toggle") ?.addEventListener("click", () => theme.toggleTheme()); </script> ``` ---

title: injectPrePaintScrollbarCSS(): void
text: injectPrePaintScrollbarCSS(): void Injects the pre-paint scrollbar-hiding CSS and class into the document. Framework-free (vanilla JS). Adds a `<style>` carrying the pre-paint scrollbar CSS and the `tv-scrollbar` class to the document root so the native scrollbar is hidden before first paint. Idempotent and a no-op on the server. This is a manual bootstrap helper for a page that wants the native bar hidden before its own script runs. It is *not* how ThemvoraScrollbar hides the bar — that happens through `createOverlayScrollbar`, which claims the hiding and gives it back on `destroy()`. Calling this directly therefore hides the bar without registering a claim, so pair it with `restoreNativeScrollbar()` if you later want the native bar back. **See also:** `ThemvoraScrollbar` **Returns** `void` ---

title: installThemeBindings(): void
text: installThemeBindings(): void Installs the delegated DOM bindings for the Themvora contracts. **See also:** `THEME_SELECTION_ATTRIBUTE`, `THEME_TOGGLE_ATTRIBUTE` **Returns** `void` Two contracts, one listener each, registered once per document: | Contract | Event | Effect | | -------- | ----- | ------ | | `[data-tv-toggle]` | `click` | `toggleTheme()` | | `[data-tv-select]` | `change` | `setFamily()` / `setMode()` from `value` | The `change` listener is the input half of `[data-tv-select]`; the output half — writing the live selection back into the element — lives in `syncSelectionControls`, and `[data-tv-pressed]` (a segmented control's `aria-pressed`) is mirrored by `syncPressedControls` on the same change. A page that renders `<ThemeToggle />` and a segmented control therefore needs no script of its own, and the two controls cannot disagree. **Delegated, not per-element.** This is the fix for the interaction bug, not a style preference. Astro bundles a component's `<script>` once per page, so a component that rendered the select cannot know how many instances the page has — `getElementById` binds one of them. And Astro's module scripts never re-execute across `<ClientRouter />` navigations, so a page you navigate back to keeps the listeners its *first* visit registered and no others. A `document`-level listener has neither problem: it is registered once and matches whatever the DOM contains at the moment the event fires. **Lazy.** Nothing here creates a runtime. The controller is resolved on the first interaction, so a page that renders a control but is never used ships the script and pays nothing else — the runtime, its persistence adapter and its cross-tab channel are still created on demand. Safe to call more than once, and safe to call on the server (a no-op). ```ts <select data-tv-select="family"> <option value="mint">mint</option> <option value="cocoa">cocoa</option> </select> <script> import { installThemeBindings } from "@themvora/astro/runtime"; installThemeBindings(); </script> ``` ---

title: requireGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T>
text: requireGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T> Returns the app-wide global runtime, throwing when none has been installed. **See also:** `getGlobalRuntime`, `setGlobalRuntime` **Returns** `ThemeRuntime<T>` — The installed runtime. ---

title: setGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(runtime): void
text: setGlobalRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(runtime): void Installs the given runtime as the app-wide global runtime and, in the browser, publishes it where the rest of Themvora looks for it. **See also:** `getGlobalRuntime` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `runtime` | `ThemeRuntime<T>` | The theme runtime to install globally. | **Returns** `void` Three publications, all of them the same runtime: 1. the module-level `globalRuntime` — what this package's hooks read; 2. `window.__themvoraRuntime` — the documented escape hatch; 3. `document.documentElement.__themvoraRuntime` plus a `theme-ready` event — which is how `@themvora/web`'s custom elements (`<themvora-scrollbar>`, `<themvora-inspector>`, `<themvora-toggle>`, …) find a runtime. They resolve it by walking **DOM ancestors** for that property, and they only fall back to waiting for `theme-ready`, which until now was dispatched solely by `<themvora-provider>`. Without these two lines an Astro app that installs its runtime from a React island had no way to use the framework-neutral elements at all — the runtime existed, but nothing in the element tree could see it. ---

title: systemModeCSSTemplate(light, dark): string
text: systemModeCSSTemplate(light, dark): string Generate the stylesheet that resolves a `"system"` selection with CSS alone — no script and no inline style. **See also:** `darkModeCSSTemplate` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `light` | `Record<string, string>` | The light theme's CSS variables. | | `dark` | `Record<string, string>` | The dark theme's CSS variables. | **Returns** `string` — Two media blocks, one per scheme, both targeting `:root`, escaped for `<style>`-element content exactly as darkModeCSSTemplate is. Use this **instead of** inlining the resolved variables whenever the mode is `"system"`. The two cannot be combined: an inline `style` on `<html>` outranks any stylesheet rule, so a page that inlines the light variables and also emits a dark media block paints light whatever the OS prefers. Measured on a production build with page scripts blocked and the OS set to dark, that combination painted `rgb(248, 250, 252)` (light); emitting both media blocks and no inline variables painted `rgb(2, 6, 23)`. `prefers-color-scheme: light` also matches when the visitor has expressed no preference — `light` is the specified default — so the light block doubles as the no-preference branch. ---

title: themvora(options): AstroIntegration
text: themvora(options): AstroIntegration Themvora Astro integration. Registers the pre-paint theme bootstrap with Astro so every page is themed before first paint (zero-flash), without requiring a client-side framework runtime. **See also:** `ThemvoraIntegrationOptions` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `ThemvoraIntegrationOptions` | The integration options (see ThemvoraIntegrationOptions). | **Returns** `AstroIntegration` — An Astro integration to register in `astro.config.ts`. **Config discovery.** The integration finds the application's `theme.config.ts` in Astro's root, trying `theme.config.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.mjs`, `.js` and `.cjs` in that order, and requires a default export — the object defineThemvoraConfig returns. Passing `config` skips discovery and accepts either the object or a path to it. **Two consumers, one declaration.** The discovered configuration is projected twice: buildBootstrap derives the blocking script from it, and the same projection is injected as `window.__THEMVORA_CONFIG__` from `<head>`. The island reads that global instead of taking theme props, so the markup the server renders and the markup the browser hydrates come from the same registry — a mismatch there is visible as the panel repainting as the real families replace the presets. `getInitialThemeState` publishes the same global on the server, because no integration runs there. When the app has no discoverable config, the built-in neutral themes are used and nothing fails. The integration owns the framework/build boundary only. Server-rendering the themed `<html>` element is handled by `@themvora/astro/provider.astro`, and interactive controls are opt-in islands — React users import the island from `@themvora/astro/client`, which is the only entry that depends on React. The bootstrap is injected at the **`head-inline`** stage, and that choice is load-bearing rather than incidental. `before-hydration` looks equivalent — both run before the island hydrates — but it ships the script as a *module* (resolved and bundled by Vite), so it executes after the browser has already painted. Measured on a prerendered page, where the server cannot know the visitor's selection and always emits the default theme: | condition | `head-inline` | `before-hydration` | |---|---|---| | OS dark, no cookie | dark at 84 ms, never corrected | light painted at 74 ms, corrected at 98 ms | | dark cookie, cold cache + slow network | dark at 518 ms, never corrected | light painted at 513 ms, corrected at 1052 ms | So `before-hydration` does not merely weaken the guarantee — it produces a visible flash of the *wrong* theme, up to ~540 ms of it. Paint ordering requires the inline head script; pre-hydration is not sufficient. For a `"system"` selection the script is not the first line of defence — CSS is. The server cannot know the visitor's preference, so it must not commit to one: an inline `style` on `<html>` outranks every stylesheet rule, which means inlining a guess would silently defeat the `prefers-color-scheme` block meant to correct it. Measured on the built example with page scripts blocked and the OS set to dark, the inline-variables-plus-dark-block combination painted the *light* canvas (`rgb(248, 250, 252)`); emitting both schemes as media blocks and no inline variables paints `rgb(2, 6, 23)`. See systemModeCSSTemplate. Client-side navigation (`<ClientRouter />`) is handled separately by createNavigationScript — the injected bootstrap is byte-identical on every page, so Astro de-duplicates it and it does not re-run, and the live theme state would otherwise be replaced by the destination page's build-time attributes. ```ts // Register the integration. No theme data. import { defineConfig } from "astro/config"; import themvora from "@themvora/astro"; export default defineConfig({ integrations: [themvora()], }); ``` ---

title: class ThemvoraScrollbar
text: class ThemvoraScrollbar **Extends** `ThemvoraRuntimeConsumer` Phase 2 — ThemvoraScrollbar (Web Component): overlay only. Creates the custom scrollbar overlay. Lifecycle: connectedCallback → resolve the runtime ↓ onRuntime → hide native bar (Phase 1) → create overlay → attach ↓ (Phase 2) later → add tv-scrollbar-ready ↓ (Phase 3) onDetach / destroy → remove overlay → restore native bar Phase 1 happens synchronously inside the overlay's construction. For static HTML served via the Vite plugin (scrollbar: true), the pre-paint script in <head> runs before first paint; for an SSR'd provider the class and CSS are in the markup. This component's own hiding is the fallback for dynamically-inserted elements (which may have already painted). The teardown is a real teardown. The hiding is claimed, not switched on, so removing the element gives the native scrollbar back instead of leaving the page with no scrollbar at all — and an attribute change swaps the overlay without ever passing through the "hidden, but nothing drawn" state. **See also:** `ThemvoraProvider` | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `constructor` | `ThemvoraScrollbar` | — | | `accessKey` | `string` | The **`HTMLElement.accessKey`** property sets the keystroke which a user can press to jump to a given element. Booleans are presence-based: present (any value except `false` or `0`) enables, absent or `false` disables. Numbers are unitless pixels. - Behaviour — `auto-hide`, `auto-hide-delay`, `hover-expand`, `draggable`, `click-to-jump`, `smooth`, `overscroll`, `touch`. - Arrows — `arrows`, `arrow-icon`, `arrow-up-icon`, `arrow-down-icon`, `arrow-left-icon`, `arrow-right-icon` (SVG markup or URL). - Geometry — `thickness`, `hover-thickness`, `radius`, `min-thumb-size`, `icon-size`, `offset` (uniform inset), `offset-top`, `offset-right`, `offset-bottom`, `offset-left` (per-side insets win over `offset`). - Motion and paint — `track-opacity`, `thumb-opacity`, `duration`, `animation-duration`, `thumb-color`, `track-color`, `active-thumb-color`, `thumb-hover-color`. Colors default to the active theme's tokens. - Placement — `z-index`, `dir` (`ltr` / `rtl` / `auto`), `axes` (comma-separated `vertical` / `horizontal`), `include` / `exclude` (comma-separated CSS selectors for the containers to track). **Properties.** None of its own beyond the standard `HTMLElement` surface. **Events.** Dispatches nothing of its own; it adds `tv-scrollbar-ready` to the element once the overlay is measured and attached. **Slots.** None — the element renders nothing into the document flow; the overlay it creates lives outside it. ---

title: ThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition>
text: ThemeController<T extends ThemeDefinition> A framework-neutral controller over the app-wide Themvora runtime. **See also:** `getThemeController`, `createThemeController` | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | readonly `runtime` | `ThemeRuntime<T>` | The underlying runtime, for anything the controller does not wrap. | | `destroy` | `void` | — | | `getFamily` | `string` | — | | `getMode` | `ThemeMode` | — | | `getResolvedMode` | `"light" \| "dark"` | — | | `getTheme` | `T` | — | | `setFamily` | `void` | — | | `setMode` | `void` | — | | `subscribe` | `__type(): void` | — | | `toggleTheme` | `void` | — | This is **not** a React hook, and not a hook of any kind: it is a plain object with getters and setters, valid in any browser context — an Astro `<script>`, a custom element, an event handler, a devtools console. Nothing here re-renders; ThemeController.subscribe is how a caller observes change. It exists so Astro does not have to borrow React's shape. A `.astro` file has no reactive component runtime, so `useTheme()` — a React hook, valid only inside a React island — is the wrong abstraction there. The Astro-idiomatic spelling is: ```ts const theme = getThemeController(); theme.toggleTheme(); ``` The React hook keeps its own shape, for React islands: ```tsx const { theme, mode, toggleTheme } = useTheme(); ``` ---

text: ThemeControllerOptions<T extends ThemeDefinition> Options for createThemeController / getThemeController. **See also:** `getThemeController` `Partial<Omit<ThemeRuntimeOptions<T>, "persistence" | "readPersistenceOnInit">> & { readouts?: boolean }` Every field is optional, and every field is an *override*. The application configuration is already in the browser — `themvora()` transports `theme.config.ts` as `window.__THEMVORA_CONFIG__` from `<head>` — so the runtime is built from that. Passing `themes` / `defaultTheme` / `initialMode` / `initialFamily` here is for a test, a storybook, or an island that deliberately wants a different registry. ---

title: createBootstrapAdapter<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeAdapter<T>
text: createBootstrapAdapter<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeAdapter<T> Creates a Bootstrap adapter. The adapter is a DOM-only, framework-free adapter: it depends only on `@themvora/core` and the DOM. On install it injects the Bootstrap compatibility stylesheet (when enabled) and a `<style>` element of CSS variables derived from the active theme, then subscribes to the runtime store and rewrites the variables whenever the theme selection changes. It does not render any component or require a React tree. On uninstall it removes the injected styles and unsubscribes from the store. **See also:** `useBootstrapTheme` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `CreateBootstrapAdapterOptions` | Adapter options. Defaults to `{}`. | **Returns** `ThemeAdapter<T>` — A `ThemeAdapter` for Bootstrap. ```ts import { createBootstrapAdapter } from "@themvora/bootstrap"; runtime.adapters.use(createBootstrapAdapter()); ``` ---

title: createBootstrapAdapter<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeAdapter<T>
text: createBootstrapAdapter<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeAdapter<T> Creates a Bootstrap adapter. The adapter is a DOM-only, framework-free adapter: it depends only on `@themvora/core` and the DOM. On install it injects the Bootstrap compatibility stylesheet (when enabled) and a `<style>` element of CSS variables derived from the active theme, then subscribes to the runtime store and rewrites the variables whenever the theme selection changes. title: @themvora/cli
text: @themvora/cli Themvora CLI — programmatic entry points. Exposes the same commands as the `themvora` binary (`generate`, `list`, `validate`, `inspect`, `diff`, `explain`, `audit`, `doctor`, `init`, `migrate`, `export`), the `run` dispatcher, and `parseArgs`, `UsageError`, `CommandExit` and `ExitCodes` for embedding or scripting. Everything else in this package — the command contract, the canonical registry accessors, the framework registry, the `init` engine and the output helpers — is internal. They are the implementation of the CLI, not an API for consumers, and exporting them would freeze an internal shape into the published surface. > Generated from `packages/cli/src` by `apps/docs/scripts/generate-api-reference.mjs`. title: cmdAudit(args): Promise<void>
text: cmdAudit(args): Promise<void> Implements the `audit` command. Audits a theme, or every shipped preset and brand, with the **canonical** scorecard — `scoreTheme()`. That is the same quality model the repository's `audit-presets.mjs` gate and the preset documentation use, so the CLI and the release gate cannot disagree about whether a preset is healthy. `audit` is deliberately stricter than `validate`: it gates on the full scorecard rather than on the frozen structural contract alone. Reads `presets` or `<file>`, plus `--json`, `--quiet` and `--strict`. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `args` | `ParsedArgs` | The parsed command-line arguments. | **Returns** `Promise<void>` ---

text: cmdCompletion(args): Promise<void> Run `themvora completion`. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `args` | `ParsedArgs` | The parsed arguments. | **Returns** `Promise<void>` The script goes to **stdout** with nothing else, so the documented install is a redirect: ```bash themvora completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/themvora ``` A status line would break that, so there is none. ---

title: cmdDiff(args): Promise<void>
text: cmdDiff(args): Promise<void> Implements the `diff` command. Compares two theme sources and reports the semantic differences. Every comparison decision comes from `@themvora/core`; this command resolves sources, renders the report, and maps failures to exit codes. Sources are the two positionals, or `--preset` / `--brand` / `--seed` for a side that has none. Explicit flags are assigned to the sides without a positional, in order, so `diff mint --brand apple` compares preset `mint` against brand `apple`. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `args` | `ParsedArgs` | The parsed command-line arguments. | **Returns** `Promise<void>` ---

title: cmdDoctor(args): Promise<void>
text: cmdDoctor(args): Promise<void> Implements the `doctor` command. Reports the health of a Themvora project: its framework, package manager, installed Themvora packages, theme configuration, and theme files. Only checks the CLI can make reliably are performed, and every finding that has a concrete correction carries it. Warnings and errors are distinct: a project with warnings is still healthy (exit `0`); an actionable failure is exit `3`. Reads an optional `<dir>` (default: the current directory), plus `--json` and `--quiet`. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `args` | `ParsedArgs` | The parsed command-line arguments. | **Returns** `Promise<void>` ---

title: cmdExplain(args): Promise<void>
text: cmdExplain(args): Promise<void> Implements the `explain` command. Explains how a theme came to be: its source, its recipe, the identity or brand anchors behind it, the contrast contract it was solved against, the semantic mapping of every role, and a validation summary. Every value comes from an existing public API — the canonical catalog, the generation metadata on the theme, the canonical scorecard. This command derives nothing, and `@themvora/core` gained no API for it. Reads `<file>` or `--preset`/`--brand`/`--seed`, plus `--json` and `--quiet`. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `args` | `ParsedArgs` | The parsed command-line arguments. | **Returns** `Promise<void>` ---

title: cmdExport(args): Promise<void>
text: cmdExport(args): Promise<void> Implements the `export` command: exports a theme file as CSS variables or JSON. Reads `--file`/`-f` (or the first positional), `--format`/`-F` (`css` or `json`), and `--output`/`-o`. Prints the exported CSS or JSON to stdout, or writes it to the output file when provided. **See also:** `parseArgs` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `args` | `ParsedArgs` | The parsed command-line arguments. | **Returns** `Promise<void>` The CSS document is formatted by core's `themeToCssDocument()`, not here. The extension's Copy CSS Variables command calls the same function, so the CSS a user copies in the editor is byte-identical to the CSS this command writes. What stays in the CLI is the file handling: `--output` and the status line. ---

title: cmdGenerate(args): Promise<void>
text: cmdGenerate(args): Promise<void> Implements the `generate` command. Generates a theme (or a light/dark pair) from one of three mutually exclusive sources — a seed color, a canonical preset, or a brand-inspired recipe — and prints it as JSON or writes it to a file. Reads `--seed`/`-s`, `--preset`, `--brand`, `--family`/`-f`, `--mode`/`-m`, `--style`, `--contrast`, `--code`/`--with-code`, `--output`/`-o` and `--dry-run`. A bare positional argument is treated as a seed color, which is the original spelling. **See also:** `parseArgs` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `args` | `ParsedArgs` | The parsed command-line arguments. | **Returns** `Promise<void>` ---

title: cmdInspect(args): Promise<void>
text: cmdInspect(args): Promise<void> Implements the `inspect` command. Prints a human-readable summary of a theme's provenance, semantic token groups, resolved colors and accessibility. A theme that carries no generation provenance is identified as such, and `migrate` is suggested when a registered migration step actually applies to it. Reads `--file`/`-f` (or the first positional) plus the `--tokens`, `--colors`, `--generation` and `--accessibility` selectors. title: generateTheme(options): GeneratedThemePair
text: generateTheme(options): GeneratedThemePair Generate a cohesive light/dark theme pair from a single seed color. Light and dark are generated **independently** from the same identity — the dark theme is not an inversion of the light one — so the brand hue survives the mode change. Every semantic pair is solved to the contrast contract with a safety margin before the theme is returned, and the seed is recorded in `meta.generation` as provenance. **See also:** `validateTheme`, `defineTheme` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `GenerateThemeOptions` | The seed color and generation options. | **Returns** `GeneratedThemePair` — A `{ light, dark }` pair of theme definitions sharing one family. ```ts const { light, dark } = generateTheme({ seed: "#d97706", family: "brand" }); ``` ---

title: ProvidedThemeProvenance
text: ProvidedThemeProvenance Provenance a theme definition declares about itself. Only markers the library itself writes are read — `meta.generation.kind` for generator output and a `pack:<name>` tag for an installed theme pack. Nothing is inferred from a theme's name, family or colours: a theme called `mint-light` is not thereby a preset. **See also:** `ProvidedThemeFamily.provenance` `{ algorithm: string; kind: "generated" } | { kind: "pack"; pack: string }` ---

title: ThemeMode
text: ThemeMode The color-mode dimension of a theme selection. - `"light"` and `"dark"` are explicit modes. - `"system"` follows the visitor's `prefers-color-scheme` preference and resolves to `"light"` or `"dark"` at selection time. `"light" | "dark" | "system"` ---

title: ThemeOverride<Name extends string>
text: ThemeOverride<Name extends string> An explicit theme override. Three equivalent ways to name the same thing: - a **variant** (`"mint-dark"`) applies exactly that definition, - a **family** (`"mint"`) applies the variant the provider resolves for the mode already in effect, - a **family/mode object** (`{ family: "mint", mode: "dark" }`) states both. All three are resolved against the provider's own registry through resolveThemeReference, so an override cannot name a theme the provider does not have, and the family form cannot pick "whichever variant came first". **See also:** `resolveThemeOverride`, `themeOverrideKey` `Name | ThemeOverrideSelection` ```ts // `themes` is the registry the provider was given. const themes = getBuiltInThemes(); <ThemeProvider themes={themes} themeOverride="mint-dark">{children}</ThemeProvider> <ThemeProvider themes={themes} themeOverride="mint">{children}</ThemeProvider> <ThemeProvider themes={themes} themeOverride={{ family: "mint" }}>{children}</ThemeProvider> ``` ---

title: themvoraVitePlugin<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemvoraVitePlugin
text: themvoraVitePlugin<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemvoraVitePlugin Vite plugin that injects the theme bootstrap as a blocking inline script at the top of `index.html`, so the persisted theme is applied before the first paint. Prevents the flash-of-wrong-theme on reload for client-rendered apps. **See also:** `ThemvoraVitePluginOptions` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `ThemvoraVitePluginOptions<T>` | Build-time options. Optional; the default discovery path needs none. | **Returns** `ThemvoraVitePlugin` — A Vite plugin, to be added to `plugins`. **Config discovery.** The plugin looks for the application's `theme.config.ts` in Vite's root (`config.root`, or `process.cwd()` when unset), trying `theme.config.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.mjs`, `.js` and `.cjs` in that order. The file must have a default export — the object defineThemvoraConfig returns. Discovery goes through Vite's own `loadConfigFromFile`, so a TypeScript config resolves its imports exactly as `vite.config.ts` does. **What it injects.** Three things, all derived from that one configuration and emitted in this order (`head-prepend`, `enforce: "pre"`): 1. a render-blocking `<style>` from createThemePrePaintCss — the fallback theme, the `prefers-color-scheme` dark fallback when the mode is `"system"`, and one rule per declared theme; 2. `window.__THEMVORA_CONFIG__`, the serializable ThemeBootstrapConfig projection the provider reads; 3. the classic blocking bootstrap script that restores the persisted selection. When `scrollbar` is enabled, the pre-paint scrollbar script follows. The stylesheet is what themes a page with JavaScript disabled; the script is what restores a saved non-default theme before the body is parsed. **Validation.** The provider in the transformed HTML is parsed and checked against the config: unknown theme names, a default theme outside the generated collection, an invalid `initial-mode`, and a provider that resolves a different initial theme all fail the build with an actionable message. Provider JSON theme definitions are added to the generated collection, so a runtime-only catalog the plugin can see is still painted. **Development.** `transformIndexHtml` runs on every dev page load, so the injected resources are always current for the running process. The *discovered config* is resolved once and memoized, so editing `theme.config.ts` needs a dev-server restart; editing `vite.config.ts` restarts Vite anyway, so the plugin's own options do not. **Production.** The resources are injected into the generated HTML at build time and run before the application bundle. They are not emitted as separate chunks. **Limitations.** The plugin only validates a provider that is present in the document it transforms; a provider inserted later from framework state is runtime-only. It does not serve SSR HTML: frameworks that render on the server (Next.js, Nuxt, Remix, Astro) have their own packages, which emit the same bootstrap from the server. Themes registered imperatively with `runtime.use()` after load are not in the generated CSS. ```ts // Nothing to configure beyond registering the plugin. import { themvoraVitePlugin } from "@themvora/core/vite"; export default defineConfig({ plugins: [react(), themvoraVitePlugin()], }); ``` ---

title: applyThemeBootstrap(plan, options): ThemeBootstrapApplied | null
text: applyThemeBootstrap(plan, options): ThemeBootstrapApplied | null Apply a ThemeBootstrapPlan to the document before first paint. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `plan` | `ThemeBootstrapPlan` | The plan built by `buildBootstrapPlan`. | | `options` | `ApplyThemeBootstrapOptions` | Storage/document/window overrides, for tests and SSR shells. | **Returns** `ThemeBootstrapApplied | null` — The state written, or `null` when there is no document to patch. This is the browser-side half of the static `boot.js` asset. It performs the same writes as the generated inline script: the `.dark` class, `color-scheme`, the canonical `data-theme*` attributes, the resolved CSS variables, and the `window.__THEMVORA_BOOTSTRAP__` handoff payload. It is idempotent. Running it twice, or running it after the Vite plugin's inline script has already painted, leaves the first result untouched — the same rule that makes an accidental plugin-plus-manual setup harmless rather than a second, conflicting initialization. ---

title: auditActionProminence(theme): ActionProminence
text: auditActionProminence(theme): ActionProminence Measure whether a theme's action fill reads as a control.

title: Why this is a third contract, not a fourth context
text: Why this is a third contract, not a fourth context 1. **semantic pair** — `primary` against `primaryForeground` must be readable. 2. **context** — where each role may be used, and with whose judgement. 3. **prominence** — a *generated* fill must separate from the canvas, because a fill that does not has stopped reading as a control. It cannot be expressed as "`primary` must clear X:1 against `background`" globally, because that would condemn every dark brand anchor. Hence the `anchored` flag: the invariant binds generated fills and merely reports anchored ones — Slack's aubergine is 1.42:1 against the dark canvas, and that is the brand being the brand. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `theme` | `ThemeDefinition` | The theme to measure. | **Returns** `ActionProminence` — The measurement, with `anchored` telling the caller which rule applies. ---
