title: Type Aliases
text: Type Aliases

title: AdapterStrategy
text: AdapterStrategy How faithfully an adapter reproduces the target library's native feel. - `exact` — only map what Themvora defines; change nothing. - `native` — behave like the library: derive missing semantic concepts (e.g. success/warning/info) and make small feel adjustments. - `aggressive` — fully emulate the library: also adjust spacing, typography, elevation, saturation and contrast. `"exact" | "native" | "aggressive"` ---

title: AnimatedGroupKey
text: AnimatedGroupKey The name of an animatable token group. `typeof ANIMATED_GROUP_KEYS[number]` ---

title: BrandColorClass
text: BrandColorClass How a reference colour is used by the generator. `"ANCHOR" | "DERIVED" | "SEMANTIC" | "IMPLEMENTATION"` ---

title: BrandProvenance
text: BrandProvenance How faithful a brand recipe is to the real brand. Required on brand recipes: a preset gallery that shows a company's colours without saying how it relates to the company is misleading. `"official" | "approximate" | "community-inspired" | "demonstration-only" | "unaffiliated"` ---

title: BrandSourceKind
text: BrandSourceKind Where a brand's reference data came from. `official-guidelines` and `official-design-system` are the strong sources: the brand publishes the values and intends them to be used. `web-reference` is weaker — a value observed on a site, which may change without notice. `"official-guidelines" | "official-design-system" | "web-reference"` ---

title: CalculateSunTimesLocationOptions
text: CalculateSunTimesLocationOptions Options accepted by `calculateSunTimes` for resolving a location when `latitude`/`longitude` are omitted. `SolarLocationInput` ---

title: CheckStatus
text: CheckStatus The outcome of one check. `"pass" | "warn" | "fail"` ---

title: ContextLevel
text: ContextLevel Whether the generator promises the context, or merely reports it. - `required` — part of the shipped guarantee. A theme that fails is a bug. - `advisory` — a use the system knows about and deliberately does not promise, because promising it would force brand colours to be desaturated. Reported so the failure is visible rather than silent. `"required" | "advisory"` ---

title: ContextOwner
text: ContextOwner Who is responsible for keeping a context true. The point of naming an owner is to make a bad screenshot cheap to triage. The first question is never "is the generator wrong?" — it is "whose promise is this?", and the answer decides whether the fix belongs in the colour engine, in a Themvora integration, or in the application that placed the role. - `generator` — the colour itself must satisfy the contract. Nothing outside the engine can fix a failure here. - `integration` — Themvora's own runtime consumes the tokens and must choose a role that satisfies the context. The scrollbar is the case. - `consumer` — the application decides where the role goes. Themvora declares the use as advisory and the consumer owns the judgement. `"generator" | "integration" | "consumer"` ---

title: ContextRequirement
text: ContextRequirement The threshold a context is held to. `decorative` is not "anything goes" — it means the role must be *visible and subordinate*, which is enforced as a relationship rather than a ratio. A border is the canonical case. `ContrastRequirement | "decorative"` ---

title: CoreColor
text: CoreColor The colour roles every Themvora theme defines. These are *semantic roles*, not library tokens. An adapter is responsible for expressing each one in its target library's own vocabulary — or for declaring that it does not need it. **See also:** `OptionalSemantic` `"background" | "foreground" | "card" | "cardForeground" | "popover" | "popoverForeground" | "primary" | "primaryForeground" | "secondary" | "secondaryForeground" | "muted" | "mutedForeground" | "accent" | "accentForeground" | "destructive" | "destructiveForeground" | "success" | "successForeground" | "border" | "input" | "ring"` ---

title: CreateRootLike<TRoot extends SyncFirstRenderRoot>
text: CreateRootLike<TRoot extends SyncFirstRenderRoot> React's `createRoot`, structurally. `__type(container: Element | DocumentFragment, options?: unknown): TRoot` ---

title: CVDType
text: CVDType The type of color vision deficiency (CVD) to simulate. `"protanopia" | "deuteranopia" | "tritanopia" | "achromatopsia"` ---

title: DiagnosticSink
text: DiagnosticSink A destination for rendered diagnostics. `__type(text: string, diagnostic: ThemeDiagnostic): void` ---

title: ForegroundPreference
text: ForegroundPreference Which ink a role prefers, when that preference is legible. `"light" | "dark"` ---

title: GeneratedThemeStatus
text: GeneratedThemeStatus The outcome of findGeneratedTheme. - `"found"` — exactly one eligible theme resolved (its `theme` is set). - `"missing"` — no generated theme is registered. - `"ambiguous"` — more than one is registered and the active selection does not pick one out. Callers must reject this rather than guess. `"found" | "missing" | "ambiguous"` ---

title: GenerationStyle
text: GenerationStyle The visual languages a theme can be generated in. `"balanced" | "soft" | "vibrant" | "editorial" | "minimal" | "brand"` ---

title: OptionalSemantic
text: OptionalSemantic Colour roles a theme *may* declare. These are capabilities rather than contract. A theme that omits them is complete; an adapter that needs one declares it in its `optional` list and must degrade gracefully when it is absent — by deriving it, or by omitting the library token entirely. Fabricating a value no consumer reads is worse than omitting it, because it looks like support. `"warning" | "warningForeground" | "info" | "infoForeground" | "error" | "errorForeground"` ---

title: PrePaintScrollbarOptions
text: PrePaintScrollbarOptions Phase 1 — Bootstrap: hide native scrollbar before first paint. This is a tiny, dependency-free, blocking `<script>` that runs before React. It does ONE thing: inject a `<style>` and add `tv-scrollbar` to `<html>` so the native scrollbar is never painted. No DOM creation. No observers. No listeners. No React. No rAF. Executes in under 1 ms. The overlay (ThemeScrollbar) handles everything else: measure, draw, animate, drag, hover, physics. When the overlay has been painted once, it adds `tv-scrollbar-ready` to `<html>` — enabling CSS fade-in. Architecture: Phase 1 — Bootstrap (this module) └─ hide native scrollbar └─ add tv-scrollbar Phase 2 — ThemeScrollbar (React / Web / Angular) └─ create overlay └─ measure └─ attach listeners (scroll, resize, pointer, wheel, MutationObserver) Phase 3 — Ready └─ tv-scrollbar-ready └─ overlay fades in via CSS Next.js (`@themvora/next`) server-renders the `tv-scrollbar` class on `<html>` and inlines `createPrePaintScrollbarCSS()` as a `<style>` in `<head>` when the `scrollbar` prop is set — so the native bar is hidden from the very first paint AND React hydrates without a class mismatch. Emitting `createPrePaintScrollbarScript()` yourself is only needed when you're not on `@themvora/next` (no SSR of the class). `void` ---

title: PresetFamily
text: PresetFamily The name of a preset theme family. `"neutral" | "oat" | "berry" | "mint" | "citrus" | "cocoa" | "plum" | "iris" | "sky" | "graphite"` ---

title: PresetKind
text: PresetKind Whether a recipe is a curated default or a brand-inspired starting point. `"default" | "brand"` ---

title: PresetOverrides
text: PresetOverrides Per-family, per-mode token overrides for the preset theme set. `Partial<Record<PresetFamily, Partial<Record<PresetVariant, PresetVariantOverride>>>>` ---

title: PresetThemeName
text: PresetThemeName The full name of a preset theme, e.g. `"oat-light"`. ``${unknown}${unknown}`` ---

title: PresetVariant
text: PresetVariant The color mode of a preset theme. `"light" | "dark"` ---

title: ProvidedThemeProvenance
text: ProvidedThemeProvenance Provenance a theme definition declares about itself. Only markers the library itself writes are read — `meta.generation.kind` for generator output and a `pack:<name>` tag for an installed theme pack. Nothing is inferred from a theme's name, family or colours: a theme called `mint-light` is not thereby a preset. **See also:** `ProvidedThemeFamily.provenance` `{ algorithm: string; kind: "generated" } | { kind: "pack"; pack: string }` ---

title: RegistryFailureReason
text: RegistryFailureReason Why a registry could not be read. `"not-a-registry" | "unsupported-construct" | "invalid-theme"` ---

title: RegistryLoadResult
text: RegistryLoadResult The outcome of reading a registry. `RegistryLoadSuccess | RegistryLoadFailure` ---

title: ScopedThemeSelection
text: ScopedThemeSelection A scoped theme selection. Either an exact theme name (or family name), or an explicit family + mode pair. Provided as a `string` for convenience — every framework wrapper accepts it. `string | { name: string } | { family: string; mode?: ThemeMode }` ---

title: ScrollbarArrowDir
text: ScrollbarArrowDir Direction of a single arrow button on an axis strip. `"up" | "down" | "left" | "right"` ---

title: ScrollbarAxis
text: ScrollbarAxis Scrollbar overlay engine — public options, runtime types and per-host runtime state. The philosophy: the browser always performs the scrolling. This module only renders a theme-aware, animated overlay that *represents* the scrollbar. It never replaces or moves native scrolling — it only synchronizes with it. `"vertical" | "horizontal"` ---

title: ScrollbarFlatOptions
text: ScrollbarFlatOptions Flat options as the adapters forward them. Every key is optional AND may be explicitly `undefined` (adapters pass their raw props straight through), so `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` does not force every call site to strip undefined keys by hand. `{ [K in keyof OverlayScrollbarOptions]: OverlayScrollbarOptions[K] }` ---

title: ScrollbarOffset
text: ScrollbarOffset The rail offset: one inset for every side, or per-side values. `number | ScrollbarOffsetSides` ---

title: SemanticRole
text: SemanticRole A status role, independent of how any library spells it. This is the *intent*: "this surface communicates a warning". How that becomes `--warning` (shadcn), `--alert-warning` (Bootstrap), `colorScheme.warning` (MUI) or nothing at all is the adapter's decision, not the theme's. `"success" | "warning" | "info" | "error"` ---

title: ThemeBootstrapConfig<T extends ThemeDefinition>
text: ThemeBootstrapConfig<T extends ThemeDefinition> The projection of ThemvoraConfig that crosses to the browser. **See also:** `toBootstrapConfig` `Pick<ThemvoraConfig<T>, "themes" | "defaultTheme" | "initialMode" | "initialFamily" | "storageKey" | "prefix" | "transition" | "scrollbar">` Two consumers read this one object, and it has to satisfy both: - the **pre-paint bootstrap**, which runs before any application code and can only resolve a selection from a registry, a fallback and a persisted key; - the **client runtime**, which is built from this global by `resolveRuntimeOptions` and therefore sees *only* what is here. The second consumer is the reason this is not simply "the bootstrap subset". When a runtime option was left out, the browser runtime silently used its default instead — `theme.config.ts` could declare `transition: { enabled: false }` and the page would still run a `document.startViewTransition` on every theme change. That is not a cosmetic difference: a view transition applies the document swap in a **later task**, so a consumer that renders from the theme store painted the new theme one frame before the document had it. So every **serializable** runtime option belongs here. What cannot cross is excluded explicitly rather than by omission: `plugins` and `adapters` hold functions, and `persistence` is a live adapter object. ---

title: ThemeChangeSource
text: ThemeChangeSource The origin of a theme change, used to attribute debug events. `"user" | "system" | "persistence" | "broadcast" | "update" | "init"` ---

title: ThemeDefinitionOrigin
text: ThemeDefinitionOrigin Which canonical API produced a theme. `"definition" | "generated" | "catalog"` ---

title: ThemeDiagnosticCode
text: ThemeDiagnosticCode A stable, machine-readable identifier for a Themvora diagnostic. Codes are part of the public contract: they are what tests assert on and what tooling can filter by. The human-readable message is deliberately *not* — it may be reworded at any time. Naming is `TV_<DOMAIN>_<CONDITION>`. Codes are added only alongside the diagnostic that actually emits them; this union is never pre-populated with speculative entries. **See also:** `ThemeDiagnostic` `"TV_MODE_INVALID" | "TV_THEME_TOKEN_MISSING" | "TV_PREPAINT_MISSING" | "TV_PREPAINT_MISMATCH" | "TV_THEME_FAMILY_UNKNOWN" | "TV_THEME_OVERRIDE_UNRESOLVED" | "TV_THEME_NEUTRAL_FALLBACK" | "TV_THEME_TOKEN_INVALID" | "TV_A11Y_CONTRAST_VIOLATION" | "TV_SCHEDULE_THEME_UNRESOLVED" | "TV_CONFIG_OPTION_INVALID" | "TV_SCROLLBAR_OPTION_INVALID" | "TV_PLUGIN_DESTROY_FAILED" | "TV_SYNC_FAILED" | "TV_GENERATION_INVALID_SEED" | "TV_GENERATION_CONTRAST_REPAIR" | "TV_GENERATION_ROLE_COLLISION" | "TV_GENERATION_CONSTRAINT_UNSATISFIED" | "TV_GENERATION_THEME_NOT_FOUND" | "TV_GENERATION_THEME_AMBIGUOUS" | "TV_DIFF_UNRESOLVED_EXTENDS" | "TV_DIFF_UNRESOLVED_SYSTEM"` ---

title: ThemeDiagnosticLevel
text: ThemeDiagnosticLevel Severity of a Themvora diagnostic. The level is a deliberate decision per diagnostic, not a default. It records what the caller is expected to do about it: - `"error"` — continuing would produce incorrect state. - `"warning"` — recoverable, but the caller very likely made a mistake. - `"deprecation"` — still supported, but scheduled to be removed. - `"info"` — useful context; never indicates a problem. **See also:** `ThemeDiagnostic` `"error" | "warning" | "deprecation" | "info"` ---

title: ThemeFamilies<T extends readonly ThemeDefinition[]>
text: ThemeFamilies<T extends readonly ThemeDefinition[]> Extract the literal theme-family union from a tuple of theme definitions. When themes are defined with `as const`, autocomplete shows the available families in `setFamily()` / `initialFamily`: ```ts const themes = [ { name: "mint-light", meta: { family: "mint", mode: "light" }, tokens: {} }, { name: "mint-dark", meta: { family: "mint", mode: "dark" }, tokens: {} }, ] as const; // ThemeFamilies<typeof themes> → "mint" ``` `FamilyOf<T[number]> extends never ? string : FamilyOf<T[number]>` ---

title: ThemeFamilyOf<T extends ThemeDefinition>
text: ThemeFamilyOf<T extends ThemeDefinition> The literal family union of a **single** theme definition type. `ThemeFamilies` below does this for a tuple; the provider's selection props are typed against the element type, so they need the same derivation one level down. Resolves to `string` when the definition does not state a literal family (a `ThemeDefinition[]` variable, a generated catalog), which keeps the dynamic-input path working. `[T["meta"] extends { family?: infer F } ? F extends string ? F : never : never] extends [never] ? string : T["meta"] extends { family?: infer F } ? F extends string ? F : string : string` ---

title: ThemeIdentifier<T extends ThemeDefinition>
text: ThemeIdentifier<T extends ThemeDefinition> Every way a caller can name a provided theme. A **variant** name (`"cocoa-dark"`) or a **family** name (`"cocoa"`) — the two forms resolveThemeReference accepts. Derived from the theme definitions the caller passes, so a statically known collection autocompletes both; a dynamically built one widens to `string` rather than becoming unusable. `T["name"] | ThemeFamilyOf<T>` ```ts const themes = [ { name: "oat-light", meta: { family: "oat", mode: "light" }, tokens: {} }, { name: "cocoa-dark", meta: { family: "cocoa", mode: "dark" }, tokens: {} }, ] as const; // ThemeIdentifier<typeof themes[number]> // = "oat-light" | "cocoa-dark" | "oat" | "cocoa" ``` ---

title: ThemeLifecycleEventName
text: ThemeLifecycleEventName Names of the lifecycle events exposed by ThemeLifecycle. `keyof ThemeLifecycleEventMap` ---

title: ThemeMode
text: ThemeMode The color-mode dimension of a theme selection. - `"light"` and `"dark"` are explicit modes. - `"system"` follows the visitor's `prefers-color-scheme` preference and resolves to `"light"` or `"dark"` at selection time. `"light" | "dark" | "system"` ---

title: ThemeModes<T extends readonly ThemeDefinition[]>
text: ThemeModes<T extends readonly ThemeDefinition[]> Extract the literal theme-mode union from a tuple of theme definitions. With `as const`, `ThemeModes<typeof themes> → "light" | "dark"`. `ModeOf<T[number]> extends never ? ThemeMode : ModeOf<T[number]>` ---

title: ThemeName
text: ThemeName Stable theme identifier used for selection and lookup. Any string is accepted; use a readable family-oriented name such as `"mint-light"` or `"dark"`. `string` ---

title: ThemeOverride<Name extends string>
text: ThemeOverride<Name extends string> An explicit theme override. Three equivalent ways to name the same thing: - a **variant** (`"mint-dark"`) applies exactly that definition, - a **family** (`"mint"`) applies the variant the provider resolves for the mode already in effect, - a **family/mode object** (`{ family: "mint", mode: "dark" }`) states both. All three are resolved against the provider's own registry through resolveThemeReference, so an override cannot name a theme the provider does not have, and the family form cannot pick "whichever variant came first". **See also:** `resolveThemeOverride`, `themeOverrideKey` `Name | ThemeOverrideSelection` ```ts // `themes` is the registry the provider was given. const themes = getBuiltInThemes(); <ThemeProvider themes={themes} themeOverride="mint-dark">{children}</ThemeProvider> <ThemeProvider themes={themes} themeOverride="mint">{children}</ThemeProvider> <ThemeProvider themes={themes} themeOverride={{ family: "mint" }}>{children}</ThemeProvider> ``` ---

title: ThemePack<T extends ThemeDefinition>
text: ThemePack<T extends ThemeDefinition> A named collection of theme definitions installable as a group. Themes installed through `use` receive a `pack:<name>` tag and replace any existing theme with the same name. `void` ---

title: ThemeScheduleStatus
text: ThemeScheduleStatus Whether the schedule is driving theme selection right now. `"active"` means the schedule is enabled and applying its light/dark selection; `"disabled"` means it has been turned off (e.g. via `schedule.disable()`). `"active" | "disabled"` ---

title: ThemeScheduleStore<T extends ThemeDefinition>
text: ThemeScheduleStore<T extends ThemeDefinition> The store surface createThemeSchedule needs. Deliberately narrower than `ThemeStore`: the runtime hands the schedule a handle whose `set` routes through the selection controller (`applyAutomaticTheme`) instead of writing the store directly, so a transition updates the effective mode and cannot be overwritten by the OS binding. A plain `ThemeStore` still satisfies this shape, so calling the factory directly keeps working unchanged. `Pick<ThemeStore<T>, "get" | "set" | "subscribe">` ---

title: ThemeTokenChangeStatus
text: ThemeTokenChangeStatus How one token path differs between the two sides. `"added" | "removed" | "changed" | "unchanged"` ---

title: TimeZoneLocation
text: TimeZoneLocation `latitude, longitude` tuple. `[latitude: number, longitude: number]` ---

title: TokenGroup
text: TokenGroup The name of a token group that can be emitted as CSS custom properties. Derived from TOKEN_GROUPS so the type and the runtime order can never disagree. `typeof TOKEN_GROUPS[number]` ---

title: TransitionPreset
text: TransitionPreset Named or explicit transition property sets. - `"smooth"`: full curated color set (colors, borders, radii, shadows). - `"subtle"`: reduced color set. - `"instant"`: only `opacity`. - `"custom"`: reserved for explicit `properties`. - `string[]`: explicit property list. `"smooth" | "subtle" | "instant" | "custom" | string[]` ---

title: ValidationLevel
text: ValidationLevel The validation levels, in escalating order. `"structural" | "semantic" | "contrast" | "visual" | "accessibility"` ---

title: Variables
text: Variables

title: ACTIONPROMINENCEFLOOR
text: ACTIONPROMINENCEFLOOR The non-text floor an action fill is held to against the canvas. `3` ---

title: ANIMATEDGROUPKEYS
text: ANIMATEDGROUPKEYS Token-category → CSS-property classification. This is the single source of truth for "which token group maps to which CSS property," so the Transition Planner builds transitions from a diff without hardcoding property lists in multiple places. `colors` intentionally maps to nothing here: theme colors flow through `@property`-registered custom properties on `:root`, so the whole `var(--theme-color-*)` graph animates by inheritance — no per-element work. Every other group is animated on the scanned elements that use it. `readonly ["colors", "radius", "spacing", "typography", "shadows", "borders", "transforms", "opacity"]` ---

title: BRANDPRESETDISCLAIMER
text: BRANDPRESETDISCLAIMER The canonical brand disclaimer. Exported so every surface that shows a brand preset — the docs pages, the README, a future gallery — states the same thing in the same words. A disclaimer that is paraphrased per page is a disclaimer that eventually contradicts itself. `"These presets are brand-inspired examples for Themvora. They are not official brand themes, and they do not imply endorsement or affiliation."` ---

title: CONTEXTRESTRICTIONS
text: CONTEXTRESTRICTIONS The declared restrictions. These are not failures — they are the design system saying what it means. A brand colour is allowed to be vivid precisely because nobody promised it would work as a paragraph. `readonly ContextRestriction[]` ---

title: CORECOLORS
text: CORECOLORS Every CoreColor, as a runtime list. `readonly CoreColor[]` ---

title: CSSDARKSELECTOR
text: CSSDARKSELECTOR The selector a pair's dark half is emitted under. Matches the convention the CLI's `export` command has always written, and the one `themvora init` uses in the generated stylesheet: an explicit class and a `data-theme` attribute, so a host can opt in with either. `".dark, [data-theme="dark"]"` ---

title: CSSROOTSELECTOR
text: CSSROOTSELECTOR The selector a single theme, or a pair's light half, is emitted under. `":root"` ---

title: default
text: default `NuxtModule<ModuleOptions>` ---

title: DEFAULTSCHEDULEDDARKTHEME
text: DEFAULTSCHEDULEDDARKTHEME The default neutral dark theme name used when `darkTheme` is omitted and no family counterpart can be derived. `"dark"` ---

title: DEFAULTSCHEDULEDLIGHTTHEME
text: DEFAULTSCHEDULEDLIGHTTHEME The default neutral theme names used when `lightTheme`/`darkTheme` are omitted and no family counterpart can be derived. `"light"` ---

title: DEFAULTTHEMETRANSITION
text: DEFAULTTHEMETRANSITION The default transition configuration applied by the runtime when transitions are enabled without explicit options. `Omit<Required<ThemeTransitionOptions>, "preset"> & Partial<Pick<ThemeTransitionOptions, "preset">>` ---

title: DEFAULTTIMEZONELOCATION
text: DEFAULTTIMEZONELOCATION Fallback used when nothing else can be resolved (New York). `TimeZoneLocation` ---

title: DEFAULTTRANSITIONPRESET
text: DEFAULTTRANSITIONPRESET The transition preset used when `ThemeTransitionOptions.preset` is omitted. `TransitionPreset` ---

title: EMPTYTHEMEDIFF
text: EMPTYTHEMEDIFF A `ThemeDiff` with every group set to `false`, representing "nothing changed". Used as the identity/empty diff so downstream stages can short- circuit when no token group differs between two themes. `ThemeDiff` ---

title: EMPTYTHEMESCHEDULESTATE
text: EMPTYTHEMESCHEDULESTATE The default, disabled ThemeScheduleState snapshot. Used as the initial state before a schedule resolves its location and themes. `ThemeScheduleState` ---

title: FOREGROUNDPREFERENCE
text: FOREGROUNDPREFERENCE The preferred foreground for each role that has one. **Only action and emphasis surfaces appear here**, and that is the whole point of the list being short. A preference is a statement about *what the surface is for*: a strong action fill wants light ink because that is what makes it read as an action rather than a disabled control. Reading inks are deliberately absent. `foreground`, `mutedForeground`, `cardForeground` and `secondaryForeground` sit on quiet surfaces whose lightness flips with the mode, so the correct ink family flips with it too — a fixed preference would be wrong in one mode. They fall through to highest contrast, which is exactly right for a role whose only job is legibility. (An earlier draft listed them as preferring "light"/"dark" and broke `mutedForeground/muted` to 4.495:1 — the property test caught it. The rule "don't give a reading ink a preference" is load-bearing.) `Readonly<Partial<Record<CoreColor, ForegroundPreference>>>` ---

title: GENERATEDTHEMEKIND
text: GENERATEDTHEMEKIND The `meta.generation.kind` value stamped by generateTheme. **See also:** `isGeneratedTheme` `"generated"` ---

title: GENERATIONSTYLENAMES
text: GENERATIONSTYLENAMES Every style name, as a runtime list. Exported publicly so the CLI and the docs can validate a `--style` argument against the real set rather than re-listing it. `readonly GenerationStyle[]` ---

title: GROUPPROPERTIES
text: GROUPPROPERTIES Maps each animatable token group to the CSS properties it drives. `colors` maps to an empty list because theme colors flow through `@property`-registered custom properties on `:root` and animate by inheritance; every other group lists the concrete CSS properties animated on the scanned elements that use them. `Record<AnimatedGroupKey, string[]>` ---

title: GROUPVARPREFIXES
text: GROUPVARPREFIXES CSS variable prefixes each token group materializes to (see `themeToCSSVariables`). `Record<keyof ThemeDiff, string[]>` ---

title: migrations
text: migrations The registered migration steps, ordered by their `from` version. Managed via registerMigration and clearMigrations. `MigrationStep[]` ---

title: OPTIONALSEMANTICS

title: PREPAINTSCROLLBARCSS
text: PREPAINTSCROLLBARCSS The CSS that hides native scrollbars while `tv-scrollbar` is present on `<html>`. Shared by the client bootstrap script and Next's SSR output so both apply identical rules. The bar is painted invisible while KEEPING its space, so the gutter that keeps content clear of the rail exists from the first frame (no load-time layout shift). Two groups: - The PAGE / window scrollbar is collapsed (`scrollbar-width: none`). Its rail auto-hides, so a reserved empty strip at the window edge would read as a missing scrollbar; the standard property also overrides the WebKit sizing below, so the page never reserves one. - INNER scroll containers keep an invisible, space-occupying scrollbar. It is sized through `::-webkit-scrollbar` (not only `scrollbar-color`) because styling those pseudo-elements is what takes Chromium/Safari off OVERLAY scrollbars — so the gutter is reserved on macOS too, where the native path would take no space. The space appears only while the container actually scrolls, exactly like a native `overflow: auto` bar. - Engines without WebKit pseudo-elements (Firefox) get the same reserve through the standard properties. `string` ---

title: SCROLLBARHIDINGSTYLEATTR
text: SCROLLBARHIDINGSTYLEATTR Marker on every stylesheet that hides the native scrollbar. Three different places can emit that CSS — this module's blocking script, `createOverlayScrollbar`, and an SSR adapter (the Astro provider renders it inline in `<head>`). A stylesheet is only removable if a teardown can find it, and an id alone cannot: the SSR output has no id, and an id is a single slot. So the marker is the contract, and the id is just a fast path. `"data-themvora-scrollbar-hiding"` ---

title: SCROLLBARHIDINGSTYLEID
text: SCROLLBARHIDINGSTYLEID `id` of the stylesheet the client-side bootstrap injects. Kept for compatibility — a teardown must find the stylesheet whoever wrote it, so restoreNativeScrollbar looks for the marker attribute below as well, and that is the one every producer sets. `"tv-scrollbar-style"` ---

title: createOpenPropsAdapter<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeAdapter<T>
text: createOpenPropsAdapter<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeAdapter<T> Creates an Open Props adapter. The adapter is a DOM-only, framework-free adapter: it depends only on `@themvora/core` and the DOM. On install it injects the Open Props compatibility stylesheet (when enabled) and a `<style>` element of CSS variables derived from the active theme, then subscribes to the runtime store and rewrites the variables whenever the theme selection changes. It does not render any component or require a React tree. On uninstall it removes the injected styles and unsubscribes from the store. **See also:** `useOpenPropsTheme` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `CreateOpenPropsAdapterOptions` | Adapter options. Defaults to `{}`. | **Returns** `ThemeAdapter<T>` — A `ThemeAdapter` for Open Props. ```ts import { createOpenPropsAdapter } from "@themvora/open-props"; runtime.adapters.use(createOpenPropsAdapter()); ``` ---

title: createThemeRoot<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeRootHandle<T>
text: createThemeRoot<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(options): ThemeRootHandle<T> Create a Themvora-owned React root for client-rendered (CSR) applications. Themvora owns the root boundary: the runtime is created once, and the initial commit is flushed synchronously so the browser's very first frame is already the themed UI. Without it, React's concurrent root can schedule the initial commit after the browser paints an empty/partial frame — visible as a flicker on reload in some applications. This is an **optional, opt-in** helper. Most applications can use the plain React API and it will be smooth: ```tsx const root = createRoot(container); root.render( <ThemeProvider defaultTheme="mint-light" initialMode="system"> <App /> </ThemeProvider>, ); ``` Reach for `createThemeRoot` when you want Themvora to own the root initialization boundary — for example a reload-sensitive demo, or an app whose providers need the Themvora runtime at composition time: ```tsx import { createThemeRoot } from "@themvora/react"; const handle = createThemeRoot({ container: document.getElementById("root")!, defaultTheme: "mint-light", initialMode: "system", transition: { enabled: true }, render: ({ runtime }) => ( <MuiThemeProvider runtime={runtime}> <App /> </MuiThemeProvider> ), }); handle.unmount(); ``` Only the FIRST commit is flushed synchronously; subsequent renders keep React's normal concurrent scheduling. `ThemeProvider` itself never calls `flushSync` — the helper owns the root, which is the one place React documents `flushSync` as appropriate. Do **not** use this helper for SSR/SSG applications — server-rendered HTML must be hydrated with `hydrateRoot()` (or a framework integration such as `@themvora/next`), not replaced by a fresh `createRoot`. **See also:** `ThemeProvider` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `options` | `CreateThemeRootOptions<T>` | — | **Returns** `ThemeRootHandle<T>` ---

title: ThemeInspector(namedParameters): Element
text: ThemeInspector(namedParameters): Element A floating developer tool that inspects the active theme. Renders a fixed toggle button and an expandable panel showing the current theme name, family, mode, selection state, token values, and emitted CSS variables — useful while building themeable UI. **See also:** `useTheme` **Returns** `Element` The panel opens above the toggle with a gap, stays dismissible via the toggle, `Escape`, or clicking outside, and matches the provider's transition duration for its own fade. ```ts <ThemeInspector /> ``` ---

title: ThemeModeButton(): Element
text: ThemeModeButton(): Element A minimal demo-style button that cycles the theme mode: `light → dark → system → light`. Renders a `<button>` whose label is the mode **actually applied**, with the configured mode shown alongside it while that is `"system"`. Cycling always follows the configured mode, so a visitor who picked "system" stays on it. Use it for demos and prototypes, or build your own control with useTheme. **See also:** `useTheme`, `useEffectiveThemeMode` **Returns** `Element` The label reads useEffectiveThemeMode rather than useThemeMode on purpose. With a sunrise/sunset schedule running, the configured mode is the visitor's standing request — `"system"`, or whichever mode they last picked — and it does not move at sunset. A label bound to it therefore kept announcing the old mode while the page changed colour. The effective mode moves with the page. ```ts <ThemeModeButton /> ``` ---

title: ThemeProvider<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(namedParameters): Element
text: ThemeProvider<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(namedParameters): Element React provider for a Themvora runtime. Creates a runtime on mount (unless a `runtime` prop is given), installs the DOM + CSS-variable bindings, injects a pre-paint bootstrap script for flash-proofing, and provides the runtime to all Themvora hooks below. Must be rendered inside the application's root. When no `runtime` prop is passed, the provider owns the runtime and destroys it on unmount; the deferred-destroy mechanism keeps the runtime alive across React StrictMode remounts. **See also:** `useTheme`, `ThemeScope`, `createThemeRoot` **Returns** `Element` **The first paint is the root's business, not the provider's.** On a client-rendered app React's concurrent root *schedules* the initial commit, so the browser can paint a frame with the root still empty before React commits — one frame, ~33 ms, plainly visible as the UI blinking on reload. The provider cannot prevent it: that frame is painted before any of the app's React code runs, so nothing the provider does in a render, an insertion effect or a layout effect is in time. It is fixed where it happens instead, with no application code: - **Vite apps** — `themvoraVitePlugin()` resolves `react-dom/client` to a shim that flushes the first `render` synchronously (`syncFirstRender`, on by default). Nothing in the app changes; `<ThemeProvider>` alone is enough. - **Anything else** — createThemeRoot is that same synchronous first commit plus runtime ownership, and stays entirely opt-in. The provider's own theme work *is* pre-paint: the bootstrap is injected in an insertion effect and a server-resolved `initial` is applied in a layout effect, so neither waits for the browser to paint. The pre-JS window is out of scope for all of them: until the entry module runs, the root is empty by definition. A themed canvas keeps that window from reading as a flash, and only a prerendered first paint puts content in it. ```ts function App() { return ( <ThemeProvider defaultTheme="mint-light" initialMode="system"> <Page /> </ThemeProvider> ); } ``` ---

title: ThemeScope(namedParameters): Element
text: ThemeScope(namedParameters): Element Applies a theme to a subtree without replacing the global runtime. The scope resolves local themes (`themes` prop) before falling back to the parent runtime's theme registry. Nested scopes override their parent within their own boundary. Theme changes are reactive: `theme`/`family`/`mode` props and global mode changes re-resolve and animate in place without remounting. **See also:** `useScopedTheme` **Returns** `Element` Scope-local transitions inherit the parent transition configuration unless explicitly overridden or disabled. First paint is server-safe: explicit selections ship resolved variables inline, while OS-dependent selections (system mode / family-following scopes) ship no inline variables plus a `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` override, so no flash occurs. ```ts <ThemeScope family="plum" mode="dark"> <Editor /> </ThemeScope> ``` ---

title: ThemeScrollbar(props): null
text: ThemeScrollbar(props): null ThemeScrollbar — overlay only. Creates the custom scrollbar overlay. Lifecycle: mount → create overlay → measure → attach listeners paint → add tv-scrollbar-ready destroy → remove overlay Props are four optional groups — `behavior`, `appearance`, `scope` and `icons` — plus `children`, which is accepted for JSX symmetry only. <ThemeScrollbar behavior={{ autoHide: true, smooth: true }} appearance={{ thickness: 8, radius: 999 }} scope={{ include: [".panel"] }} icons={{ up: <ArrowUpIcon />, size: 12 }} /> <ThemeScrollbar behavior={{ autoHide: true, smooth: true }} appearance={{ thickness: 8, radius: 999 }} icons={{ up: <ArrowUpIcon />, down: <ArrowDownIcon /> }} /> **See also:** `ThemeProvider` | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `props` | `ThemeScrollbarProps` | — | **Returns** `null` ---

title: useEffectiveThemeMode(): "light" | "dark"
text: useEffectiveThemeMode(): "light" | "dark" Subscribe to the mode actually **applied** — `"light"` or `"dark"`, never `"system"`. This is the value a control that says "you are in dark mode" must render. useThemeMode reports the request, which is the right thing for a three-way light/dark/system picker but the wrong thing for a toggle or a label: with `mode: "system"` it never changes, and with a sunrise/sunset schedule running it stays on the configured value while the page changes underneath it. Updates for every cause — a click, an OS appearance change, a schedule transition — because it subscribes to the appearance rather than to the selection. ```tsx const effectiveMode = useEffectiveThemeMode(); return {effectiveMode === "dark" ? "Dark" : "Light"}; ``` **See also:** `useThemeMode`, `useThemeSchedule` **Returns** `"light" | "dark"` ---

title: useGeneratedTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): T
text: useGeneratedTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): T The theme produced by `generateTheme()` and registered with the provider. Returns the registered theme that carries the generator's origin marker (`meta.generation.kind === "generated"`) — never a shipped preset, and never inferred from a theme's id, family or colors. Generate one and pass the result to `ThemeProvider`: ```tsx const generated = generateTheme({ seed: "#635BFF", family: "brand" }); <ThemeProvider themes={[generated.light, generated.dark]}>{children}</ThemeProvider> ``` When both halves of one `generateTheme()` call are registered, the theme the active selection resolves to is returned. If several generated themes are registered and none is active, the call throws rather than guessing. Throws `ThemeError` with code `TV_GENERATION_THEME_NOT_FOUND` when the provider holds no generated theme, and `TV_GENERATION_THEME_AMBIGUOUS` when several are registered and the active selection does not identify one. Re-resolves on every settled change to the registry, store, or selection; if the generated theme is later removed, the same error is raised at the next render rather than a stale theme being returned. **See also:** `useThemeValue` **Returns** `T` — The registered generated theme. ---

title: useProvidedThemes<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): readonly ProvidedThemeFamily<T>[]
text:
useProvidedThemes>(): readonly ProvidedThemeFamily[] The themes this provider was given, grouped by family. Returns exactly the collection supplied to the nearest `ThemeProvider` — not the built-in catalog, and not every theme that exists in the project. Build a theme picker from it instead of enumerating a separate preset source: ```tsx const themes = useProvidedThemes(); return themes.map((family) => (

{family.name}

{family.variants.map((variant) => ( ))}
)); ``` The collection is reactive: a `themes` prop change, a `runtime.use(pack)` install or a registry mutation re-renders the consumer. Entries keep their identity while their content is unchanged, so `React.memo` and dependency arrays behave. **See also:** `useTheme`, `normalizeProvidedThemes` **Returns** `readonly ProvidedThemeFamily[]` — The provider's theme families, in supplied order. ---

title: useScopedTheme(ref, selection, transition?): RefObject<{ destroy: void; getTheme: void; refresh: void; setLocalThemes: void; setTransition: void; update: void } | null>
text: useScopedTheme(ref, selection, transition?): RefObject<{ destroy: void; getTheme: void; refresh: void; setLocalThemes: void; setTransition: void; update: void } | null> Headless scoped-theming hook: applies a scoped theme selection to an arbitrary element (by ref) without rendering a wrapper component. Useful when the scoped element is not a plain `div` — e.g. a custom component that forwards a ref — or when `ThemeScope`'s wrapper would break layout. Must be called inside `ThemeProvider`. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --------- | ---- | ----------- | | `ref` | `RefObject<HTMLElement \| null>` | Ref to the element that receives the scoped theme variables. | | `selection` | `ScopedThemeSelection \| null` | Scoped selection to apply. Pass `null` to remove the scope (destroys any active binding). | | `transition` | `boolean \| ThemeTransitionOptions` (optional) | Transition override for this scope's changes. Inherits the provider transition when omitted. | **Returns** `RefObject<{ destroy: void; getTheme: void; refresh: void; setLocalThemes: void; setTransition: void; update: void } | null>` — A ref holding the active scoped binding (for advanced access). ```ts const elRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null); useScopedTheme(elRef, { family: "plum", mode: "dark" }); return <div ref={elRef} />; ``` ---

title: useSetThemeFamily<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): type(family: ThemeFamilies<readonly T[]>): void
text: useSetThemeFamily<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): type(family: ThemeFamilies<readonly T[]>): void Get a stable `setFamily` function (does not re-render on change). **See also:** `useThemeFamily` **Returns** `__type(family: ThemeFamilies<readonly T[]>): void` ---

title: useSetThemeMode<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): type(mode: ModesOf<T>): void
text: useSetThemeMode<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): type(mode: ModesOf<T>): void Get a stable `setMode` function (does not re-render on change). **See also:** `useThemeMode` **Returns** `__type(mode: ModesOf<T>): void` ---

title: useTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): { effectiveMode: "light" | "dark"; family: string; mode: ThemeMode; setFamily: type(family: ThemeFamilies): void; setMode: type(mode: ModesOf): void; theme: T; toggleTheme: type(): void }
text: useTheme<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): { effectiveMode: "light" | "dark"; family: string; mode: ThemeMode; setFamily: type(family: ThemeFamilies): void; setMode: type(mode: ModesOf): void; theme: T; toggleTheme: type(): void } The primary Themvora hook. Returns the current theme, mode, family and the selection controls. When you pass the theme tuple element type, `setFamily` and `setMode` are constrained to the families/modes defined in your registry (the built-in set is used below so the example stands alone): ```ts import { getBuiltInThemes } from "@themvora/core"; const themes = getBuiltInThemes(); const { theme, mode, family, setMode, setFamily, toggleTheme } = useTheme<typeof themes[number]>(); setFamily("mint"); // autocomplete suggests your families setMode("dark"); ``` **See also:** `useThemeValue`, `useThemeMode`, `useEffectiveThemeMode`, `useThemeFamily` **Returns** `{ effectiveMode: "light" | "dark"; family: string; mode: ThemeMode; setFamily: __type(family: ThemeFamilies): void; setMode: __type(mode: ModesOf): void; theme: T; toggleTheme: __type(): void }` ---

title: useThemeBatch(): type(callback: type(): void): void
text: useThemeBatch(): type(callback: type(): void): void Get a batch function that defers all selection changes and DOM writes to a single flush. **See also:** `useTheme` **Returns** `__type(callback: __type(): void): void` ---

title: useThemeFamily(): string
text: useThemeFamily(): string Subscribe to the current selection family. **See also:** `useSetThemeFamily` **Returns** `string` ---

title: useThemeHistory(): { canRedo: boolean; canUndo: boolean; clear: type(): void; redo: type(): void; undo: type(): void }
text: useThemeHistory(): { canRedo: boolean; canUndo: boolean; clear: type(): void; redo: type(): void; undo: type(): void } Subscribe to the runtime history (undo/redo/canUndo/canRedo/clear). **See also:** `useThemeTimeTravel` **Returns** `{ canRedo: boolean; canUndo: boolean; clear: __type(): void; redo: __type(): void; undo: __type(): void }` ---

title: useThemeLifecycle<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): { on: type<K extends keyof ThemeLifecycleEventMap<ThemeDefinition<string>>>(event: K, listener: type(data: ThemeLifecycleEventMap<T>[K]): void): type(): void }
text: useThemeLifecycle<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): { on: type<K extends keyof ThemeLifecycleEventMap<ThemeDefinition<string>>>(event: K, listener: type(data: ThemeLifecycleEventMap<T>[K]): void): type(): void } Subscribe to runtime lifecycle events (theme changed, mode changed, …). The handler is typed per event name, so `on("beforeThemeChange", ({ next }) => …)` gives you the theme definitions rather than `unknown` — the same precision `runtime.lifecycle.on` has in `@themvora/core`. **See also:** `useTheme` **Returns** `{ on: __type<K extends keyof ThemeLifecycleEventMap<ThemeDefinition<string>>>(event: K, listener: __type(data: ThemeLifecycleEventMap<T>[K]): void): __type(): void }` ---

title: useThemeMode(): ThemeMode
text: useThemeMode(): ThemeMode Subscribe to the current selection mode ("light" | "dark" | "system"). This is the mode the visitor **asked for**. While a sunrise/sunset schedule is running, or while the selection is `"system"`, the appearance on screen can differ from it — use useEffectiveThemeMode to display what is actually applied. **See also:** `useEffectiveThemeMode`, `useSetThemeMode` **Returns** `ThemeMode` ---

title: useThemePacks(): type(pack: ThemePack<any>): void
text: useThemePacks(): type(pack: ThemePack<any>): void Get a function that applies a theme pack to the runtime. **See also:** `useTheme` **Returns** `__type(pack: ThemePack<any>): void` ---

title: useThemeRestore(): type(snapshot: ThemeRuntimeSnapshot): void
text: useThemeRestore(): type(snapshot: ThemeRuntimeSnapshot): void Get a restore function that re-applies a previously captured snapshot. **See also:** `useThemeSnapshot` **Returns** `__type(snapshot: ThemeRuntimeSnapshot): void` ---

title: useThemeRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T>
text: useThemeRuntime<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeRuntime<T> Get the active Themvora runtime from context. Throws when used outside a `ThemeProvider`. Pass the theme tuple element type to type the runtime's store/selection against your registry — any registry works, so the built-in set is used here to keep the example self-contained: ```ts import { getBuiltInThemes } from "@themvora/core"; const themes = getBuiltInThemes(); const runtime = useThemeRuntime<typeof themes[number]>(); ``` **See also:** `ThemeProvider`, `useTheme` **Returns** `ThemeRuntime<T>` ---

title: useThemeSchedule(): ThemeSchedule | null
text: useThemeSchedule(): ThemeSchedule | null Reactive access to the runtime's sunrise/sunset scheduling controller. Requires the runtime to be created with the `scheduled` option (see `ThemeProvider` / `createThemeRuntime`). Returns `null` when the provider has no schedule configured. ```tsx const schedule = useThemeSchedule(); schedule?.enable(); schedule?.disable(); // schedule.enabled, schedule.active, schedule.sunrise, schedule.sunset, // schedule.nextTransition ... re-render reactively. ``` **See also:** `ThemeProvider`, `useTheme` **Returns** `ThemeSchedule | null` The returned controller is a **reactive view**: its state reads come from the subscription below, not from the live controller. That is what makes it safe to render during SSR — the subscription hydrates from EMPTY_THEME_SCHEDULE_STATE, the same snapshot the server rendered, and only adopts the live state after mount. Returning the raw controller instead (which is what this hook used to do, discarding the subscription it had just created) handed consumers the *live* value during the hydration render, so React saw a mismatch against the server HTML and re-rendered the tree. ---

title: useThemeSnapshot(): type(): ThemeRuntimeSnapshot
text: useThemeSnapshot(): type(): ThemeRuntimeSnapshot Get a snapshot function that captures the full runtime state. **See also:** `useThemeRestore` **Returns** `__type(): ThemeRuntimeSnapshot` ---

title: useThemeTimeTravel(): { history: HistoryEntry<ThemeDefinition<string>>[]; jump: type(index: number): void }
text: useThemeTimeTravel(): { history: HistoryEntry<ThemeDefinition<string>>[]; jump: type(index: number): void } Subscribe to the history timeline and get a `jump(index)` function. **See also:** `useThemeHistory` **Returns** `{ history: HistoryEntry<ThemeDefinition<string>>[]; jump: __type(index: number): void }` ---

title: useThemeTokens<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeTokens | undefined
text: useThemeTokens<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): ThemeTokens | undefined Subscribe to the current theme's token groups. **See also:** `useThemeValue` **Returns** `ThemeTokens | undefined` ---

title: useThemeValue<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): T
text: useThemeValue<T extends ThemeDefinition<string>>(): T Subscribe to the current theme definition (re-renders on change). **See also:** `useTheme` **Returns** `T` ---

title: useToggleTheme(): type(): void
text: useToggleTheme(): type(): void Get a stable `toggleTheme` function (flips light ⇄ dark). **See also:** `useThemeMode` **Returns** `__type(): void` ---

title: CreateThemeRootOptions<T extends ThemeDefinition>
text: CreateThemeRootOptions<T extends ThemeDefinition> **Extends** `Omit<ThemeProviderProps<T>, "children" | "runtime">` Options for `createThemeRoot`. Everything `ThemeProvider` accepts (except `children` and `runtime`, which this helper manages), plus: - `container` — the DOM node the root mounts into. - `render` — the application's full composition. Receives the Themvora runtime so dependent library configuration can be derived from it: ```tsx createThemeRoot({ container, defaultTheme: "mint-light", initialMode: "system", render: ({ runtime }) => ( <MuiThemeProvider runtime={runtime}> <App /> </MuiThemeProvider> ), }); ``` Composition belongs in JSX, so arbitrary provider trees (MUI, Chakra, React Query, Redux, Router, …) are fully under the application's control. `MuiThemeProvider` above is the `@themvora/mui` adapter provider, which takes the runtime directly. `render` is the primary (and only) composition mechanism — there is no separate `children` option. | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `adapters` (optional) | `ThemeAdapter<T>[]` | Library adapters installed when the runtime is created. The runtime owns the registry and notifies every adapter whenever the theme changes; it never knows anything about the libraries themselves. | | `broadcast` (optional) | `ThemeSelectionBroadcastAdapter \| null` | Cross-tab broadcast adapter. When omitted, a `BroadcastChannel`-based adapter on channel `"theme-selection"` is created; pass `null` to disable cross-tab sync. | | `container` | `Element \| DocumentFragment` | The DOM node this root mounts into. | | `cssVariables` (optional) | `false \| CSSVariablesOptions` | CSS-variable binding configuration. `false` disables the binding. | | `defaultTheme` (optional) | `ThemeIdentifier<T>` | Theme to activate when no persisted or explicit selection exists. Accepts a **variant** name (`"cocoa-dark"`) or a **family** name (`"cocoa"`); a family resolves to the variant the mode contract picks (see resolveThemeReference). A variant also supplies its own mode unless `initialMode` is given. | | `dom` (optional) | `false \| DOMBindingOptions` | DOM attribute/class binding configuration. `false` disables the binding. | | `initial` (optional) | `InitialThemeResolution<T>` | Explicit initial theme resolution, bypassing default + persistence based resolution. | | `initialFamily` (optional) | `ThemeIdentifier<T>` | The family resolved on first load. When themes are defined with `as const`, this is constrained to the families defined in `themes` (autocomplete). A **variant** name is accepted too and normalised to its family — the variant's mode is used only when `initialMode` is absent, so an explicit mode always wins. | | `initialMode` (optional) | `"system" \| ThemeModes<readonly T[]>` | The mode resolved on first load: `"light" \| "dark" \| "system"`. When themes are defined with `as const`, this is constrained to the modes defined in `themes` plus `"system"` (autocomplete). | | `persistence` (optional) | `ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter \| null` | Persistence adapter for the theme selection. Pass `null` to disable persistence entirely. | | `plugins` (optional) | `ThemePlugin<T>[]` | Runtime plugins installed at creation. | | `prefix` (optional) | `string` | CSS custom property prefix used by the CSS-variables binding. | | `readPersistenceOnInit` (optional) | `boolean` | Whether a persisted selection is read at runtime creation. | | `render` | `__type(context: { runtime: ThemeRuntime<T> }): ReactNode` | Render the application tree. Called with the Themvora runtime so other library providers can derive their configuration from it. | | `scheduled` (optional) | `false \| ScheduledThemeOptions<T>` | Sunrise/sunset scheduling configuration. `false` disables scheduling. | | `storageKey` (optional) | `string` | The `localStorage` key the default persistence adapter reads and writes. | | `themeOverride` (optional) | `ThemeOverride<ThemeIdentifier<T>>` | An explicit theme to apply, outranking a saved selection. Unlike defaultTheme, which is only a fallback, an override is applied even when `localStorage` or a cookie already names another theme — which is what makes "preview this theme" expressible as a prop. It is a one-shot signal, not a controlled selection: it is applied when its value changes, it is never re-asserted on later renders, and it does not write to persistence. See ThemeOverride. | | `themes` (optional) | `readonly T[]` | Initial theme definitions. Duplicate names are dropped (first wins). When omitted, the registry starts empty. | | `transition` (optional) | `boolean \| ThemeTransitionOptions` | Transition configuration. `true` enables transitions with defaults, `false` disables them, and an object provides explicit options. | | `view` (optional) | `Window` | The `window` to bind to. Defaults to the global `window` when available; omit (or pass `undefined`) in SSR environments. | ---

A **variant** name is accepted too and normalised to its family — the variant's mode is used only when `initialMode` is absent, so an explicit mode always wins. | | `initialMode` (optional) | `"system" \| ThemeModes<readonly T[]>` | The mode resolved on first load: `"light" \| "dark" \| "system"`. When omitted, the provider creates an internal runtime (owning `dom` and `cssVariables` itself) and destroys it on unmount. | | `scheduled` (optional) | `false \| ScheduledThemeOptions<T>` | Sunrise/sunset scheduling configuration. `false` disables scheduling. | | `storageKey` (optional) | `string` | The `localStorage` key the default persistence adapter reads and writes. | | `themeOverride` (optional) | `ThemeOverride<ThemeIdentifier<T>>` | An explicit theme to apply, outranking a saved selection. title: ThemeScopeProps
text: ThemeScopeProps Props for the ThemeScope component. Accepts `theme` (exact selection), `family`/`mode` (family-based selection), `themes` (scope-local definitions), and `transition`. | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `children` | `ReactNode` | The scoped subtree. | | `className` (optional) | `string` | Additional class applied to the scope wrapper element. | | `family` (optional) | `string` | Theme family for the scoped subtree. When `mode` is omitted the scope follows the provider's current mode (light/dark/system). | | `mode` (optional) | `ThemeMode` | Mode for a family-based scope. Optional — defaults to the provider's current mode so `family="plum"` flips light/dark with the page. | | `style` (optional) | `CSSProperties` | Inline styles applied to the scope wrapper element. Merged over the resolved theme variables, so user styles win on conflicts. | | `theme` (optional) | `string` | Exact theme name, family name, or a `{ family, mode }`-style object. When `family`/`mode` are also passed, `theme` wins (it's the explicit selection). Omit to follow the global selection inside a new boundary. | | `themes` (optional) | `readonly ThemeDefinition<string>[]` | Local theme definitions for genuinely isolated components. Resolved FIRST (they shadow same-named parent themes), then the provider's registry falls back — no second runtime is created. | | `transition` (optional) | `boolean \| ThemeTransitionOptions` | Transition for this scope's own theme changes. `undefined` inherits the `<ThemeProvider/>` transition, `false` disables it, `true` inherits, and an object is merged over the provider's config (local keys win). | ---

title: ThemeScrollbarAppearance
text: ThemeScrollbarAppearance **Extends** `Pick<OverlayScrollbarOptions, "arrows" | "thickness" | "hoverThickness" | "radius" | "minThumbSize" | "offset" | "trackOpacity" | "thumbOpacity" | "zIndex" | "duration" | "animationDuration" | "thumbColor" | "trackColor" | "activeThumbColor" | "thumbHoverColor">` Appearance — the look/size of every strip. | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `activeThumbColor` (optional) | `string` | Custom thumb color while the user is dragging it. When set, overrides the theme-derived active color. Default `undefined` (uses `thumbColor` or theme-derived). | | `animationDuration` (optional) | `number` | rAF easing time constant (ms) for smooth thumb travel. Default `180`. | | `arrows` (optional) | `boolean` | Show the up/down (or left/right) navigation buttons like native browser scrollbars. Clicking scrolls a step; holding repeats. Default `true`. | | `duration` (optional) | `number` | CSS transition duration (ms) for thickness/opacity/color. Default `250`. | | `hoverThickness` (optional) | `number` | Thumb thickness while hovered / dragged — only used when `hoverExpand` is true. Default `thickness + 4`. | | `minThumbSize` (optional) | `number` | Minimum thumb travel size. Default `32`. | | `offset` (optional) | `ScrollbarOffset` | Distance from the container edges to the rail. A number insets every side equally; an object sets individual sides, with omitted sides defaulting to the component default (`4`, except `left`, which defaults to `0`). `0` is a value, not "unset": a side set to `0` gets no inset at all and the rail sits flush against that edge, like a native scrollbar. That holds for every host, **including the page/window scrollbar** — `offset: 0` puts the document rail hard against the viewport edge rather than a few px in. The rail follows the writing direction (a vertical rail sits on the inline-end edge), so in RTL it uses `left`. The content is kept clear of the rail by the native scrollbar gutter the component reserves, not by extra padding, so no content width is taken and nothing reflows. | | `radius` (optional) | `number` | Thumb corner radius in px. Default `999`. | | `thickness` (optional) | `number` | Resting thumb thickness (width for vertical, height for horizontal). Default `8`. | | `thumbColor` (optional) | `string` | Custom thumb color (any CSS color string). When set, overrides the theme-derived color. Default `undefined` (theme-derived). | | `thumbHoverColor` (optional) | `string` | Custom thumb color while hovered. When set, overrides the theme-derived hover color. Default `undefined` (uses `thumbColor` or theme-derived). | | `thumbOpacity` (optional) | `number` | Thumb opacity while visible. Default `0.7`. | | `trackColor` (optional) | `string` | Custom track color (any CSS color string). When set, overrides the theme-derived color. Default `undefined` (theme-derived). | | `trackOpacity` (optional) | `number` | Track strip opacity (0 = invisible). Default `0.25`. | | `zIndex` (optional) | `number` | Z-index for the overlay strips. Defaults to the tracked container's own `z-index` (so the scrollbar stays inside its container's stacking order — e.g. a rail inside a sticky header never floats above that header). Containers that declare no z-index get `0`; the document scrollbar gets `55`, which is above typical sticky headers (50) and below full-screen modal backdrops (60) — the window bar is chrome, so a fixed header must not hide it. Overriding lets you force scrollbars above fixed headers/modals if you need to. | ---

title: ThemeScrollbarBehavior
text: ThemeScrollbarBehavior **Extends** `Pick<OverlayScrollbarOptions, "autoHide" | "hoverExpand" | "draggable" | "clickToJump" | "smooth" | "overscroll" | "axes" | "touch" | "dir">` Behavior — how the overlay scrolls and hides. | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `autoHide` (optional) | `boolean` | Fade the thumb/track out while idle. Default `true` (macOS-style). | | `autoHideDelay` (optional) | `number` | Idle (ms) before a revealed strip fades out. Default `900`. | | `axes` (optional) | `ScrollbarAxis[]` | Which axes to render. Defaults to both. | | `clickToJump` (optional) | `boolean` | Clicking the empty track scrolls smoothly to that position. Default `true`. | | `dir` (optional) | `"ltr" \| "rtl" \| "auto"` | Text direction. Defaults to the resolved `dir` / CSS `direction`. | | `draggable` (optional) | `boolean` | Allow dragging the thumb to scroll. Default `true`. | | `hoverExpand` (optional) | `boolean` | Grow the strip on hover / drag. Default `false` (thickness stays constant so the scrollbar never shifts while scrolling). | | `overscroll` (optional) | `boolean` | Subtly compress the thumb at the scroll boundaries (rubber-band feel). Default `true`. | | `smooth` (optional) | `boolean` | Use rAF-lerped (eased) thumb motion instead of a hard snap. Default `true`. | | `touch` (optional) | `boolean` | Native (touch) devices: keep native scrollbars by default. Pass `true` to force the overlay on coarse-pointer devices. Default `false`. | ---

title: ThemeScrollbarIcons
text: ThemeScrollbarIcons Arrow button icons (any `ReactNode` — JSX, inline SVG, text, …). | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `arrow` (optional) | `ReactNode` | Icon for all arrow directions (individual overrides win). | | `down` (optional) | `ReactNode` | Icon for the "scroll down" button. | | `left` (optional) | `ReactNode` | Icon for the "scroll left" button. | | `right` (optional) | `ReactNode` | Icon for the "scroll right" button. | | `size` (optional) | `number` | Arrow glyph size, in CSS px, for all four directions. Clamped to the button's usable area, so it never overflows a thin rail. Omit to keep the default sizing. | | `up` (optional) | `ReactNode` | Icon for the "scroll up" button. | ---

title: ThemeScrollbarProps
text: ThemeScrollbarProps Props for the ThemeScrollbar overlay component. Options are grouped into `behavior`, `appearance`, and `icons` — but every option is also accepted as a flat, top-level prop (flat props win over the grouped ones). | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `appearance` (optional) | `ThemeScrollbarAppearance` | The look and size of every rail. | | `behavior` (optional) | `ThemeScrollbarBehavior` | How the overlay scrolls and hides. | | `children` (optional) | `ReactNode` | Renders nothing visible; kept for API symmetry (the overlay is created against the runtime, not the component tree). It is deliberately ignored by option resolution and change detection. | | `icons` (optional) | `ThemeScrollbarIcons` | Arrow button icons, plus the shared glyph size. | | `scope` (optional) | `ThemeScrollbarScope` | Which scrollable containers the overlay tracks. | ---

title: ThemeScrollbarScope
text: ThemeScrollbarScope Scope — which scrollable containers the overlay tracks. This decides *where* the scrollbar appears, not how it looks, so it is its own group rather than part of `appearance`. | Member | Type | Description | | ------ | ---- | ----------- | | `exclude` (optional) | `string[] \| null` | Skip these containers when tracking. | | `include` (optional) | `string[] \| null` | Scope the overlay to these containers (document is always tracked). | ---

title: Related docs
text: Related docs - [Families & Modes](/core-concepts) — A selection is a family (which palette) plus a mode (light/dark/system); every framework exposes the same read/write surface for it. - [Theme Discovery & Overrides](/advanced-features) — A provider exposes exactly the themes it was given — grouped by family, with variants and resolved tokens — and accepts an explicit one-shot themeOverride that outranks a saved selection. - [Runtime](/architecture) — One runtime per app owns the store, selection, registry, history, lifecycle and adapters; every framework binding is a thin view over it. - [ThemeScope](/scoped-theme) — Apply a different family/mode (or a local theme definition) to a subtree, with scoped CSS variables and pre-paint support. - [Persistence](/persistence) — Persist the selection across reloads and requests, with fingerprint validation, storage adapters and theme migrations. - [Theme generation](/theme-studio) — Generate a complete, accessible light/dark theme pair from a single seed color, ready to drop into the runtime. - [Plugins](/plugins) — Extend the runtime through a first-class plugin manager and adapter registry; theme packs install ready-made behaviour. - [Custom scrollbar](/custom-scrollbar) — Themed overlay scrollbars that match the active theme and pre-paint before hydration. - [DevTools](/devtools) — Inspect and drive the live runtime from a panel: adapters, history, snapshots and performance entries. - [React](/framework-guides/react) — the framework integration

title: @themvora/remix/react-router
text: @themvora/remix/react-router React Router Framework Mode entry point. React Router's root route owns the document and runs a loader for each request, which is the same contract this package already implements for Remix v2. The runtime layer is framework-neutral — it uses React and the standard `Request` object, never a `@remix-run/*` import — so the same exports apply to both targets. This entry point exists so a React Router project can name its integration explicitly: ```ts import { createThemeDocument } from "@themvora/remix/react-router"; ``` `createThemeDocument` accepts one static configuration and returns `resolveInitial(request)`, a `Document` component that owns the blocking head script, `<html>` shell and runtime provider, and a standalone `Provider`. Remix v2 consumers can keep importing from `@themvora/remix`. > Generated from `packages/remix/src` by `apps/docs/scripts/generate-api-reference.mjs`. Do not edit by hand — run `pnpm --filter @themvora/docs api:generate`.

title: Functions
