title: COMPONENTCSS
text: COMPONENTCSS The document-level stylesheet for the built-in elements. Exported so consumers can inspect it, and so the injection is testable without parsing the DOM. `string` ---

title: COMPONENTSTYLEID
text: COMPONENTSTYLEID The `id` of the injected stylesheet element. `"themvora-elements-style"` ---

title: PREPAINTSCROLLBARCSS
text: PREPAINTSCROLLBARCSS The CSS that hides native scrollbars while `tv-scrollbar` is present on `<html>`. Shared by the client bootstrap script and Next's SSR output so both apply identical rules. The bar is painted invisible while KEEPING its space, so the gutter that keeps content clear of the rail exists from the first frame (no load-time layout shift). Two groups: - The PAGE / window scrollbar is collapsed (`scrollbar-width: none`). Its rail auto-hides, so a reserved empty strip at the window edge would read as a missing scrollbar; the standard property also overrides the WebKit sizing below, so the page never reserves one. - INNER scroll containers keep an invisible, space-occupying scrollbar. It is sized through `::-webkit-scrollbar` (not only `scrollbar-color`) because styling those pseudo-elements is what takes Chromium/Safari off OVERLAY scrollbars — so the gutter is reserved on macOS too, where the native path would take no space. The space appears only while the container actually scrolls, exactly like a native `overflow: auto` bar. - Engines without WebKit pseudo-elements (Firefox) get the same reserve through the standard properties. `string` ---

title: THEMEREADYEVENT
text: THEMEREADYEVENT Dispatched once by `<themvora-provider>` after its runtime exists and its first theme has been applied. Custom elements are upgraded in document order, so a provider normally initializes before its descendants. This event covers the remaining case — an element defined or inserted after the provider — and the reconnection case, where a provider that was removed and re-added creates a *new* runtime. The payload carries no detail: read state from the runtime (`getProviderRuntime(providerEl)`). `"theme-ready"` ---

title: THEMESCHANGEEVENT
text: THEMESCHANGEEVENT Dispatched by `<themvora-provider>` after an attribute change replaced its theme catalog. A catalog change can leave the active theme untouched — the runtime preserves a selection that is still valid — so `store.subscribe()` alone cannot tell a consumer that the set of available themes moved. This event reports exactly that, once per applied catalog change. It is not dispatched on initialization; THEME_READY_EVENT covers that. `"themes-change"` ---

title: Related docs
text: Related docs - [Families & Modes](/core-concepts) — A selection is a family (which palette) plus a mode (light/dark/system); every framework exposes the same read/write surface for it. - [Theme Discovery & Overrides](/advanced-features) — A provider exposes exactly the themes it was given — grouped by family, with variants and resolved tokens — and accepts an explicit one-shot themeOverride that outranks a saved selection. - [Runtime](/architecture) — One runtime per app owns the store, selection, registry, history, lifecycle and adapters; every framework binding is a thin view over it. - [ThemeScope](/scoped-theme) — Apply a different family/mode (or a local theme definition) to a subtree, with scoped CSS variables and pre-paint support. - [Theme generation](/theme-studio) — Generate a complete, accessible light/dark theme pair from a single seed color, ready to drop into the runtime. - [Zero-flash bootstrap](/zero-flash) — Paint the correct theme on the first frame: a blocking script plus server-resolved initial state, with a Vite plugin for SPA builds. - [Custom scrollbar](/custom-scrollbar) — Themed overlay scrollbars that match the active theme and pre-paint before hydration. - [DevTools](/devtools) — Inspect and drive the live runtime from a panel: adapters, history, snapshots and performance entries. - [Web Components](/framework-guides/web) — the framework integration

title: One Runtime
text: One Runtime The heart of the library is a single framework-agnostic runtime that wires the store, registry, selection, persistence, broadcast, DOM bindings, history, lifecycle, and plugins together. ```ts import { createThemeRuntime } from "@themvora/core"; const runtime = createThemeRuntime({ themes: getBuiltInThemes(), // default: built-in themes defaultTheme, // fallback theme name initialMode, // "light" | "dark" | "system" initialFamily, // e.g. "plum" persistence, // localStorage adapter by default broadcast, // BroadcastChannel adapter by default dom, // DOM attribute binding options (false to disable) cssVariables, // CSS variable binding options (false to disable) transition, // smooth transitions scheduled, // sunset/sunrise auto switching plugins, // lifecycle + token transform plugins }); ``` Once created, the runtime immediately: 1. Resolves the initial theme from `defaultTheme` / `initialMode` / `initialFamily` (or persisted selection). 2. Registers every theme in the registry. 3. Wires the store, selection controller, persistence, and broadcast. 4. Applies DOM attributes and CSS variables via the bindings.

title: Runtime API
text: Runtime API Every feature hangs off the `runtime` object. Each entry below shows the property and a minimal usage snippet.

title: runtime.store
text: runtime.store The reactive store holding the **active theme**. `get()` reads it, `set()` replaces it, `subscribe()` reacts to changes, and `batch()` coalesces multiple writes into a single notification. ```ts const theme = runtime.store.get(); // current theme const unsubscribe = runtime.store.subscribe((t) => { console.log("theme changed:", t.name); }); runtime.store.set(myTheme); // apply immediately runtime.store.batch(() => { // coalesce several writes runtime.store.set(a); runtime.store.set(b); }); unsubscribe(); ```

title: runtime.registry
text: runtime.registry Every registered theme, powering dynamic theming. Register, unregister, replace, look up, and group themes by family. ```ts runtime.registry.register(myTheme); // add a theme runtime.registry.registerMany([a, b, c]); // add several runtime.registry.unregister("plum-dark"); // remove by name runtime.registry.replace("plum-dark", newDark); // swap in place runtime.registry.get("plum-light"); // find by name runtime.registry.has("plum-light"); // boolean runtime.registry.list(); // all themes runtime.registry.getFamilies(); // ["default", "plum", ...] runtime.registry.getThemesByFamily("plum"); // plums only ```

title: runtime.selection
text: runtime.selection Mode + family resolution. Handles persistence and broadcast for you, and keeps the store in sync. ```ts runtime.selection.setMode("dark"); // "light" | "dark" | "system" runtime.selection.setFamily("mint"); // switch palette runtime.selection.toggleTheme(); // flip light <-> dark runtime.selection.getSelection(); // { mode: "dark", family: "mint" } ```

title: runtime.themes
text: runtime.themes A read-only list of all registered themes — handy for rendering pickers, galleries, or walking families. ```ts for (const theme of runtime.themes) { console.log(theme.name, theme.meta?.family, theme.meta?.mode); } const plums = runtime.themes.filter( (t) => t.meta?.family === "plum", ); ```

title: runtime.update(tokens)
text: runtime.update(tokens) **Live theme editing**: merge partial tokens into the active theme and re-apply. The perfect primitive for theme studios and design-time tweaking. ```ts runtime.update({ colors: { primary: "#6366f1", accent: { hover: "#4f46e5" }, }, radius: { lg: "16px" }, }); ```

title: runtime.use(pack)
text: runtime.use(pack) Install a **theme pack** at runtime. A pack is a named bundle of themes; every theme in it is stamped with a `pack:<name>` tag. ```ts runtime.use({ name: "brand", themes: [ { name: "apple-light", meta: { family: "apple", mode: "light" }, tokens }, { name: "apple-dark", meta: { family: "apple", mode: "dark" }, tokens }, ], }); ```

title: runtime.batch(cb)
text: runtime.batch(cb) Run a callback atomically — intermediate state changes are suppressed until the callback finishes. ```ts runtime.batch(() => { runtime.update({ colors: { primary: "#000" } }); runtime.selection.setMode("dark"); runtime.selection.setFamily("plum"); }); // subscribers fire exactly once, with the final theme ```

title: runtime.snapshot() / runtime.restore(snapshot)
text: runtime.snapshot() / runtime.restore(snapshot) Serialize the full runtime state — theme, selection, history, and registry — and restore it later. Ideal for time travel and demo replay. ```ts const snapshot = runtime.snapshot(); // { theme, selection, history: [], registry: { themes } } // ... make changes ... runtime.restore(snapshot); // back to exactly how it was ```

title: runtime.history
text: runtime.history Built-in undo/redo, capped at 50 steps by default. Records full theme snapshots with timestamps. ```ts runtime.history.undo(); // step back runtime.history.redo(); // step forward runtime.history.jump(2); // jump to any point in time runtime.history.canUndo(); // boolean runtime.history.canRedo(); // boolean runtime.history.getHistory(); // HistoryEntry[] { theme, timestamp } runtime.history.clear(); // wipe the timeline ```

title: runtime.lifecycle
text: runtime.lifecycle A typed event bus for the theme pipeline. Subscribe with `on()` (returns an unsubscribe function) and react to typed payloads. ```ts const off = runtime.lifecycle.on("beforeThemeChange", ({ current, next }) => { console.log(`leaving ${current.name}, entering ${next.name}`); }); runtime.lifecycle.on("afterApply", ({ theme }) => { document.title = `Theme — ${theme.name}`; }); off(); // unsubscribe ```

title: runtime.destroy()
text: runtime.destroy() Full teardown: unsubscribes every listener, removes DOM/CSS bindings, closes the broadcast channel, and clears registry, history, and lifecycle. ```ts runtime.destroy(); ```

title: Layers
text: Layers - **Store** — minimal reactive state holding the active theme. `get`, `set`, `subscribe`, `batch`. - **Registry** — every registered theme, powering dynamic theming, theme packs, and family lookups. - **Selection** — mode + family resolution with persistence & broadcast, driving the store. - **Adapters** — CSS variables, DOM attributes, system theme, scoped themes, scheduled themes, transitions. - **Resolvers** — token references, expressions, and derived colors resolved lazily at runtime. - **Plugins** — hook into the lifecycle and transform tokens; official plugins ship for persistence, history, animations, accessibility, scheduling, debugging, and devtools. - **Bootstrap** — blocking inline script for zero flash of incorrect theme, plus a `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` fallback.

title: How a Theme Change Flows Through the Runtime
text: How a Theme Change Flows Through the Runtime ``` setFamily("plum") → selection.setFamily() → persistence.set({ mode, family }) // save → broadcast.post({ mode, family }) // sync other tabs → resolve theme for family + mode → lifecycle.emit("beforeThemeChange") → plugins.onBeforeThemeChange → store.set(theme) → lifecycle.emit("afterThemeChange") → DOM binding: data-theme, data-theme-mode, .dark class → CSS variables binding: --theme-* variables → lifecycle.emit("beforeApply" / "afterApply") → history records a snapshot ```

title: Bootstrap: Zero Flash of Wrong Theme
text: Bootstrap: Zero Flash of Wrong Theme Before any JS runs, a blocking inline script reads the persisted selection, resolves the effective mode (`system` → `prefers-color-scheme`), and applies CSS variables + DOM effects. ```ts import { createThemeBootstrapScript, buildThemeCssMap, getBuiltInThemes, } from "@themvora/core"; // buildThemeCssMap/createThemeBootstrapScript take the registry explicitly; // the built-in set is a valid registry, so no theme file is needed. const themes = getBuiltInThemes(); const cssMap = buildThemeCssMap(themes); // name + family:mode → variables const script = createThemeBootstrapScript({ themes, defaultTheme: "light", initialMode: "system", storageKey: "theme-selection", prefix: "theme-", }); // inject `script` into <head> before first paint ``` The `@themvora/next` provider does all of this automatically — it reads cookies on the server, renders the resolved theme, and emits the blocking script.

title: Independent packages
text: Independent packages Themvora is a set of independently installable packages, not a single bundle: - Installing a framework integration (`@themvora/react`, `@themvora/vue`, `@themvora/svelte`, `@themvora/solid`, `@themvora/angular`, `@themvora/next`, `@themvora/nuxt`, `@themvora/astro`, `@themvora/remix`) installs that binding and the `@themvora/core` runtime it declares as a normal dependency — no unrelated framework packages and no component-library adapters. The guides still install core explicitly so the runtime version is visible in your own manifest. - Adapters are separate packages, installed only when explicitly wanted. Their framework wrappers live behind subpaths (`/react`, `/vue`, `/svelte`, `/solid`, `/angular`) with optional peers. - `@themvora/core` has zero runtime dependencies.

title: Accessibility First Theming
text: --- title: "Accessibility-first theming: contrast checks and CVD simulation" date: 2026-07-07 description: "How Themvora's accessibility toolkit keeps themes readable — WCAG contrast ratios, full-theme audits and color-vision-deficiency simulation — all at runtime." tags: accessibility, wcag, contrast, cvd --- A gorgeous palette that fails WCAG contrast is a bug, not a design choice. Theme Kit ships a runtime accessibility toolkit so you can catch contrast failures and color-vision problems *before* your users do.

title: Contrast ratios, live
text: Contrast ratios, live `getContrastRatio(foreground, background)` returns the WCAG 2.x ratio, and `validateThemeContrast(theme)` audits every semantic token pair against the AA/AAA thresholds: ```ts import { getContrastRatio, validateThemeContrast } from "@themvora/core"; getContrastRatio("#111111", "#ffffff"); // → 19.56 const audit = validateThemeContrast(theme); // full AA/AAA audit ```

title: Auditing a whole theme
text: Auditing a whole theme `validateThemeContrast` walks every semantic token pair — text-on-surface, text-on-primary, borders, and more — and returns a structured report of failures: ```ts import { validateThemeContrast } from "@themvora/core"; const result = validateThemeContrast(theme, { themes: [theme] }); // { valid: false, checks: [{ foregroundToken, backgroundToken, // foreground, background, ratio, passesAANormal, passesAALarge, // passesAAANormal, passesAAALarge }] } ```

title: Color-vision deficiency simulation
text: Color-vision deficiency simulation `simulateCVD(color, type)` converts a color as seen with protanopia, deuteranopia or tritanopia, and `simulateThemeForCVD` does the same for an entire theme. Combined with the runtime, you can preview *exactly* what a user with CVD sees: ```ts import { simulateThemeForCVD } from "@themvora/core"; const deuteranopic = simulateThemeForCVD(theme, "deuteranopia"); ```

title: Built-in accessibility profiles
text: Built-in accessibility profiles For teams that need guaranteed contrast, Themvora ships `getAccessibilityProfiles` with **High Contrast** and **Large Text** presets — drop them in as theme packs and let users opt in. Every feature above is demonstrated live on `/accessibility`, where you can check any two colors, audit the current theme, and apply a CVD-simulated theme to this very site.

title: Multi Window Sync
text: --- title: "Keeping every tab in sync: multi-window theming without a backend" date: 2026-07-21 description: "How Themvora synchronizes theme changes across tabs and windows using BroadcastChannel, SharedWorker and StorageEvent — with a graceful cascade of fallbacks." tags: sync, broadcastchannel, sharedworker, storageevent --- When a user flips to dark mode in one tab, every other open tab of your app should follow instantly — no refresh, no polling, no backend. Themvora ships three transport strategies and a cascade that picks the best one available.

title: The cascade
text: The cascade `createMultiWindowSync()` probes the environment and selects the first transport that works: 1. **BroadcastChannel** — the modern, dedicated channel for same-origin messaging. Zero setup, instant delivery. 2. **SharedWorker** — a shared thread all tabs talk to. Useful when you also want cross-tab coordination beyond theming. 3. **StorageEvent** — the classic `localStorage` + `storage` event pair. Works everywhere, including older browsers. ```ts import { createThemeRuntime, createMultiWindowSync } from "@themvora/core"; const runtime = createThemeRuntime({}); const sync = createMultiWindowSync({ channelName: "my-app-themes", }); // Wire incoming selections into the runtime sync.subscribe((selection) => { runtime.selection.setMode(selection.mode); runtime.selection.setFamily(selection.family); }); // Broadcast a local change to every other tab sync.post({ mode: "dark", family: "slate" }); ``` Each selection change is broadcast to the other windows, which apply it locally. The `createThemeSelectionBroadcast()` adapter does the same for raw selection updates when you only care about family + mode.

title: Why this matters
text: Why this matters Theme state is *global UI state*. If one tab shows light and another shows dark, your app feels broken. Multi-window sync turns theming into a true single-user-interface across the whole browsing session — and it's the same pattern the docs site's Playground demo shows with a real second tab.

title: Caveats
text: Caveats - BroadcastChannel and SharedWorker require **secure contexts** (HTTPS or `localhost`). - StorageEvent fires in *other* tabs, not the one that wrote — which is exactly what we want. - Keep the channel name stable across your app; a mismatch silently disables sync.

title: Persistence Sync
text: --- title: "Persistence and multi-window sync, explained" date: 2026-08-18 description: "How Themvora remembers the user's choice across reloads and keeps every tab in sync — persistence adapters, BroadcastChannel, SharedWorker, and the StorageEvent fallback." tags: persistence, sync, adapters --- Two things make theming feel like it's actually "saved": the theme survives a reload, and it stays consistent across tabs. Both are harder than they look — and both are solved by small, replaceable adapters in Themvora.

title: Persistence: the selection outlives the page
text: Persistence: the selection outlives the page The runtime persists the *selection* — `{ mode, family }` — not the theme definition: ```ts import { createThemeRuntime, createPersistencePlugin } from "@themvora/core"; const runtime = createThemeRuntime({ plugins: [createPersistencePlugin()], // writes { mode, family } to localStorage under "theme-selection" }); ``` On the next load, the runtime reads the saved selection and resolves the theme before first paint. The default persistence adapter is a thin wrapper over `localStorage` with a `storage` event subscription, so the docs site itself survives a hard refresh with your exact family and mode.

title: Custom keys and storage
text: Custom keys and storage Pass `key` to avoid collisions when multiple apps share an origin, or swap the underlying storage: ```ts createPersistencePlugin({ key: "my-app-theme" }); ``` Because persistence is an adapter (`get`/`set`/`remove`/`subscribe`), you can back it with `sessionStorage`, cookies, IndexedDB, or a server round-trip — the runtime doesn't care.

title: Multi-window sync: every tab follows
text: Multi-window sync: every tab follows Two tabs each run their own runtime. When tab A flips to dark, tab B should too. Themvora ships `createMultiWindowSync()`, which picks the best available transport: ```ts import { createMultiWindowSync } from "@themvora/core"; const sync = createMultiWindowSync({ prefer: "auto" }); sync.subscribe((selection) => { runtime.selection.setMode(selection.mode); runtime.selection.setFamily(selection.family); }); sync.post({ mode: "dark", family: "slate" }); ``` The transport cascade is: 1. **BroadcastChannel** — the modern same-origin channel. Instant, zero storage writes. 2. **SharedWorker** — a shared thread every tab talks to; useful when you also coordinate beyond theming. 3. **StorageEvent** — the classic `localStorage` + `storage` event pair; works in every browser that supports localStorage.

title: Pairing persistence and sync
text: Pairing persistence and sync They solve different problems and work together: - **Persistence** survives reloads — it writes the selection to storage and reads it at bootstrap. - **Sync** propagates changes *while the app is running* — other open tabs update instantly. A theme change in one tab is written to storage (persistence) and broadcast to other tabs (sync) in the same tick. A tab that opens later reads the persisted selection; tabs that were already open get the live update.

title: Replaceable by design
text: Replaceable by design Both adapters implement tiny interfaces, so they're drop-in replaceable: - `ThemeSelectionPersistenceAdapter` — `get/set/remove/subscribe` over `{ mode, family }` - `ThemeSelectionBroadcastAdapter` — `post/subscribe/destroy` over the same selection shape Roll your own (a server-backed persistence adapter, an iFrame messaging sync) and pass it straight to the runtime options `persistence` and `broadcast`. The rest of the library — transitions, SSR bootstrap, scoped themes — composes on top without knowing which adapters you chose. Try it on this site: open the docs in two tabs, switch families in one, and watch the other follow instantly.

title: Scoped Themes
text: --- title: "Scoped themes: isolate a subtree without leaving the runtime" date: 2026-08-17 description: "Scope a theme to a single region — a video player, an embedded widget, a legacy component — with ThemeScope, the themvora-scope element, or an imperative binding." tags: scoped, islands, advanced --- Global theming is the common case, but some regions of a page need their own theme: a video player with a dark chrome on a light page, an embedded widget from another team, a code editor with a custom palette. Scoped themes give you that island without spinning up a second runtime.

title: The scope primitive
text:
The scope primitive Every framework exposes a `ThemeScope` that wraps a subtree and themes only it: ```tsx import { ThemeScope } from "@themvora/react"; export function VideoPlayerPage() { return (

Watch

{/* Dark chrome no matter what the page theme is */}
); } ``` Everything inside the scope resolves `plum-dark`; everything outside keeps following the page theme. The scope renders a boundary, applies scoped CSS variables inline, and cleans up when it unmounts.

title: Scope by family and mode
text: Scope by family and mode You don't have to pin an exact theme — a scope can follow a family while staying in sync with the page's light/dark mode: ```tsx <ThemeScope family="plum"> {/* Plum-light in light mode, plum-dark in dark mode */} <BrandedWidget /> </ThemeScope> ``` Or you can pin `family` and `mode` together. The scoped selection is resolved against the same registry as the global one, so everything stays consistent.

title: Imperative scoping for raw elements
text:
Imperative scoping for raw elements When you don't control JSX — a video player, legacy DOM, or an element from another library — scope the element directly: ```ts import { createScopedThemeBinding, getBuiltInThemes } from "@themvora/core"; const player = document.getElementById("player")!; // createScopedThemeBinding takes the registry positionally; the built-in set // is a valid registry, so no theme file is needed. const themes = getBuiltInThemes(); const binding = createScopedThemeBinding(themes, player, "plum-dark"); // Later: update the selection in place, or tear down binding.update("mint-light"); binding.destroy(); ``` Web Components get a declarative element instead: ```html

Scoped to plum-dark

 ```

title: Local themes for genuinely isolated islands
text: Local themes for genuinely isolated islands Sometimes a region needs themes that don't exist in the global registry — a component that ships its own palette. The `themes` prop layers local definitions on top: ```tsx import { defineTheme } from "@themvora/core"; const compactTheme = defineTheme({ name: "compact-light", meta: { family: "compact", mode: "light" }, tokens: { /* ... */ }, }); <ThemeScope themes={[compactTheme]} theme="compact-light"> <Toolbar /> </ThemeScope> ``` Local themes resolve first, then the provider's registry falls back — no second runtime is created. A late-loaded theme pack can update the scope in place via `setLocalThemes`.

title: Nesting scopes
text: Nesting scopes Scopes nest naturally: the inner scope wins within its boundary, and each scope inherits transitions from its parent scope or the provider. ```tsx <ThemeScope theme="mint-light"> <Dashboard /> <ThemeScope theme="plum-dark"> <CodeEditor /> </ThemeScope> </ThemeScope> ``` The page, the dashboard, and the editor can all show different themes at once — each with its own scope boundary, variables, and transition timing.

title: When to use scopes
text: When to use scopes - **Embedded/legacy content** you can't restyle - **Video players, maps, editors** that ship their own dark theme - **Multi-tenant widgets** that should look like their tenant, not the host - **Demo/showcase surfaces** that must stay on-brand regardless of the app theme Scopes keep those islands isolated from the global theme — while still participating in the same runtime, transition engine, and persistence layer.

title: Semantic Tokens
text: --- title: "Semantic tokens: why you theme meanings, not components" date: 2026-08-16 description: "Themvora themes semantic tokens — background, foreground, primary, muted — instead of component classes. Here's why that scales to every framework and every component library." tags: tokens, design-systems, concepts --- Component-based theming asks "what color is a button?" and then writes `.button { background: #6366f1 }`. That works until you have three button variants, a dark mode, and a second component library to theme. Semantic tokens flip the question: theme *meanings*, and let every component resolve its own look from them.

title: Tokens, not hex values
text: Tokens, not hex values Instead of hard-coding colors into components, you define a small set of semantic meanings: ```ts import { defineTheme } from "@themvora/core"; export const lightTheme = defineTheme({ name: "app-light", meta: { family: "app", mode: "light" }, tokens: { colors: { background: "#fafafa", foreground: "#18181b", card: "#ffffff", cardForeground: "#18181b", popover: "#ffffff", popoverForeground: "#18181b", primary: "#6366f1", primaryForeground: "#ffffff", secondary: "#f4f4f5", secondaryForeground: "#18181b", accent: "#f4f4f5", accentForeground: "#18181b", muted: "#f4f4f5", mutedForeground: "#71717a", destructive: "#ef4444", destructiveForeground: "#ffffff", success: "#16a34a", successForeground: "#ffffff", border: "#e4e4e7", input: "#e4e4e7", ring: "#6366f1", }, radius: { lg: "12px" }, }, }); ``` Components consume the meaning — `primary`, `muted`, `border` — never a literal color. When the theme changes, every consumer updates together.

title: The cascade: tokens → CSS variables → components
text:
The cascade: tokens → CSS variables → components At runtime Themvora flattens tokens into CSS custom properties: ``` --theme-color-background: #fafafa; --theme-color-primary: #6366f1; --theme-color-mutedForeground: #71717a; --theme-radius-lg: 12px; ``` Your components reference the variables (or the framework hook), so the whole tree re-themes in one DOM update: ```tsx import { useThemeTokens } from "@themvora/react"; function Card() { const tokens = useThemeTokens(); return (
{children}
); } ```

title: Why meanings scale
text: Why meanings scale - **One theme, many surfaces** — `primary` means "the main action color" everywhere: buttons, links, focus rings, active states. - **Dark mode for free** — swap the token set, not the components. A component written against tokens renders correctly in both modes with zero changes. - **Framework-agnostic** — the same tokens feed React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Web Components, and CSS-only Tailwind projects. The runtime is the shared contract. - **Component-library adapters** — Themvora can map tokens into MUI, Chakra, Ant Design, shadcn/ui, Bootstrap, and more, because those libraries already accept token-ish inputs.

title: Extending tokens safely
text: Extending tokens safely Tokens are plain objects, so they compose: ```ts import { extendTheme } from "@themvora/core"; // Add a brand family without touching the base export const brandLight = extendTheme("app-light", { meta: { family: "brand", mode: "light" }, colors: { primary: "#0ea5e9", // override just what you need }, }); ``` `extendTheme` merges deeply — nested `colors`, `radius`, `shadows`, and the `code` block all inherit unless overridden. You can layer a family, a mode, or a brand on top of a base theme.

title: Semantic tokens and accessibility
text: Semantic tokens and accessibility Because contrast pairs are *semantic* (`foreground` on `background`, `primary` on `primaryForeground`), Themvora can audit them: ```ts import { getBuiltInThemes, validateThemeContrast } from "@themvora/core"; // Pass a theme list to resolve `extends` chains before auditing. const result = validateThemeContrast(theme, { themes: getBuiltInThemes() }); // { valid, checks: [{ foregroundToken, backgroundToken, ratio, passesAALarge, … }] } ``` A component that consumes `foreground` on `background` is automatically checked — no manual mapping from "component X uses color Y" required. The whole docs site you're reading runs on this: every card, button, and code block reads from the live theme's tokens. That's the semantic-token payoff — theming that stays honest at scale.

title: Solar Time Theming
text: --- title: "Theming by the clock: switch to dark mode at your local sunset" date: 2026-07-14 description: "Use Themvora's scheduled option and NOAA solar math to switch light and dark modes based on actual sunrise and sunset for the user's coordinates." tags: scheduling, solartimes, dark-mode --- Hard-coded "dark mode starts at 8pm" ignores where your user lives. In summer a Mumbai user's sunset is minutes away from a Helsinki user's sunrise. Themvora's `calculateSunTimes` implements the standard NOAA solar calculation so your theme follows the *actual* sun.

title: Scheduled runtime option
text: Scheduled runtime option Pass `scheduled` to the runtime and it computes today's sunrise/sunset, then switches the theme at the right moment: ```ts import { createThemeRuntime } from "@themvora/core"; const runtime = createThemeRuntime({ scheduled: { // Everything optional. lightTheme/darkTheme adapt to the currently // selected theme family (fallback: neutral light/dark), and each // visitor's timezone is detected for their local sunrise/sunset. // Optional overrides: // lightTheme: "mint-light", darkTheme: "mint-dark", // timeZone: "Asia/Kathmandu", // pin a timezone // latitude: 51.5072, longitude: -0.1276 // …or exact coordinates }, }); ``` No `latitude`/`longitude` means the location is resolved from the visitor's IANA timezone (the tz database's reference city per zone) on the client, so a Mumbai user gets Mumbai's sunrise/sunset and a Helsinki user gets Helsinki's — the same `scheduled` block works for everyone, anywhere, with no network call. No `lightTheme`/`darkTheme` means the schedule follows the visitor's selected theme family (e.g. `plum-dark` → `plum-light`/`plum-dark`), falling back to Themvora's neutral `light`/`dark` themes. The runtime re-checks on an interval, so a visitor crossing time zones re-themes correctly.

title: Standalone utility
text: Standalone utility `calculateSunTimes(date, latitude?, longitude?)` returns `{ sunrise, sunset }` as `Date`s — with no coordinates it auto-detects the visitor's timezone. It's usable for any scheduling you want to build yourself, from theme switching to "good morning" toasts: ```ts import { calculateSunTimes } from "@themvora/core"; // Auto-detected from the visitor's timezone. const { sunrise, sunset } = calculateSunTimes(new Date()); // …or pin a location. const { sunrise: london, sunset: londonSet } = calculateSunTimes( new Date(), { timeZone: "Europe/London" }, ); const { sunrise: paris, sunset: parisSet } = calculateSunTimes( new Date(), 48.8566, 2.3522, ); ```

title: The Playground shows it live
text: The Playground shows it live Open `/playground` and pick any timezone in the world (or drag the latitude/longitude sliders, or pick a city). The sun-path diagram redraws and the suggested mode flips the live site theme as you cross a location's daylight boundary — the demo and the library are the same code path.

title: Theme Families
text: --- title: "Beyond light and dark: theming with independent families and modes" date: 2026-08-15 description: "Theme families let users switch colors independently from light/dark mode — giving you plum-light, plum-dark, mint-light, mint-dark, and every combination from a single API." tags: families, modes, concepts --- A single light/dark toggle is enough for many apps, but it breaks down when you need more than one palette. A corporate dashboard might offer "Plum" and "Mint" families — each with its own light and dark mode. With families, those modes are independent dimensions.

title: The problem with one-dimensional toggles
text: The problem with one-dimensional toggles A typical dark mode implementation stores a single boolean: `isDark`. Your app is either light or dark. But what if you want: - A **Plum** palette (purple primary) with both light and dark modes - A **Mint** palette (green primary) with its own light and dark - A **High Contrast** family for accessibility With a boolean toggle, every palette is a separate theme. You'd need `plum-light`, `plum-dark`, `mint-light`, `mint-dark` — and the user can't switch palette without switching mode.

title: Families: two independent dials
text:
Families: two independent dials Themvora separates the concept of **family** (the color palette) from **mode** (light/dark/system): ```ts import { useTheme } from "@themvora/react"; function ThemePicker() { const { theme, mode, family, setMode, setFamily, toggleTheme } = useTheme(); return (

Active: {theme.name}

); } ``` The user picks a family (Plum → Mint) and a mode (light → dark) independently. The runtime resolves `family: "plum", mode: "dark"` to `plum-dark` automatically.

title: How themes are organized
text: How themes are organized Themes in Themvora carry a `meta` field that declares their family and mode: ```ts import { defineTheme } from "@themvora/core"; export const plumLight = defineTheme({ name: "plum-light", meta: { family: "plum", mode: "light", label: "Plum Light" }, tokens: { /* ... */ }, }); export const plumDark = defineTheme({ name: "plum-dark", meta: { family: "plum", mode: "dark", label: "Plum Dark" }, tokens: { /* ... */ }, }); ``` The registry indexes themes by family and mode, so `resolveInitialTheme({ themes, family: "plum", mode: "system" })` resolves to the correct theme — and re-resolves when the user switches family or the OS preference changes.

title: The nine built-in families
text: The nine built-in families Themvora ships nine families out of the box — oat, berry, mint, citrus, cocoa, plum, iris, sky, and graphite — each with a light and dark mode. You can add your own by defining themes with the same `meta.family` and `meta.mode` structure.

title: Families in the runtime
text: Families in the runtime The runtime's `selection` controller manages both dimensions: ```ts runtime.selection.setFamily("mint"); // switches the palette runtime.selection.setMode("dark"); // switches the mode runtime.selection.toggleTheme(); // light ↔ dark, same family // Read the current state const { family, mode } = runtime.selection.getSelection(); ``` The theme resolves forward: `family + mode → theme name → theme definition`. This means every family/mode combination is valid, even if you haven't defined a theme for it — the runtime falls back to the family's default.

title: Why families matter
text: Why families matter - **User choice** — let users pick both personality (family) and comfort (mode) - **Brand consistency** — every family carries its own on-brand colors, but the mode switch is independent - **Accessibility** — a high-contrast family coexists with your main palette, and users can combine it with their preferred mode - **SSR-safe** — both dimensions are persisted, bootstrapped, and restored across reloads with no extra effort

title: Zero Flash Theming
text: --- title: "Zero flash: how ThemeProvider avoids a wrong-theme flash on every load" date: 2026-07-28 description: "The three techniques Themvora uses to guarantee a user never sees a flash of incorrect theme — blocking bootstrap scripts, SSR CSS variables and cookie-based fingerprinting." tags: next, rsc, ssr, performance --- Every theming library has to answer the same question: what does the user see between "HTML arrives" and "JavaScript runs"? If the answer is *the wrong theme*, you have a flash of incorrect theme (FOIT). Themvora attacks this from three directions at once. ## 1. Resolve the theme on the server With `@themvora/next`, the `ThemeProvider` is a server component. It reads the `theme` cookie, validates the selection against the configured themes, and resolves the *initial theme before a single byte of HTML is sent*: ```tsx import { ThemeProvider } from "@themvora/next"; export default function RootLayout({ children }) { return ( <ThemeProvider defaultTheme="light"> {children} </ThemeProvider> ); } ``` The server-rendered `<html>` arrives already carrying `data-theme="dark"` and the correct inline `--theme-color-*` variables, so first paint is correct. ## 2. Block with a bootstrap script Cookies aren't always there — a returning user's first request, an authenticated route, or a misconfigured proxy. For those cases Themvora emits a small **blocking bootstrap script** inside `<head>` that runs before first paint. It reads the persisted selection from `localStorage`, falls back to `prefers-color-scheme`, and flips `data-theme` before the browser paints: ```ts import { createThemeBootstrapScript, getBuiltInThemes } from "@themvora/core"; const script = createThemeBootstrapScript({ themes: getBuiltInThemes(), defaultTheme: "light" }); // → a self-contained <script> string you can inline in <head> ``` ## 3. Ship the CSS variables in the SSR HTML Because the resolved theme's tokens are flattened on the server, the `--theme-color-*` variables are present in the initial HTML itself. There is no "CSS loads late" gap — the tokens the first paint needs are already there, and `@themvora/next` even pre-paints the dark-mode CSS via `useServerInsertedHTML`. ## The result - **First paint is always correct** — no theme, no layout flash. - **No runtime dependency for correctness** — the site is themed even with JavaScript disabled. - **Fingerprinting** keeps the persisted selection honest: a cookie that names a theme you no longer ship is safely rejected. Try it yourself — this very documentation site runs on exactly this pipeline.

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - A project that `themvora init` already integrated Add a theme source to a project `init` already set up. ```bash themvora add preset mint themvora add brand apple themvora add seed "#6366f1" --family indigo ``` <!-- cli-command:generated:start -->

title: Synopsis — Add a theme source to an existing project
text: Synopsis — Add a theme source to an existing project ```text Usage: themvora add <preset|brand|seed> <value> [options] ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<kind>` | The source kind to add. | | `<value>` | The preset id, brand id, or seed colour. |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `--dir <path>` | Project directory. Defaults to the current directory. | — | | `--family <name>` | Theme family name, for a seed source. | — | | `--style <name>` | Generation style, for a seed source. Run `themvora list styles` for the available values. | — | | `--plan` | Print what would happen and exit. Never writes. | — | | `--dry-run` | Print the plan and exit. Never writes. | — | | `--force` | Replace the registry even when it was not generated by Themvora. | — | | `--json` | Emit the plan or the report as JSON on stdout. | — | | `--quiet` | Suppress progress output. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | the registry was updated, or already had the source | | `1` | command/runtime error, or a registry that cannot be extended | | `2` | usage/argument error, or no Themvora registry |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora add preset mint themvora add brand apple themvora add seed "#6366f1" --family indigo themvora add preset iris --dir ./my-app themvora add preset iris --plan ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end -->

title: How it works
text: How it works `init` writes a theme registry and records **the sources it was built from** in a machine-readable line in that file: ```ts /** * Themvora application configuration. * * Generated by `themvora init`. * … * Source: preset mint. * themvora:sources: [{"kind":"preset","id":"mint"}] */ ``` `add` decodes that list, appends its own source, resolves everything through the same source resolver `init` uses, and regenerates the file with the same renderer. Nothing is parsed back out of the TypeScript — the alternative would break the moment a formatter reformatted the file. That also means `add` is exactly as safe as `init`: - **Idempotent.** Adding a source the registry already has reports `Already present — nothing changed` and writes nothing. - **Non-destructive.** The file is regenerated only when it carries Themvora's generated header. A registry you maintain by hand is never rewritten. - **Stable defaults.** Adding a source never changes the theme the app opens with — the first source's default stays the default.

title: Where the themes go
text: Where the themes go | Project | Registry file | | ------- | ------------- | | React, Vue, Svelte, Solid (Vite) | `theme.config.ts` | | Next.js App Router | `themvora.themes.ts` | The file is the single declaration the integration reads, so nothing else has to change. Restart the dev server and the new themes are selectable.

title: Working with an existing project
text: Working with an existing project `add` uses `--dir` rather than a positional, because both positionals name the source: ```bash themvora add preset iris --dir ./my-app themvora add brand github --dir ./packages/web ```

title: Previewing
text: Previewing ```bash themvora add preset iris --plan themvora add preset iris --dry-run --json ``` Both print what would change and write nothing.

title: When it refuses
text: When it refuses `add` stops rather than guessing in three cases, and each says what to do: - **No registry.** The project has not been integrated — run `themvora init`. - **A hand-written registry.** The file exists but was not generated by Themvora, so `add` will not rewrite it. - **A registry with no source record.** The file predates the source line. Re-run `themvora init` to regenerate it, then add the source again.

title: Synopsis — Audit a theme or the shipped presets
text: Synopsis — Audit a theme or the shipped presets ```text Usage: themvora audit <file|presets> [options] ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<scope>` | A theme file to audit, or `presets` to audit every shipped preset and brand. |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `--strict` | Treat warnings as failures, as the repository's preset gate does. | — | | `--json` | Emit the audit report as JSON on stdout. | — | | `--quiet` | Print only themes that fail or warn, plus the summary. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | audit passed | | `3` | audit failed (checks are listed) | | `1` | command/runtime error | | `2` | usage/argument error |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora audit presets themvora audit theme.json themvora audit presets --strict --json ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end --> ## Examples ```bash # Every shipped preset and brand themvora audit presets # One theme file themvora audit theme.json # Warnings are failures too themvora audit presets --strict ``` ## The scorecard Both scopes use `scoreTheme()` — the same quality model the repository's `audit-presets.mjs` release gate and the preset documentation use. There is one audit system, so the CLI and the release gate cannot disagree about whether a preset is healthy. | Check | What it asserts | | ----- | --------------- | | `structural` | Every core role is present and a valid colour | | `semantic` | `destructive` / `success` are still in their colour families | | `text-contrast` | Every text pair meets its floor | | `ui-contrast` | Every non-text UI pair meets its floor | | `surface-hierarchy` | `background` / `card` / `popover` / `border` are distinguishable | | `muted-hierarchy` | The muted scale is ordered and separated | | `accent-collision` | `accent` and `primary` do not collide | | `cvd` | Status roles stay distinguishable under colour-vision deficiency | | `contexts` | Every semantic usage the components promise is satisfied | ## Output ``` Shipped presets and brands oat-light 9/9 PASS oat-dark 9/9 PASS ... discord-dark 9/9 PASS 28 theme(s) 28 pass 0 with warnings 0 fail Audit passed. ``` A failing theme names the checks that failed and their measured values: ``` forest-light 6/9 FAIL ui-contrast: input/background 1.40; input/card 1.45; surface-hierarchy: card/popover ΔL 0.000 ``` `--quiet` prints only the themes that fail or warn, plus the summary. ## Strict mode `--strict` treats warnings as failures, mirroring the repository's `audit-presets.mjs --strict-ui`. A preset that only warns is reported but does not fail the audit by default. ## Scope `audit presets` audits every entry in the canonical catalog — the 9 default presets and the 5 brand recipes, both modes: **28 themes**. The repository's own `audit-presets.mjs` additionally covers the neutral baseline and the accessibility profiles (which are exempt by design, since they exist *to* deviate), and checks snapshot drift against a frozen test fixture. Those are repository concerns; `audit presets` is the user-facing equivalent, on the same scorecard. ## JSON output ```bash themvora audit presets --json ``` ```json { "scope": "presets", "strict": false, "subjects": [ { "id": "mint", "label": "Mint", "themes": [ { "name": "mint-light", "valid": true, "issues": [], "checks": [{ "id": "structural", "label": "Structural", "status": "pass" }], "passed": 9, "total": 9, "failed": false, "warned": false } ] } ], "summary": { "subjects": 14, "themes": 28, "passed": 28, "warned": 0, "failed": 0 } } ``` A failing run still emits the report **and** exits `3`. ## Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | Audit passed. | | `3` | Audit failed — a theme failed a check, or a warning under `--strict`. | | `1` | A source was accepted but could not be used (unreadable file, invalid JSON or JSONC). | | `2` | Usage error: no scope, or an unknown scope. | ## Next Steps - [Validate a theme](./validate) - [Explain a theme](./explain) - [CLI reference](./reference) ## Related - [Theme generation](../../theme-generation) - [Accessibility](../../accessibility) - [API Reference](../../api-reference) Next: [migrate](/cli/migrate).

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - @themvora/cli installed (globally, locally, or via npx) A **brand recipe** is a brand-inspired starting point: a documented reference colour, pinned as an anchor, and a full theme derived from it. ```bash themvora list brands themvora generate --brand apple ``` > **Brand recipes are brand-inspired, not official.** They are Themvora's own > interpretations, generated by Themvora's own engine. They are not published, > reviewed, or endorsed by the companies named, and using one does not make your > product affiliated with them. Check the brand's own guidelines before shipping > anything that imitates their identity.

title: What a recipe records, and what Themvora derives
text: What a recipe records, and what Themvora derives This distinction is the whole point of the feature, so it is worth being exact. **Recorded — the documented input.** Each recipe names one publicly documented reference and one anchor colour taken from it. That is the only brand-specific data Themvora stores: ```text apple reference Apple · official-guidelines https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/color design system: yes · light/dark: yes anchor light primary #007aff System Blue provenance approximate ``` **Derived — Themvora's own output.** Everything else in the theme is produced by the generator from that anchor: the surfaces, borders, muted and accent roles, the dark-mode counterparts, and the contrast repair. None of it is copied from the brand's site or design system, and none of it is claimed to be theirs. `themvora explain` shows both halves side by side, and is the way to check what a recipe actually pins: ```bash themvora explain --brand apple ``` The `provenance` field states how faithful the recipe is. Every shipped brand is `approximate`: the anchor is documented, the rest is derived.

title: The five recipes
text: The five recipes | Recipe | Character | Style | Anchor | Reference | | ------ | --------- | ----- | ------ | --------- | | `apple` | Brand-inspired · Blue accent · Restrained | `brand` | `#007aff` | Apple HIG | | `github` | Brand-inspired · Primer blue · Systematic | `brand` | `#0969da` | GitHub Primer | | `vercel` | Brand-inspired · Monochrome · Geist neutral | `minimal` | `#000000` | Vercel Geist | | `slack` | Brand-inspired · Aubergine · Bold | `brand` | `#4a154b` | Slack brand | | `discord` | Brand-inspired · Blurple · Playful | `brand` | `#5865f2` | Discord brand | Browse them with the colours applied on the [brand preset gallery](/presets/brand).

title: Using a recipe
text: Using a recipe ```bash # Generate a file themvora generate --brand apple --output theme.json # Start a project on it themvora init my-app --framework react --brand apple # Add it to an existing project's registry themvora add brand github ```

title: There is no per-brand shorthand
text: There is no per-brand shorthand ```bash themvora generate --apple # ✗ not shipped ``` The shorthand form does not exist, and the docs do not show it. A brand is named with `--brand <id>`, like every other registry value, because that is the only spelling the parser accepts — and because a flag per brand would be a second registry in the command surface.

title: Discovering the ids
text: Discovering the ids ```bash themvora list brands # a table, with character, style and provenance themvora list brands --json # the full entries themvora list brands --ids # just the identifiers, one per line ```

title: Recipes are not scraped
text: Recipes are not scraped A recipe is authored data in the Themvora repository, reviewed like any other source file. The CLI never fetches a brand's website, never reads their CSS, and never copies their stylesheet — `generate --brand` runs entirely offline against the shipped catalog. That is also why a recipe can be *approximate* and still be useful: it is honest about what it pins (one documented colour) rather than pretending to reproduce a design system.

title: Ci
text: # CI & Automation

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - Project-local `@themvora/cli` install (or `npx @themvora/cli`) - CI runner with access to git and node The CLI is deterministic and non-blocking: it reads a theme or a project, prints, exits, and waits for nothing. That makes it a natural build step. `init` is the one command with an interactive mode, and it never reaches for it here. With `CI` set, with a redirected stdin, or under `--json`, `--quiet`, `--plan` or `--dry-run`, it behaves exactly like every other command: a missing value is a usage error naming the flag that supplies it. ```bash # Non-interactive by construction: every value a prompt would ask for is given. themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react ``` `--styling` defaults to plain CSS, which is also what the wizard preselects — so a pipeline that names no styling produces the same project a person would get by pressing Enter. Say which one you want and the question never comes up: ```bash themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react --styling tailwind themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react --styling css ```

title: Run everywhere
text: Run everywhere `themvora` (installed) or `npx --yes @themvora/cli` behaves the same on npm, pnpm, yarn, bun, cmd, PowerShell, bash, and zsh. Prefer a **project-local install** in CI so the version is locked and reviewed: ```json { "scripts": { "theme:validate": "themvora validate themes/" } } ```

title: Exit codes make it a gate
text: Exit codes make it a gate Every command uses the same four codes, so a pipeline can switch on them without parsing output: | Code | Meaning | Raised by | | ---- | ------- | --------- | | `0` | Success | all | | `1` | Command/runtime error, or a blocked write | all | | `2` | Invalid arguments, or a missing precondition | all | | `3` | Validation, audit, verification or health failure | `validate`, `audit`, `init`, `doctor` | The distinction that matters for a gate: `1` and `2` mean the command could not do its job, while `3` means it did the job and the *subject* failed. ```bash themvora validate themes/ if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "theme invalid — rejecting" exit 1 fi ```

title: Three levels of theme check
text: Three levels of theme check Pick the one that matches what you want to block on: ```bash themvora validate theme.json # structural: schema, required tokens, references, contrast themvora audit theme.json # the full quality scorecard — stricter than validate themvora audit presets # the same scorecard over every shipped preset ``` `validate` answers "is this a well-formed theme". `audit` answers "is this a *good* theme", and gates on the scorecard. A theme can pass `validate` and fail `audit`, which is the point of having both.

title: Machine-readable output
text: Machine-readable output Every command that reports supports `--json`, and the payload goes to stdout alone — progress and diagnostics go to stderr, so a JSON payload is never polluted. JSON output never contains terminal escape sequences, and colour is off automatically when stdout is not a TTY. ```bash themvora validate theme.json --json | jq '.valid' themvora diff before.json after.json --json | jq '.summary' themvora doctor . --json ```

title: Project checks
text: Project checks If the repository *consumes* Themvora rather than just holding theme files, check the project too: ```bash themvora doctor . # framework, package manager, packages, config, theme files themvora doctor . --json # the same, as data ``` `doctor` exits `3` on an actionable health failure — a missing integration, an invalid theme file, an unreadable config — and `0` when the only findings are warnings.

title: Writes are explicit, and previewable
text: Writes are explicit, and previewable Nothing in the CLI writes as a side effect of a read: - **Theme commands** write only to a destination you name (`--output`, or `--write` for `migrate` in place). The default is stdout. - **`init` and `add`** edit files, but every one of them can be previewed with `--plan` or `--dry-run`, which render the same plan object `apply` consumes and write nothing at all. - **`init` never replaces a file it did not generate** without `--force`, and `add` refuses a registry it does not own. That makes a "check, then apply" pipeline straightforward: ```bash themvora init . --framework react --plan # review in the log themvora init . --framework react --no-install ```

title: GitHub Actions
text: GitHub Actions ```yaml name: Validate Themes on: pull_request: push: branches: [main] jobs: themes: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile - run: pnpm exec themvora validate themes/ - run: pnpm exec themvora audit themes/ - run: pnpm exec themvora doctor . ```

title: Automation-friendly behaviours
text: Automation-friendly behaviours - **No prompts, ever.** A missing required value is a usage error with an actionable message; no run can block waiting for input. - **`--json` is stable and documented**, so scripts do not parse human output. - **Deterministic per project.** A script in `package.json` fixes the version, so machines agree. - **Offline by default.** The theme commands never touch the network. Only `init` on a *new* project invokes a scaffolder, and `--plan`/`--dry-run` never do. - **Pre-build step.** Run `theme:generate` before `next build`, `vite build`, or a Tailwind pass so `theme.json` / `theme.css` exist first.

title: For contributors, not CI
text: For contributors, not CI Shell completion is a developer convenience rather than a pipeline step, but it is worth mentioning in a setup script: ```bash themvora completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/themvora ``` Registry values (presets, brands, styles, frameworks) are resolved by the script at completion time, so it never goes stale when Themvora is upgraded.

text: Next Steps - [Validate your themes](./validate) - [Audit against the scorecard](./audit) - [Export to JSON or CSS](./export) - [View CLI reference](./reference)

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - A shell: bash, zsh, fish or PowerShell Emit a shell completion script for the `themvora` CLI. ```bash themvora completion bash themvora completion zsh themvora completion fish themvora completion powershell ``` The script goes to stdout with nothing else, so the documented install is a redirect: ```bash # bash themvora completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/themvora # zsh — either on your $fpath, or sourced themvora completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_themvora" # fish themvora completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/themvora.fish # PowerShell themvora completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression ``` <!-- cli-command:generated:start -->

title: Synopsis — Emit a shell completion script
text: Synopsis — Emit a shell completion script ```text Usage: themvora completion <shell> ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<shell>` | One of: bash, zsh, fish, powershell. |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `--shell <name>` | The shell to generate for (or pass it positionally). One of: `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, `powershell`. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | success | | `2` | usage/argument error | | `1` | command/runtime error |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora completion bash themvora completion zsh themvora completion fish themvora completion powershell ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end -->

title: What completes
text: What completes - **Command names**, including aliases (`gen`, `ls`), with descriptions where the shell renders them. - **Flags**, scoped to the command you are typing. - **Closed value sets** — `--mode light|dark|both`, the `list` selectors, the shell names. - **Registry values** — presets, brands, styles and `init` frameworks.

title: Registry values are resolved, not embedded
text: Registry values are resolved, not embedded The script does not contain a copy of any value list. It asks the installed CLI: ```bash themvora list presets --ids ``` That matters for two reasons. A preset added to Themvora shows up in your completions without regenerating anything, and a completion can never offer an identifier the installed CLI would reject — the list *is* the CLI's own registry. The result is cached in a shell variable for the session, so a Tab press costs at most one process, once. `list --ids` is the machine-readable mode this relies on: it prints the identifiers, one per line, and nothing else. ```bash themvora list presets --ids themvora list frameworks --ids ```

title: Coverage is structural
text: Coverage is structural Commands, aliases and flags come from the same command contract that renders `themvora --help` and the generated reference, so a flag cannot be completable without also being documented and parseable — or the other way round.

title: Synopsis — Diff two themes semantically
text: Synopsis — Diff two themes semantically ```text Usage: themvora diff <a> <b> [options] ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<a>` | First source: a theme file, a preset id, or a brand id. Resolved as file, then preset, then brand. Omit to use a flag instead. (optional) | | `<b>` | Second source, resolved the same way. Omit to use a flag instead. (optional) |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `--preset <id>` | Use a canonical preset as a source, filling the first side without a positional. Run `themvora list presets` for the available values. | — | | `--brand <id>` | Use a brand recipe as a source. Repeat for the other side. Run `themvora list brands` for the available values. | — | | `--seed <color>` | Use a theme generated from this seed as a source. Repeat for the other side. | — | | `--mode <mode>` | Compare only this visual mode. One of: `light`, `dark`. | — | | `--all` | Include unchanged tokens in the report. | — | | `--json` | Emit the diff report as JSON on stdout. | — | | `--quiet` | Print per-mode counts without the per-token rows. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | compared (whether or not differences exist) | | `1` | command/runtime error | | `2` | usage/argument error |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora diff mint iris themvora diff theme.json --preset mint themvora diff --brand apple --preset mint --mode light themvora diff mint iris --json ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end --> ## Examples ```bash # Two presets themvora diff mint iris # A file against a preset themvora diff theme.json --preset mint # Two brand recipes themvora diff --brand apple --brand github # A seed against a preset themvora diff --seed "#3366ff" --preset mint ``` ## Sources Each side takes exactly one source. A positional is resolved in a fixed order — **an existing file, then a preset id, then a brand id** — and the label in the output always states which branch was taken, so the precedence is never a guess: ``` a: file theme.json b: preset mint ``` A value that looks like a path (it contains a separator or ends in `.json`) is always treated as a file, so a mistyped filename reports `cannot read file` rather than being mistaken for an unknown id. Use `--preset`, `--brand`, or `--seed` when a side has no positional. The flags fill the sides without a positional, **in the order you type them**: ```bash themvora diff mint --brand apple # a = preset mint, b = brand apple themvora diff --brand apple --preset mint # a = brand apple, b = preset mint themvora diff --seed "#111111" --seed "#222222" # a and b are seeds ``` ## Output ``` mint-light → iris-light a: preset mint b: preset iris light Canvas background #e9f3ee → #f1f1f6 foreground #131d18 → #191a1f Actions primary #32936c → #5d5fea primaryForeground #0a140f → #fbfbff radius lg 18px → 16px 20 changed · 0 added · 0 removed · 2 unchanged dark ... ``` Sections are the canonical role groups — **Canvas**, **Surfaces**, **Actions**, **States**, **Interaction** — for colours, and the token group name (`radius`, `spacing`, …) for everything else. Only groups with changes are shown. - Unchanged tokens are hidden by default. Pass `--all` to include them. - `--quiet` prints only the per-mode counts. - A mode only one side provides says so in words rather than listing every token as added. - Identical themes print `… are identical (N tokens compared).` ### Provenance is reported separately Themes generated from different seeds but with identical tokens are *the same theme* for every rendering purpose, so they are not reported as changed. Provenance differences appear as a trailing note instead: ``` provenance differs: seed, style ``` ## Modes There are two visual modes, `light` and `dark`. `--mode` restricts the comparison to one of them, and is rejected if a source does not have it: ```bash themvora diff mint iris --mode light ``` `--mode system` is rejected: `"system"` is a **selector** over the concrete light/dark pair, not a mode that can be compared. ## JSON output `--json` emits the report on stdout, with nothing else mixed in. ```bash themvora diff mint iris --json ``` ```json { "version": 1, "a": { "name": "mint-light", "family": "mint", "mode": "light" }, "b": { "name": "iris-light", "family": "iris", "mode": "light" }, "hasChanges": true, "modes": { "light": { "mode": "light", "present": "both", "changes": [ { "path": "colors.primary", "group": "colors", "role": "primary", "roleGroup": "actions", "status": "changed", "before": "#32936c", "after": "#5d5fea" } ], "counts": { "added": 0, "removed": 0, "changed": 20, "unchanged": 2, "total": 22 }, "byGroup": [{ "group": "colors", "added": 0, "removed": 0, "changed": 19, "unchanged": 2 }] } }, "provenance": { "a": { "algorithm": "semantic-v2", "seed": "#059669", "style": "soft", "anchored": [] }, "b": { "algorithm": "semantic-v2", "seed": "#6366f1", "style": "balanced", "anchored": [] }, "changed": true, "differing": ["seed", "style"] }, "summary": { "added": 0, "removed": 0, "changed": 20, "unchanged": 2, "total": 22 } } ``` `version` is the **report schema** version, independent of the theme schema and the package version. `counts` is always complete, whatever `--all` is set to; only `changes` is filtered. Ordering is deterministic — groups follow the canonical token-group order, colours follow the canonical role order, and nothing in the report depends on the host's locale. ## Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | Compared successfully — **whether or not differences exist**. | | `1` | A source was accepted but could not be used (unreadable file, invalid JSON or JSONC, an unresolvable `mode: "system"`). | | `2` | Usage error: an unresolvable source, two sources for one side, `--mode system`, or a mode a source does not have. | > `diff` exits `0` when the themes differ. A `git diff --exit-code`-style > "nonzero means different" would collide with `1` meaning *runtime error* in > this CLI's exit-code contract, so it is deliberately not provided. ## Next Steps - [Validate a theme](./validate) - [Inspect a theme](./inspect) - [CLI reference](./reference) ## Related - [Themvora Quick Start](../quickstart) - [Theme generation](../../theme-generation) - [API Reference](../../api-reference) Next: [migrate](/cli/migrate).

title: Synopsis — Check a Themvora project's health
text: Synopsis — Check a Themvora project's health ```text Usage: themvora doctor [dir] [options] ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<dir>` | Project directory to check. Defaults to the current directory. (optional) |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `--json` | Emit the health report as JSON on stdout. | — | | `--quiet` | Show only warnings and errors. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | healthy (warnings alone do not fail) | | `3` | an actionable health failure | | `1` | command/runtime error | | `2` | usage/argument error |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora doctor themvora doctor ./my-app themvora doctor --json ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end --> ## Examples ```bash # The current directory themvora doctor # Another project themvora doctor ./my-app ``` ## Output ``` themvora doctor — /path/to/project ✓ Project manifest healthy-app — 3 dependencies ✓ Package manager pnpm ✓ Framework React (Vite) ✓ Themvora packages @themvora/core, @themvora/react ✓ Theme config theme.config.ts ✓ Theme files 2 valid, generated by semantic-v2 healthy ``` Every finding that has a concrete correction carries it: ``` ! Package manager 2 lockfiles found: package-lock.json, yarn.lock → Keep one lockfile; several let different tools resolve different trees. ✗ Themvora packages none installed → Install @themvora/core (and the integration for your framework). ``` ## What it checks | Check | Level | | ----- | ----- | | `project` | **error** if `package.json` is missing or unparseable | | `package-manager` | **warning** for no lockfile, or several | | `framework` | **warning** when nothing is detected | | `framework-support` | **info** when the framework is a library integration but not an `init` target | | `themvora-packages` | **error** when none are installed | | `framework-integration` | **warning** when the framework is in use but its integration is not installed | | `theme-config` | **error** when `theme.config.*` exists without `@themvora/core`; **warning** when it is missing | | `theme-files` | **error** for an unreadable, malformed, or structurally invalid theme file (comments and trailing commas are accepted, as in `validate`) | | `generator-metadata` | **warning** when a theme was generated by an older algorithm than the current one | Framework detection reads dependencies and prefers the **most specific** match: a Next.js app also depends on `react`, so Next.js wins. ## Warnings are not failures A project with warnings is still healthy: | State | Exit | | ----- | ---- | | No errors | `0` — including a warnings-only project | | Any error | `3` | | Not a directory, or an unreadable project | `1` | ## JSON output ```bash themvora doctor --json ``` ```json { "directory": "/path/to/project", "framework": { "id": "react", "displayName": "React", "initSupported": true }, "packageManager": "pnpm", "findings": [ { "id": "theme-config", "level": "warning", "title": "Theme config", "detail": "no theme.config.ts found", "fix": "Add a theme.config.ts so the pre-paint bootstrap and the runtime read one registry." } ], "summary": { "errors": 0, "warnings": 1, "info": 5, "healthy": true } } ``` `--quiet` prints only warnings and errors. ## Next Steps - [Audit a theme](./audit) - [Explain a theme](./explain) - [CLI reference](./reference) ## Related - [Themvora Quick Start](../quickstart) - [Zero-flash theming](../../zero-flash) - [API Reference](../../api-reference) Next: [migrate](/cli/migrate).

title: Synopsis — Explain how a theme was produced
text: Synopsis — Explain how a theme was produced ```text Usage: themvora explain <file> [options] ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<file>` | Theme file to explain. A preset id or brand id is also accepted. (optional) |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `--preset <id>` | Explain a canonical preset. Run `themvora list presets` for the available values. | — | | `--brand <id>` | Explain a brand recipe, including its pinned anchors. Run `themvora list brands` for the available values. | — | | `--seed <color>` | Explain a theme generated from this seed. | — | | `--json` | Emit the explanation as JSON on stdout. | — | | `--quiet` | Omit the semantic mapping, keeping the recipe and validation. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | success | | `1` | command/runtime error | | `2` | usage/argument error |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora explain --preset mint themvora explain --brand apple themvora explain --seed "#6366f1" themvora explain theme.json ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end --> ## Examples ```bash themvora explain --preset mint themvora explain --brand apple themvora explain --seed "#6366f1" themvora explain theme.json ``` A preset or brand id is also accepted positionally, resolved the same way [`diff`](./diff) resolves its sources: an existing file, then a preset id, then a brand id. ## Output ``` source resolved preset mint kind curated preset family mint style soft character Cool · Soft · Restrained tags cool, soft, restrained radius 18px temperature neutral seed #059669 algorithm semantic-v2 constraint contract text 4.5:1 large text 3:1 ui 3:1 semantic mapping mint-light Canvas background #e9f3ee foreground #131d18 Body text on the page canvas muted #dfe9e4 mutedForeground #5e6662 Supporting text on the canvas Actions primary #32936c primaryForeground #0a140f The label on a primary action ... validation light valid · 9/9 checks · text 9/9 · ui 7/7 dark valid · 9/9 checks · text 9/9 · ui 7/7 ``` Each section answers one of the plan's questions: | Section | Answers | | ------- | ------- | | `source` | Where this theme came from, and how it was resolved | | `identity` | For a brand recipe: the reference material, the pinned anchors, and any normalization | | `constraint contract` | The contrast floors the theme was solved against | | `semantic mapping` | Every role, its resolved value, and the usage core promises for it | | `validation` | The canonical scorecard, per mode | ## Brand recipes A brand source adds an `identity` block, drawn from the recipe's own reference data: ``` identity reference Apple · official-guidelines https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/color design system: yes · light/dark: yes anchors 2 pinned light primary #007aff System Blue dark primary #007aff System Blue normalized every anchor survived exactly ``` - **`anchors`** are the brand values the generator pins exactly rather than generating around. - **`normalized`** lists anchors the solver had to move to keep the theme readable. When nothing moved it says so. (No shipped brand currently reports a moved anchor — the channel is reported honestly and is empty.) - The canonical brand disclaimer is printed verbatim, so a page that shows a brand preset states the same thing everywhere. ## What it does not explain Two things the CLI deliberately does not report, because core does not expose them: - **Derived seed identity** (hue, chroma, temperature) for a `--seed` source. The identity layer is internal to the generation engine, which keeps all colour math in one module. `explain --seed` reports the seed, the style and the contract instead. - **Solver repairs** for non-brand sources. The generator exposes no repair data for a seed, and its internal report returns empty adjustment lists. ## JSON output `--json` emits the same explanation as a document: ```json { "source": { "kind": "preset", "id": "mint", "label": "preset mint" }, "recipe": { "name": "Mint", "family": "mint", "kind": "curated preset", "style": "soft", "character": "Cool · Soft · Restrained", "tags": ["cool", "soft", "restrained"], "radius": "18px", "temperature": "neutral", "seed": "#059669", "algorithm": "semantic-v2", "provenance": null, "brandColor": null, "disclaimer": null }, "identity": null, "contract": { "text": 4.5, "largeText": 3, "ui": 3 }, "modes": { "light": { "name": "mint-light", "roles": [ { "path": "colors.foreground", "role": "foreground", "roleGroup": "Canvas", "value": "#131d18", "usage": "Body text on the page canvas" } ], "validation": { "valid": true, "issues": [], "score": { "passed": 9, "total": 9, "checks": [] }, "contrast": { "pairs": 16, "text": { "total": 9, "passing": 9 }, "ui": { "total": 7, "passing": 7 } } } } } } ``` `identity` is `null` for a preset, a seed, and a theme file — only a brand recipe has one. ## Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | Explained successfully. | | `1` | A source was accepted but could not be used (unreadable file, invalid JSON or JSONC). | | `2` | Usage error: no source, more than one source, an unresolvable id, or an invalid seed. | ## Next Steps - [Diff two themes](./diff) - [Inspect a theme](./inspect) - [CLI reference](./reference) ## Related - [Theme generation](../../theme-generation) - [Presets](../presets) - [API Reference](../../api-reference) Next: [migrate](/cli/migrate).

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - Theme JSON file(s) to export - Project with @themvora/cli installed or npx access Export theme tokens to **CSS variables** or a **flat JSON map** for another system.
