title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - Project with @themvora/cli installed or npx access Generate a complete theme from one of three sources: a **seed color**, a canonical **preset**, or a brand-inspired **brand** recipe. By default it derives a light + dark pair; `--mode light|dark` writes a single theme. <!-- cli-command:generated:start -->

title: Synopsis — Generate a theme from a seed, preset, or brand
text: Synopsis — Generate a theme from a seed, preset, or brand ```text Usage: themvora generate [options] ```

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `-s, --seed <color>` | Source hex color (#rrggbb). | `#6366f1` | | `--preset <id>` | Generate from a canonical preset. Run `themvora list presets` for the available values. | — | | `--brand <id>` | Generate from a brand-inspired recipe. Run `themvora list brands` for the available values. | — | | `-f, --family <name>` | Family name for the theme name. | `default` | | `-m, --mode <mode>` | Which mode(s) to emit. One of: `light`, `dark`, `both`. | `both` | | `--style <name>` | Visual language. Seed generation only. Run `themvora list styles` for the available values. | — | | `--contrast <level>` | Contrast contract to solve for. One of: `AA`. | `AA` | | `--code` | Also generate a tokens.code syntax palette. Seed generation only. | — | | `-o, --output <file>` | Write JSON to a file instead of stdout. | — | | `--dry-run` | Print what would be written without writing it. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | success | | `2` | usage/argument error | | `1` | command/runtime error |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" themvora generate --preset mint themvora generate --brand apple --output theme.json themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --style editorial --mode light ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end --> > The CLI requires a hex seed (`#rrggbb`), e.g. `#6366f1`. In bash, zsh, and > PowerShell the leading `#` starts a comment, so always quote the seed in a > terminal: `--seed "#6366f1"`. Package managers (npm, pnpm, yarn) also run > `package.json` scripts through a shell, so keep the quotes there too — the > quotes are a shell concern, not part of the flag itself.

title: Three sources
text: Three sources Exactly one source may be given per invocation. They are mutually exclusive, and supplying two is a usage error (`2`) rather than a silent winner. | Source | Flag | What it does | | ------ | ---- | ------------ | | Seed | `--seed <color>` (or a bare positional) | Generates a new palette from one colour. | | Preset | `--preset <id>` | Emits a curated preset, exactly as shipped. | | Brand | `--brand <id>` | Emits a brand-inspired recipe, exactly as shipped. | With no source at all, `generate` keeps its original behaviour: it derives from the default seed `#6366f1`. ```bash themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" themvora generate --preset mint themvora generate --brand apple ``` Run `themvora list presets` / `themvora list brands` to see the identifiers.

title: Presets and brands are not re-derived
text: Presets and brands are not re-derived `--preset` and `--brand` read the **resolved** theme from the canonical catalog, so the output is byte-for-byte the preset the documentation shows. The CLI never re-runs a recipe, which is why a preset can never drift from its docs page. ```bash themvora generate --preset mint --mode light ``` ```json { "name": "mint-light", "meta": { "family": "mint", "mode": "light", "label": "Mint Light", "generation": { "algorithm": "semantic-v2", "seed": "#059669", "style": "soft" } } } ```

title: Seed-only options
text: Seed-only options A recipe pins its own family, style and curated tokens. Combining `--preset` or `--brand` with `--style`, `--code`, or `--family` is rejected with an explanation rather than silently ignored — the options below apply to seed generation only.

title: Unknown values
text: Unknown values An unknown id exits `2` and names the registry to consult. A near miss is corrected: ```bash $ themvora generate --brand appple Usage: themvora generate [options] unknown brand "appple" — did you mean "apple"? — run "themvora list brands" to see the available brands ```

title: Writing to a file
text: Writing to a file `--output <file>` writes the JSON to a file. The confirmation line goes to **stderr**, so stdout stays free for a payload and the command can be piped. `--dry-run` performs no write at all: it reports what would happen on stderr and still prints the payload to stdout, so the result is inspectable without touching the filesystem. ```bash themvora generate --preset mint --output theme.json --dry-run # stderr: would write theme.json (2894 bytes, preset "mint" (style soft)) ```

title: What the generator derives
text: What the generator derives Given a seed, `generate` (via `generateTheme`) derives the full semantic color set: `background`, `foreground`, `card`, `popover`, `primary`, `primaryForeground`, `secondary`, `muted`, `accent`, destructive (with their foregrounds), `border`, `input`, `ring`, plus a `radius.lg` scale. The same model that builds the default presets is exposed here, so a generated family fits the rest of Themvora.

title: Light + dark pair (default)
text: Light + dark pair (default) ```bash themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --family indigo --output theme.json ``` Writes: ```json title="theme.json" { "light": { "name": "indigo-light", "meta": { "family": "indigo", "mode": "light", "label": "Indigo Light", "order": 10 }, "tokens": { "colors": { "background": "#f8fafc", "foreground": "#0f172a", "card": "#ffffff", "cardForeground": "#0f172a", "popover": "#ffffff", "popoverForeground": "#0f172a", "primary": "#6366f1", "primaryForeground": "#ffffff", "secondary": "#e4e4f1", "secondaryForeground": "#0f172a", "muted": "#efeff5", "mutedForeground": "#64748b", "accent": "#c6c6ec", "accentForeground": "#0f172a", "destructive": "#ef4444", "destructiveForeground": "#ffffff", "success": "#22c55e", "successForeground": "#ffffff", "border": "#d9d9e8", "input": "#d9d9e8", "ring": "#6366f1" }, "radius": { "lg": "8px" } } }, "dark": { "name": "indigo-dark", "meta": { "family": "indigo", "mode": "dark", "label": "Indigo Dark", "order": 20 }, "tokens": { "colors": { "background": "#020617", "foreground": "#f8fafc", "card": "#0f172a", "cardForeground": "#f8fafc", "popover": "#0f172a", "popoverForeground": "#f8fafc", "primary": "#9596ea", "primaryForeground": "#020617", "secondary": "#060846", "secondaryForeground": "#f8fafc", "muted": "#050638", "mutedForeground": "#94a3b8", "accent": "#151651", "accentForeground": "#f8fafc", "destructive": "#f87171", "destructiveForeground": "#020617", "success": "#4ade80", "successForeground": "#020617", "border": "#080a5e", "input": "#080a5e", "ring": "#9596ea" }, "radius": { "lg": "8px" } } } } ```

title: A single mode
text: A single mode ```bash themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --family indigo --mode light \ --output indigo-light.json ```

title: Code tokens (opt-in)
text: Code tokens (opt-in) Not every theme needs a syntax-highlighting palette. Pass `--code` to also generate a `tokens.code` block — a cohesive set of `--theme-code-*` variables (keyword, string, number, function, type, comment, …) derived from the seed hue, with distinguishable light/dark variants: ```bash themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --family indigo --code \ --output indigo.json ``` The generated `light.tokens.code` (dark mirrors it with inverted colors): ```json "code": { "background": "#ffffff", "foreground": "#0f172a", "keyword": "#1b1ebc", "string": "#1c7d33", "number": "#a04a00", "function": "#1641d0", "type": "#0e6f73", "comment": "#64748b" } ``` Without `--code` no `code` block is emitted, so themes stay lean.

title: Print to stdout
text: Print to stdout ```bash themvora generate --seed "#10b981" --family mint ```

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | Generated (file written or printed). | | `1` | A command or runtime error. | | `2` | Invalid source combination, unknown preset/brand, or invalid `--seed`/`--mode`/`--style`. |

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - Project with @themvora/cli installed or npx access Create a project, or integrate Themvora into one you already have. `init` has a different job from `generate`. `generate` turns a seed, preset or brand into theme data and writes a file. `init` works on a *project*: ```text project directory ↓ detect or choose framework ↓ choose a theme source ↓ scaffold (a new project) or integrate (an existing one) ↓ install the Themvora packages ↓ wire the provider, passing the theme registry as props ↓ verify by running the project's own build and typecheck ``` The goal is not to write a configuration file. The goal is: > **Run `themvora init …` and end with an actually working, minimally themed > application.** <!-- cli-command:generated:start -->

title: Synopsis — Integrate Themvora into a project, or create one
text: Synopsis — Integrate Themvora into a project, or create one ```text Usage: themvora init [dir] [options] ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<dir>` | Project directory. Created when it does not exist. Defaults to the current directory. (optional) |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `--framework <id>` | Target framework. Required for a new project; overrides detection in an existing one. Run `themvora list frameworks` for the available values. | — | | `--preset <id>` | Generate the theme from a canonical preset. Run `themvora list presets` for the available values. | — | | `--brand <id>` | Generate the theme from a brand-inspired recipe. Run `themvora list brands` for the available values. | — | | `--seed <color>` | Generate the theme from a seed colour. | — | | `--styling <engine>` | Styling engine for the generated app: `css` (plain semantic stylesheet, no extra dependency) or `tailwind` (Tailwind v4 via @themvora/tailwind). Plain CSS is the default in both modes: the wizard asks this as "Would you like to use Tailwind CSS with Themvora?" and preselects `css`, and a run without a terminal resolves to the same value. Supplying the flag skips the question. In an existing project it only rewrites the stylesheets `init` generated — one you wrote yourself needs --force. | `css` | | `--tool <name>` | Package manager to drive the framework generator and install dependencies: `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` or `bun`. When omitted, detection decides: the corepack `packageManager` field, then the lockfile, then npm. The interactive wizard preselects the manager you invoked the CLI with. `--package-manager` is accepted as a compatibility alias. One of: `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `bun`. | — | | `--example` | Accepted and ignored. The showcase is always generated; kept so older scripts do not break. | — | | `--plan` | Print what would happen and exit. Never writes or installs. | — | | `--dry-run` | Print the file operations and exit. Never writes, installs or scaffolds. | — | | `--no-install` | Skip dependency installation. Build/typecheck verification is then skipped and reported as skipped, not failed, because it needs those dependencies. | — | | `--force` | Replace files that exist and were not generated by themvora init. | — | | `--json` | Emit the plan or the report as JSON on stdout. | — | | `--quiet` | Suppress progress output. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | the project was created or integrated and verified | | `3` | the project was written but a verification step failed | | `1` | command/runtime error, or existing files block the run | | `2` | usage/argument error | | `130` | the interactive wizard was cancelled (Ctrl+C); nothing was written |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora init themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react --styling tailwind themvora init my-app --tool npm --framework next --styling css themvora init my-app --tool npm --framework next themvora init my-app --package-manager pnpm --framework react themvora init my-app --framework next --preset mint themvora init my-app --framework react --plan themvora init my-app --framework react --no-install ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end -->

title: Interactive project creation
text: Interactive project creation Run `themvora init` with no directory, in a terminal, and the CLI opens a guided wizard: ```text ? What would you like to name your project? my-app ? Which package manager would you like to use? pnpm ? Which framework would you like to use? React ? Would you like to use Tailwind CSS with Themvora? No — Plain CSS ``` Four questions, in that order: | Question | Asked when | | -------- | ---------- | | Project name | No directory was given, and the current directory is not already a project | | Package manager | `--tool` was not supplied, and nothing in the target identifies one | | Framework | `--framework` was not supplied, and the target is a new project | | Tailwind or plain CSS | `--styling` was not supplied, and the target is a new project | The last question has **No — Plain CSS** preselected — the same value a run without a terminal uses. *Yes — Tailwind CSS* installs the Tailwind integration instead. Explicit flags win, and nothing already supplied is asked for again: | Command | What it asks | | ------- | ------------ | | `themvora init` | name, package manager, framework, styling | | `themvora init my-app` | package manager, framework, styling | | `themvora init my-app --tool pnpm` | framework, styling | | `themvora init my-app --framework react` | package manager, styling | | `themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react` | styling | | `themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react --styling css` | nothing | Once the answers are in, the wizard hands over to the normal pipeline: it validates the configuration, scaffolds the framework with its official generator, integrates Themvora, installs the dependencies once, runs the project's own build and typecheck, and prints the command that starts the app. ```bash # Interactive project creation themvora init # Explicit project configuration themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react # Next.js with npm themvora init my-app --tool npm --framework next # Vue with bun themvora init my-app --tool bun --framework vue # Backward-compatible package-manager option themvora init my-app --package-manager pnpm --framework react ``` `themvora init .` is never a name question: a directory was named, so it is scaffolded in place.

title: Cancelling
text: Cancelling Ctrl+C at any question exits `130` and writes nothing. The questions run before a plan exists, so there is no half-scaffolded directory to clean up — and that includes the styling question, which is asked before a single file is written.

title: When the wizard does not run
text: When the wizard does not run There is no wizard without a terminal. `--json`, `--quiet`, `--plan`, `--dry-run`, `CI`, `TERM=dumb`, and a redirected stdin all keep `init` non-interactive — and a missing value then becomes a usage error that names the flag supplying it: ```text $ themvora init my-app --json Usage: themvora init [dir] [options] a new project needs --framework <id> (supported: react, next, vue, svelte, solid) ```

title: Package managers
text: Package managers `--tool` selects the package manager that drives the framework's generator and performs the dependency install: ```bash themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react themvora init my-app --tool bun --framework vue ``` | Value | Scaffolder invocation | Install | | ----- | --------------------- | ------- | | `npm` | `npm create vite@latest …` · `npx --yes create-next-app@latest …` | `npm install` | | `pnpm` | `pnpm create vite@latest …` · `pnpm dlx create-next-app@latest …` | `pnpm add` | | `yarn` | `yarn create vite@latest …` · `yarn dlx create-next-app@latest …` | `yarn add` | | `bun` | `bun create vite …` · `bunx create-next-app@latest …` | `bun add` | `--package-manager <name>` is the same option under its earlier spelling. Both resolve to one internal value; supplying both with **different** values is an argument conflict rather than a silent choice: ```text $ themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --package-manager yarn --framework react Usage: themvora init [dir] [options] --tool and --package-manager disagree (--tool pnpm and --package-manager yarn) — pass a single package manager ``` When neither flag is given, detection decides, in this order: 1. the corepack `packageManager` field, because it is an explicit declaration; 2. the first lockfile found; 3. `npm`, when there is neither. Several lockfiles are reported as a warning rather than silently resolved. A manager you named explicitly is checked before anything runs: if `pnpm` is not on `PATH`, `init` stops with an actionable error instead of quietly installing with npm. The wizard's menu preselects the manager that invoked the CLI, so `pnpm init` lands on pnpm. That is a default in a prompt, not a fourth detection rule: a non-interactive run has nobody to suggest it to, and falls back to npm.

title: Supported frameworks
text: Supported frameworks ```bash themvora init my-app --framework react themvora init my-app --framework next themvora init my-app --framework vue themvora init my-app --framework svelte themvora init my-app --framework solid ``` `init` currently scaffolds and integrates **React + Vite, Next.js App Router, Vue 3 + Vite, Svelte 5 + Vite, and Solid + Vite**. Themvora may support additional frameworks at the package level — Angular, Nuxt, Astro and Remix are fully supported by their own packages and documented — but that does **not** mean the CLI scaffolder supports every one of them yet. | Framework | Target | Build system | Rendering | | --------- | ------ | ------------ | --------- | | React | React + Vite | Vite | Client | | Next.js | App Router | Next | Server | | Vue | Vue 3 + Vite | Vite | Client | | Svelte | Svelte 5 + Vite | Vite | Client | | Solid | Solid + Vite | Vite | Client | `themvora list frameworks` prints the same set, from the same registry. Asking for a published-but-unsupported framework says so explicitly rather than reporting an unknown name: ```bash themvora init my-app --framework nuxt # "nuxt" is a supported Themvora integration but is not an `init` target yet # — init supports: react, next, vue, svelte, solid ```

title: A new project
text: A new project ```bash themvora init my-app --framework react ``` The project is created with the framework's **own** generator — `create-vite` or `create-next-app` — and Themvora then integrates into the result. Themvora does not ship a copy of anyone's starter template, because such a copy is stale the moment that framework changes its template. After scaffolding, the integration is computed from the generator's real output rather than from an assumption about it, and the project is verified by running its own `build` and `typecheck` scripts.

title: Installation happens once, and it is Themvora's
text: Installation happens once, and it is Themvora's The generators can install dependencies themselves, and every one of them asks first — `create-vite` with *"Install with npm and start now?"*. That question is suppressed, because for a Themvora starter either answer is wrong: the CLI installs the framework packages regardless, so answering *No* still ends in an install and answering *Yes* installs the tree twice. `init` therefore passes each generator its own documented non-interactive flag — `--no-interactive` for `create-vite`, `--skip-install` for `create-next-app` — and runs **one** install itself, after the integration has finished editing `package.json`: ```text scaffold (no install) ↓ integrate — write the theme module, the showcase, the provider props ↓ record build-time dependencies in package.json (Tailwind only) ↓ install once, with the selected package manager ↓ verify — the project's own build and typecheck ``` Tailwind's compiler and its plugin are `devDependencies`, and package managers only take a dev flag for a whole command — so the obvious implementation is a second `add -D` right after the first. That is two full resolutions of one dependency tree for one new project, and it is not what happens here. The integration writes those two entries into `package.json` first, which means the single install already sees them and produces one lockfile entry set. `--no-install` is still supported and still means "install nothing": it drops Themvora's install step, and the generator's install is already suppressed. The manifest is still written in full, so a `pnpm install` you run yourself produces the same project. The dependency-backed verification steps are then reported as **skipped** rather than failed, because a build that cannot resolve its dependencies is not evidence that the generated code is broken. The development server is never started automatically. `init` prints the command that starts it, with the selected manager's own syntax: ```text Project created successfully! Next steps: cd /path/to/my-app pnpm run dev ```

title: An existing project
text: An existing project ```bash themvora init . --framework react ``` The framework is detected from `package.json`; `--framework` overrides detection. Two properties matter more than the features here: - **Your files are not replaced.** A file that is wholly Themvora's — the theme module and the showcase components — is written only when it does not exist. If you already have one of your own, `init` stops and asks for `--force`. The application root is a special case: in a project Themvora scaffolded it is replaced, and in one you already had it is left alone entirely. - **Running it twice does nothing the second time.** Re-running `init` on an integrated project reports `0 created · 0 updated` and leaves the tree byte-identical. That is asserted by the test suite, not assumed. When a file is not in a shape `init` recognises — a root element it cannot match, a `plugins` array written unusually — it does **not** guess. It reports the exact snippet to add, under `manual steps`.

title: Theme sources
text: Theme sources | Flag | Result | | ---- | ------ | | _(none)_ | Core's built-in neutral `light` / `dark` pair | | `--preset <id>` | A canonical preset from the catalog | | `--brand <id>` | A brand-inspired recipe from the catalog | | `--seed <color>` | A theme generated from the seed | ```bash themvora init my-app --framework react --preset mint themvora init my-app --framework react --brand apple themvora init my-app --framework react --seed "#3366ff" ``` Presets and brands are read from the same catalog the docs pages render, so the theme written into your project is byte-for-byte the theme the docs show. A seed goes through `generateTheme`. The resolved theme is validated **before** anything is written.

title: The generated project
text: The generated project The generated application is the **Themvora showcase** — the same interactive reference the docs site renders, not a placeholder: ```text Themvora Theming that survives contact with a real app [Read the docs] [Next.js guide] [Custom themes] [Playground] Mode Light Dark System Preset family [mint] [themvora] [citrus] [cocoa] [berry] … [Toggle light / dark] ┌─ Theme controls ────────────────┐ │ live preview · swatches · tokens │ └──────────────────────────────────┘ ┌─ Scoped to cocoa ───────────────┐ │ a subtree pinned to one family │ └───────────────────────────────────┘ ``` Every colour comes from a semantic token. The generated stylesheet contains no literal colour, and the generated components contain none either — which is what makes a theme switch visibly real, and what makes the showcase a correct reference for the semantic system rather than a decorative demo. The showcase UI is its own component rather than living in the application root, and there is exactly one provider boundary: ```text src/ ├── main.tsx mounts the app; the provider boundary lives here ├── App.tsx composes the showcase ├── index.css the generated stylesheet ├── components/ │ ├── ThemvoraDefault.tsx the showcase UI │ └── ThemeSwitcher.tsx the light/dark control └── themes/ └── themes.ts the theme module ``` Each framework uses its own conventions for the same split: | Framework | Provider | Application root | Showcase | Theme module | Stylesheet | | --------- | -------- | ----------------- | -------- | ------------ | ---------- | | React | `src/main.tsx` | `src/App.tsx` | `src/components/` | `src/themes/themes.ts` | `src/index.css` | | Next.js | `app/layout.tsx` | `app/page.tsx` | `components/` | `themes/themes.ts` | `app/globals.css` | | Vue | `src/App.vue` | `src/App.vue` | `src/components/` | `src/themes/themes.ts` | `src/style.css` | | Svelte | `src/App.svelte` | `src/App.svelte` | `src/components/` | `src/themes/themes.ts` | `src/app.css` | | Solid | `src/App.tsx` | `src/App.tsx` | `src/components/` | `src/themes/themes.ts` | `src/index.css` | The app opens in a **light** theme. The provider receives `initialMode="light"` and the source's light theme by name, so a first run looks the same for every visitor instead of following the operating system. A selection the user has already made still wins, as the runtime's persistence contract requires.

title: The theme module
text: The theme module `themes/themes.ts` is the one file that names colours, and it is generated from canonical core APIs rather than copied from a template. It exports: | Export | What it is | | ------ | ---------- | | `themvora` | the custom `themvora` light/dark pair | | `selection` | the families the app offers — the source's own, plus the four demo families | | `presetThemes` | `getPresetThemes()` filtered by `selection` — the canonical presets, referenced rather than copied | | `sourceThemes` | themes the catalog cannot serve (a brand, a seed, the neutral pair), written out | | `themes` | everything the application registers | | `defaultTheme` | the theme the app opens with, typed against the registry's own names | | `scopedFamily` / `scopedThemes` | the family the scoped demo pins to, resolved from the registry rather than hardcoded | The `shadows` group is deliberately absent from the custom pair: shadow tokens are CSS box-shadow values, so a bare colour would emit an unusable `--theme-shadow-sm`. Empty optional groups are omitted for the same reason.

title: --example
text: --example The showcase is the starter. There is no minimal variant to opt out of, so `--example` changes nothing about what is written. The flag is still accepted so that scripts written against an earlier release keep working.

title: Styling
text: Styling ```bash themvora init my-app --framework react # plain CSS — the default themvora init my-app --framework react --styling css # plain CSS, explicitly themvora init my-app --framework react --styling tailwind # Tailwind CSS ``` `--styling` chooses how the generated application is styled, and it defaults to plain CSS — in the wizard and outside it. In a terminal the wizard asks the same question — *Would you like to use Tailwind CSS with Themvora?* — with **No — Plain CSS** preselected. Pressing Enter and running `themvora init` with no terminal both produce the same project. Passing the flag skips the question entirely. Plain CSS is the default because it is the only choice that adds no build-time dependency: a project that a script generates, or that someone accepts without thinking about it, should not acquire a CSS framework it never asked for. Tailwind is one answer away, at the prompt or with `--styling tailwind`. **`tailwind`** writes a Tailwind CSS v4 entry point that imports `tailwindcss` and then `@themvora/tailwind`, whose `@theme` mapping turns Themvora's tokens into utilities — `bg-background`, `text-foreground`, `bg-card`, `border-border`, `bg-primary`. It adds `@themvora/tailwind` to the dependencies, and `tailwindcss` plus the framework's own plugin (`@tailwindcss/vite`, or `@tailwindcss/postcss` for Next.js) to `devDependencies`, and registers the plugin in the build configuration. **`css`** writes one global stylesheet that reads the same tokens through `var(--theme-color-background)`, `var(--theme-color-card)`, `var(--theme-color-primary)` and friends. It adds no dependency at all, and no build configuration — there is nothing to compile. Either way the showcase contains **one** styling system: no `:root` palette, no `prefers-color-scheme` block, no literal colour in a component. Switching themes repaints the whole showcase in both, including the page itself — the document background and text come from the theme, not from the browser default. The two variants do not produce the same markup with a different stylesheet bolted on. The `css` variant renders component classes (`class="card"`) that the generated stylesheet defines from semantic variables. The `tailwind` variant renders Tailwind utilities (`class="grid gap-4 rounded-xl border border-border bg-card p-6"`) and defines **no** component classes at all — its stylesheet is the Tailwind entry point plus a body rule. What they do share is everything that makes the app an app: the same page, the same cards and controls, the same theme switcher, the same responsive breakpoints, the same tokens. Choosing plain CSS is a choice about how the stylesheet is written, not a downgrade to an unstyled page. `--styling` is deliberately not called `--style`: `--style` already means a theme *generation* style (`themvora generate --style minimal`), which is a different concern. And there is no `--tailwind`/`--no-tailwind` pair — two flags for one setting is how a CLI ends up with two ways to say the same thing and no way to say which won.

title: Styling an existing project
text: Styling an existing project `--styling` is a choice about a project `init` is about to create. In an existing project it can only reach the files `init` generated: a stylesheet you wrote yourself is a conflict, not a target, so the run tells you which of the two it found instead of quietly restyling your app. ```text ! --styling tailwind only rewrites the stylesheets `init` generated — a stylesheet you wrote yourself is left alone unless you pass --force ``` If you do want the matching rules in a project you already have, pass `--force` to replace its root stylesheet, or copy them across yourself.

title: A fresh project versus an existing one
text: A fresh project versus an existing one The two workflows are deliberately different. For a project `init` scaffolded, the CLI owns the generated structure. It writes the showcase, and it **removes the scaffold's own unused files** — the demo stylesheet that declares a second palette, the demo component, the logo assets the generated UI never renders. A file is removed only when it is a known artifact of that framework's template *and* nothing left in the project refers to it, so a dangling import is never produced. For an existing project, none of that happens. The CLI adds its own files and reports anything it cannot do safely as a manual step with the exact snippet. Your `App`, your stylesheets and your build configuration are left alone — including any Tailwind setup you already have. Nothing registers a Themvora plugin in your build: initialization is provider props.

title: The plan and dry run
text: The plan and dry run ```bash themvora init my-app --framework react --plan themvora init my-app --framework react --dry-run ``` Both are built from the **same plan object** a real run applies, so the preview cannot drift from the outcome. Neither writes a file, installs a package or invokes a scaffold — `--dry-run` never runs an external generator. For a new project the preview is computed before the generator has run, so the files Themvora owns are exact while the edits to the generator's own files are resolved afterwards. The plan says so.

title: Options
text: Options | Flag | Effect | | ---- | ------ | | `--no-install` | Skip dependency installation entirely; verification is then reported as skipped | | `--tool <name>` | Drive the generator and the install with `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` or `bun` | | `--package-manager <name>` | Compatibility alias for `--tool`; the two must agree | | `--force` | Replace files that exist and were not generated by `init` | | `--json` | Emit the plan or the report as JSON | | `--quiet` | Suppress progress output | The package manager is detected from the lockfile, and the corepack `packageManager` field wins over a lockfile because it is an explicit declaration. Several lockfiles is reported as a warning rather than silently resolved. See [Package managers](#package-managers) for the full precedence and the commands each choice produces.

title: What is wired
text: What is wired Initialization is **provider props**. There is no configuration file and no build plugin: ```text themes/themes.ts ↓ <ThemeProvider themes={themes} defaultTheme={...} initialMode="light" transition={...}> ↓ pre-paint bootstrap ``` One module, one consumer. The provider paints `<html>` before the first paint — its own contract, so a client-rendered app needs neither `themvoraVitePlugin()` nor a hand-rolled pre-paint script. React uses the same path; `createThemeRoot` remains the documented entry for server rendering. Next.js follows the same shape. `@themvora/next`'s `ThemeProvider` renders `<html>` and `<body>` itself and resolves the initial theme on the server, so there is no Vite plugin either, and the registry is passed to the provider as a prop. Client hooks come from `@themvora/next/client`, never from the package root.

title: Next.js 16 and Cache Components
text: Next.js 16 and Cache Components `create-next-app` now enables **Cache Components** by default, and the generated layout needs **nothing extra** — in particular no `export const instant = false`. That mode rejects a route that reads request data (`cookies()`, `headers()`) outside a `<Suspense>` boundary, and Next's remedy for such a route is the `instant = false` opt-out. `@themvora/next`'s provider keeps that read *inside* a boundary instead: the `<html>`/`<head>`/`<body>` shell resolves from the configured default alone, and the persisted selection is resolved in a nested server component beneath `<Suspense>`. The route therefore prerenders as a static shell with a dynamic, request-aware hole, so there is nothing to opt out of. The visitor's theme still reaches the first paint through two mechanisms that agree with each other: the blocking bootstrap script in `<head>` reads the theme cookies in the browser and writes the resolved theme onto `<html>` before the first frame, and the Suspense-gated server component resolves the same cookies for the client runtime and the streamed, server-rendered subtree. `init` leaves your `next.config.ts` alone either way.

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | The project was created or integrated, and verified | | `3` | The project was written, but a verification step failed | | `1` | Command or runtime error, or existing files block the run | | `2` | Usage or argument error | | `130` | The interactive wizard was cancelled (Ctrl+C); nothing was written | A verification failure exits `3` rather than `0` deliberately: `init` claims to produce a *working* application, so a project that does not build is not a success. A cancellation exits `130` — `128 + SIGINT`, the conventional shell value — so a wrapper script can tell "the user changed their mind" from "the command failed".

title: Safety
text: Safety `init` modifies your project, so the guarantees are explicit: - Nothing is derived from an untrusted value into a command. The one piece of user input that reaches a child process — the scaffolded directory name — is validated against a conservative character set first. - Every generated path is resolved and checked against the project root, so no registry value or theme name can write outside the project. - Commands are passed as argument arrays. A shell is used only on Windows, where the package managers are `.cmd` shims that cannot be launched otherwise. - The exact command being run is printed before it runs. - No remote template repository is ever downloaded by Themvora's own logic; scaffolding is delegated to the ecosystem's official generator.

title: Synopsis — Inspect a theme
text: Synopsis — Inspect a theme ```text Usage: themvora inspect <file> [options] ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<file>` | Theme file to inspect. |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `-f, --file <path>` | Theme file to inspect (or pass it positionally). | — | | `--tokens` | Show semantic token groups only. | — | | `--colors` | Show resolved color tokens only. | — | | `--generation` | Show generation provenance only. | — | | `--accessibility` | Show contrast and relationship diagnostics only. | — | | `--json` | Emit the summary as JSON on stdout. | — |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora inspect theme.json themvora inspect theme.json --generation themvora inspect theme.json --accessibility --json ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end --> ## Examples ```bash themvora inspect themes/plum-dark.json themvora inspect theme.json # a light + dark pair # One section at a time themvora inspect theme.json --generation themvora inspect theme.json --tokens themvora inspect theme.json --colors themvora inspect theme.json --accessibility # Machine-readable themvora inspect theme.json --json ``` With no selector, every section is shown. ## Output For a single theme: ``` Theme: mint-light Mode: light Family: mint Label: Mint Light Version: N/A Provenance: Algorithm semantic-v2 Seed #059669 Style soft Tokens: colors: 21 items radius: 1 items Colors: background #f8fbf9 foreground #12211a primary #0a8f5f ... Accessibility: contrast 9/9 text · 7/7 ui pairs meet the floor relationships no issues ``` For a `{ light, dark }` pair, each theme is printed with its own index: ```text Theme 1: mint-light ... Theme 2: mint-dark ``` ## Provenance `Provenance` reports the generation metadata the theme carries — the algorithm, the seed it was generated from, the style, and any roles pinned to a brand anchor. It is read straight from `meta.generation`; nothing is inferred. A theme with no provenance is labelled as such, and `inspect` only suggests `migrate` when a registered migration step actually applies to the file: ``` Provenance: not recorded — this theme was not produced by the generator. ``` ## Accessibility The `Accessibility` section reuses core's own checks: the canonical `measureThemeContrast()` measurement for the ratio counts, and `validateThemeLevels()` for the relationship and CVD diagnostics. `inspect` never re-derives a ratio. Note that this section is diagnostic. A hand-authored theme can report issues here and still be perfectly valid — see [validate](./validate) for why the two commands draw that line where they do. ## JSON output `--json` emits the same data as a document. For a single theme the theme object is the root; for a pair it is `{ "themes": [ … ] }`. ```bash themvora inspect theme.json --json ``` ```json { "themes": [ { "name": "mint-light", "mode": "light", "family": "mint", "generation": { "algorithm": "semantic-v2", "seed": "#059669", "style": "soft", "anchored": [] }, "tokens": { "groups": [{ "name": "colors", "count": 21 }] }, "colors": { "background": "#f8fbf9" }, "accessibility": { "pairs": 16, "text": { "total": 9, "passing": 9 }, "ui": { "total": 7, "passing": 7 }, "diagnostics": [] } } ] } ``` ## Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | Inspected successfully. | | `1` | File not found, unreadable, or not parseable as JSON or JSONC. | | `2` | No theme file supplied. | ## Next Steps - [Migrate themes to new schema](./migrate) - [Export current tokens](./export) - [Validate theme structure](./validate) - [CLI reference](./reference) ## Related - [Themvora Quick Start](../quickstart) - [Custom Themes](../../custom-themes) - [API Reference](../../api-reference) Next: [migrate](/cli/migrate).

title: Overview
text: # CLI Overview **Themvora CLI** is the command-line toolkit for creating, validating, migrating, inspecting, and exporting Themvora themes — and for wiring Themvora into a project. It wraps the same **Themvora core** design system that every `@themvora/*` framework package consumes, so a theme built in the terminal is literally the same JSON shape a React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Next, Nuxt, Astro, Remix, Tailwind, or plain HTML app reads at runtime. ```bash # npm — `-g` is npm's global-install flag (pnpm: `pnpm add --global`, yarn: `yarn global add`) npm install -g @themvora/cli themvora --help ```

title: Why a CLI?
text: Why a CLI? Themvora has two audiences, and they need different interfaces: - **Applications** depend on the runtime packages — `@themvora/core`, `@themvora/react`, `@themvora/next`, the adapters — at build time and run. - **Developers and build pipelines** work on the theme *files* and on the *project* that consumes them — create, check, compare, inspect, migrate and export themes; scaffold a project; add a theme to one — without opening an editor. The CLI is a standalone developer tool for that second audience. It doesn't run in your app; you run it when you author a theme or set a project up.

title: The two halves
text: The two halves The command set has a file half and a project half, and the difference matters for what each command is allowed to touch. | | Commands | Reads | Writes | | --- | -------- | ----- | ------ | | **Themes** | `generate` `validate` `inspect` `diff` `explain` `audit` `migrate` `export` | a theme file | only where you name a destination | | **Registries** | `list` `completion` | the canonical catalogs | nothing | | **Projects** | `init` `add` `doctor` | a project directory | targeted edits, and only with your consent | The theme commands are pure: a theme in, text out. The project commands are the ones that edit files, and they are built to refuse rather than guess.

title: How a theme moves through the CLI
text: How a theme moves through the CLI ```text list ──→ which brands, presets, styles and frameworks exist? ↓ seed color · preset · brand ↓ generateTheme ──→ theme.json ↓ validateTheme ──→ schema + tokens + contrast ↓ inspect ──→ what is inside this theme? ↓ diff ──→ how does it differ from another? ↓ explain ──→ where did it come from? ↓ audit ──→ does it pass the quality scorecard? ↓ use in the runtime ── @themvora/core provider ↓ migrate ── when the theme schema changes ↓ export ── CSS variables / JSON for another system ``` `list` is the discovery half: it reads the same canonical registries `generate` resolves against, so the identifiers it prints are exactly the ones the generator accepts.

title: Or let the CLI set the project up
text: Or let the CLI set the project up ```text init ──→ scaffold or integrate a project ↓ theme.config.ts ──→ the single theme declaration ↓ add ──→ extend that registry with another source ↓ doctor ──→ is the project still healthy? ``` `init` scaffolds with the framework's **own** generator and then integrates into the result, and it verifies the outcome by running the project's own build and typecheck. A project it created is verified end to end — the generated app builds, and the theme is applied on first paint. Run it with no arguments in a terminal and it becomes a short guided wizard: ```bash themvora init ``` It asks for the project name, the package manager, the framework, and whether to use Tailwind CSS, then does everything else itself — scaffold, integration, one dependency install, build and typecheck. Nothing is mandatory about the prompts: supply the values as flags and it runs straight through, which is how it behaves in CI either way. ```bash themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react ```

title: Package vs. command
text: Package vs. command | npm package | terminal command | | ------------------- | ------------------ | | `@themvora/cli` | `themvora` | The package is installed globally, and the packager links the `themvora` executable into your shell's bin directory. You type `themvora`, not `@themvora/cli`.

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - **Node.js 18+** (any modern release). No browser package is needed. - For the theme commands, a plain JSON theme file. A file is either a **pair** (`{ "light": …, "dark": … }`, generated by `--mode both`) or a **single** theme (`{ "name", "meta", "tokens" }`, from `--mode light|dark`). - For `init` and `add`, a project directory.

title: What the CLI does not do
text: What the CLI does not do It is not a build tool, a daemon, or an editor. Specifically: - **It never scaffolds a project by hand.** `init` delegates to `create-vite` or `create-next-app` and integrates into the output, because a copy of someone else's starter template is stale the moment they change it. - **It never publishes or versions anything.** It does not bump your `package.json` versions and does not run a release. - **It never rewrites a file it does not own.** A generated artifact is regenerated; a file you maintain is left alone, or reported as a conflict. - **It never writes without being asked.** `--plan` and `--dry-run` are inert, and the theme commands write only to a destination you name. - **It only prompts where a person is.** `init` opens a guided wizard when it has questions and a terminal to ask them in. Every other command, and `init` itself under `--json`, `--quiet`, `--plan`, `--dry-run`, in CI, or with a redirected stdin, reports a missing required value as a usage error with an actionable message instead. Scripts and pipelines never wait for input.

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - @themvora/cli installed (globally, locally, or via npx) A **preset** is a curated recipe: a seed colour, a generation style, and a character, pinned together so the result is reproducible. Presets are the shortest path from "I need a theme" to a complete light/dark pair. ```bash themvora list presets themvora generate --preset mint ```

title: The nine presets
text: The nine presets | Preset | Character | Style | Seed | | ------ | --------- | ----- | ---- | | `oat` | Warm · Soft · Neutral | `soft` | `#b45309` | | `berry` | Warm · Vibrant | `vibrant` | `#db2777` | | `mint` | Cool · Soft · Restrained | `soft` | `#059669` | | `citrus` | Warm · Vibrant · Bright | `vibrant` | `#d97706` | | `cocoa` | Warm · Deep · Editorial | `editorial` | `#92400e` | | `plum` | Violet · Editorial | `editorial` | `#7c3aed` | | `iris` | Cool · Balanced | `balanced` | `#6366f1` | | `sky` | Cool · Soft · Airy | `soft` | `#0ea5e9` | | `graphite` | Neutral · Minimal | `minimal` | `#52525b` | Every preset produces a `<id>-light` and `<id>-dark` theme. Browse them with the colours applied on the [preset gallery](/presets).

title: Using a preset
text: Using a preset **Generate a file** — the theme is written out, nothing else changes: ```bash themvora generate --preset mint --output theme.json ``` **Start a project** — `init` registers the preset with the framework provider: ```bash themvora init my-app --framework react --preset mint ``` **Extend a project** — `add` appends it to the project's existing registry, so both presets become selectable: ```bash themvora add preset iris ```

title: Discovering the ids
text: Discovering the ids ```bash themvora list presets # a table, with character, style and seed themvora list presets --json # the full registry entries themvora list presets --ids # just the identifiers, one per line ``` Every identifier comes from the same registry `generate`, `init` and `add` resolve against, so `list` cannot print a preset the generator would reject. A preset id is also the value `--preset` accepts everywhere: ```bash themvora generate --preset mint themvora init my-app --framework vue --preset mint themvora add preset mint ```

title: Where the values come from
text: Where the values come from A preset is a **recipe**, not a snapshot. `generateTheme` derives the full token set from the seed using the pinned style, which is why two runs of the same preset produce byte-identical output and why a preset never carries hand-tuned colours that could drift from the generator. `--style` overrides the style a preset pins: ```bash themvora generate --preset mint --style editorial ```

title: Presets vs. brands vs. seeds
text: Presets vs. brands vs. seeds | | What it is | When to use it | | --- | ---------- | -------------- | | **Preset** | A curated seed + style + character | You want a considered theme, fast | | **[Brand](/cli/brands)** | A brand-inspired recipe with documented anchors | You want something recognisable | | **Seed** | Just a colour | You have a brand colour of your own | All three resolve to the same thing — a pair of `ThemeDefinition` objects — so they are interchangeable in every command that accepts a theme source.

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - npm, pnpm, yarn, or bun installed - No Themvora project setup required to start A complete five-minute workflow: generate a theme from a seed, validate it, inspect it, and export CSS variables — then wire the JSON into a Themvora provider.

title: Two ways to start
text: Two ways to start This page follows the **file** path: produce a theme, check it, and hand it to your app. If you would rather the CLI set the project up for you — scaffold it, wire the provider, and verify it builds — start with [`init`](/cli/init) instead: ```bash # Guided: asks for the project name, package manager, framework and styling themvora init # Or say what you want and skip the questions themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react --preset mint # Same project, with Tailwind CSS instead of the default plain CSS themvora init my-app --tool pnpm --framework react --styling tailwind ``` Either way it scaffolds with the framework's own generator, installs the dependencies once, and runs the project's build and typecheck before it reports success. Plain CSS is the default; the styling choice changes how the starter is written, not what it contains: same page, same components, same theme tokens. Both paths end in the same place: the same `ThemeDefinition` objects, consumed by the same provider.

title: 1. Install
text: 1. Install ```bash npm install -g @themvora/cli # or, without installing: npx --yes @themvora/cli ... ```

title: 2. Generate
text: 2. Generate Not sure what to generate? List the canonical registries first — the identifiers they print are exactly the ones the generator accepts: ```bash themvora list presets themvora list brands ``` Derive a complete **light + dark pair** from one seed color: ```bash themvora generate \ --seed "#6366f1" \ --family indigo \ --output theme.json ``` `--family` becomes the theme name and label prefix (`indigo-light`, `indigo-dark`). The generator also derives the secondary, muted, accent, border, ring, destructive, and background/foreground colors from the seed. Or start from a curated recipe instead of a raw colour: ```bash themvora generate --preset mint --output theme.json themvora generate --brand apple --output theme.json ``` Omit `--output` to print the JSON to stdout, or ask for one mode only: ```bash themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --mode light --output light.json themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --mode dark --output dark.json ``` The default `--mode both` writes a `{ light, dark }` pair — one definition per mode, each carrying its own `meta` (family + mode) and token set: ```json title="theme.json" { "light": { "name": "indigo-light", "meta": { "family": "indigo", "mode": "light", "label": "Indigo Light", "order": 10 }, "tokens": { "colors": { "background": "#f8fafc", "foreground": "#0f172a", "primary": "#6366f1", "border": "#d9d9e8", "ring": "#6366f1" }, "radius": { "lg": "8px" } } }, "dark": { "name": "indigo-dark", "meta": { "family": "indigo", "mode": "dark", "label": "Indigo Dark", "order": 20 }, "tokens": { "colors": { "background": "#020617", "foreground": "#f8fafc", "primary": "#9596ea", "border": "#080a5e", "ring": "#9596ea" }, "radius": { "lg": "8px" } } } } ```

title: 3. Validate
text: 3. Validate ```bash themvora validate theme.json # ✓ Theme is valid: indigo-light + indigo-dark ``` `validate` checks the schema, required semantic tokens, inheritance, references, and contrast. It returns exit code `3` when validation fails: ```bash themvora validate theme.json # ✗ Theme is invalid: indigo-dark # - Missing token: `colors.primary` ```

title: 4. Inspect
text: 4. Inspect ```bash themvora inspect theme.json # Theme 1: indigo-light # Mode: light # Family: indigo # Tokens: # colors: 21 items ```

title: 5. Export for another system
text: 5. Export for another system ```bash themvora export theme.json --format css --output theme.css ``` ```css :root { --theme-color-background: #f8fafc; --theme-color-primary: #6366f1; } ```

title: 6. Bring the theme into your app
text: 6. Bring the theme into your app The JSON the CLI writes is exactly what a provider consumes: ```tsx // React / Next.js import { ThemeProvider } from "@themvora/react"; import raw from "./theme.json"; const themes = raw.light ? [raw.light, raw.dark] : [raw]; export function App() { return <ThemeProvider themes={themes} defaultTheme="light">{/* UI */}</ThemeProvider>; } ``` If you would rather not wire this by hand, [`init`](/cli/init) writes that provider, a `theme.config.ts`, and the zero-flash bootstrap for you — and then runs your project's own build to prove it works.

text: Where to go next The five steps above are the file workflow. title: Environment & non-interactive mode
text: Environment & non-interactive mode Every command except `init` is non-interactive by construction. `init` has a guided wizard, and it runs only when a terminal is attached and the invocation is not `--json`, `--quiet`, `--plan` or `--dry-run`; in every other context it reports a missing value as a usage error that names the flag supplying it. Otherwise the CLI always respects `--output` for file writes, never overwrites without being told to, and prints plain text when colour or animation is unavailable. Colour follows `NO_COLOR` and `FORCE_COLOR`; animation and prompts are disabled in CI, on `TERM=dumb`, and whenever stdout or stdin is not a TTY.

title: themvora: command not found

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - @themvora/cli installed (globally, locally, or via npx) A **generation style** is the visual language the generator works in. It decides how much chroma the surfaces carry, how the secondary and accent roles relate to the primary hue, how strong borders are, and how deep the dark mode goes. ```bash themvora list styles themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --style editorial ```

title: The six styles
text: The six styles `balanced` is the default and the reference point. The others each move a small number of parameters in one direction, so the difference between any two is legible rather than arbitrary. | Style | Character | Secondary | Accent | Borders | | ----- | --------- | --------- | ------ | ------- | | `balanced` | The reference. Even surfaces, restrained accents | neutral | analogous | medium | | `soft` | Warmer surfaces, gentler primaries, tinted secondary | tinted | analogous | light | | `vibrant` | Higher chroma, wider accent split | tinted | split-complementary | strong | | `editorial` | Deeper primaries, very low surface chroma, strong rules | neutral | complementary | strong | | `minimal` | No surface chroma at all, muted primary, hairline borders | neutral | analogous | very light | | `brand` | The seed is the anchor; the widest lightness band of the six | neutral | analogous | light | The last column is a summary. Concretely, the parameters that move are the surface chroma, the primary chroma multiplier, the secondary and accent hue relationships, the neutral temperature, the border strength, the dark surface depth, and the band the primary's lightness is clamped into.

title: brand is different on purpose
text: brand is different on purpose The other five styles *interpret* the seed. `brand` treats it as an anchor: the primary is allowed to stay as dark as `#000000` or as light as `#ffffff`, which is why its lightness band is the widest of the six. A near-black brand stays near-black instead of being lifted into a mid-tone. Contrast repair still applies — it moves the ink first and the surface only as far as it must — so a `brand` theme remains accessible. That is why four of the five [brand recipes](/cli/brands) use it, and `vercel` does not: a monochrome identity reads better through `minimal`.

title: Using a style
text: Using a style ```bash # On a seed themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --style editorial # On a seed added to a project themvora add seed "#6366f1" --family indigo --style soft # Overriding the style a preset pins themvora generate --preset mint --style vibrant ``` `--style` is accepted wherever a seed is generated. A preset or brand already pins a style, and passing `--style` overrides it.

title: Discovering the values
text: Discovering the values ```bash themvora list styles # the six names themvora list styles --ids # just the identifiers, one per line themvora list styles --json # the registry ``` The names come from the generator's own `GENERATION_STYLE_NAMES`, so the CLI cannot accept a style the engine does not implement.

title: Styles are not themes
text: Styles are not themes A style does not produce a theme on its own — it is a parameter of generation: ```text seed colour + style ──→ generateTheme ──→ theme.json ``` Two runs with the same seed and style produce byte-identical output. That is what makes a [preset](/cli/presets) reproducible: a preset is exactly a seed, a style and a character, pinned together.

title: Synopsis — Validate a theme
text: Synopsis — Validate a theme ```text Usage: themvora validate <file> [options] ``` | Argument | Description | | -------- | ----------- | | `<file>` | Theme file to validate. |

title: Options
text: Options | Option | Description | Default | | ------ | ----------- | ------- | | `-f, --file <path>` | Theme file to validate (or pass it positionally). | — | | `--json` | Emit a machine-readable report on stdout. | — | | `--quiet` | Suppress the success summary. Errors are still printed. | — |

title: Exit codes
text: Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | theme is valid | | `3` | validation failed (issues are listed) | | `1` | command/runtime error | | `2` | usage/argument error |

title: Examples
text: Examples ```bash themvora validate theme.json themvora validate theme.json --json themvora check theme.json ``` > Generated from `packages/cli/src/command-schema.json` — the same contract `themvora --help` renders. <!-- cli-command:generated:end --> ## Examples ```bash themvora validate theme.json themvora validate themes/berry.json themvora validate theme.json --json ``` The file may be a single theme or a `{ light, dark }` pair; both are validated. ### Comments and trailing commas Theme files may be JSONC. `//` and `/* … */` comments and trailing commas are accepted — this is a syntax excerpt, not a complete theme: ```jsonc { // The brand colour. "name": "brand-light", "tokens": { "colors": { "primary": "#4f46e5", // trailing commas are fine too }, }, } ``` The same parser is used by the VS Code extension (`parseThemeJson()` in `@themvora/core`), so a commented theme behaves identically in the editor and in CI — diagnostics, hovers and colour swatches included. **Only** comments and trailing commas are tolerated. Unquoted keys, single-quoted strings and other JSON5 syntax are not: `JSON.parse` still decides what the values are, and the tolerance is applied by blanking the extra syntax first. Package manifests such as `package.json` are read as strict JSON and are unaffected. A genuinely malformed file still fails, and the message says where the parser gave up: ```text Error: file is not valid JSON or JSONC: themes/broken.json — Expected double-quoted property name in JSON at position 17 (line 3 column 1) ``` ## What it checks `validate` reports the layers Themvora core actually provides. Each layer comes from the shipped API — there is no second validator inside the CLI. | Layer | Source | Decides the exit code? | | ----- | ------ | ---------------------- | | `required` | `validateTheme()` — the frozen contract | **Yes** | | `structure` | `validateThemeLevels()` | No — reported | | `semantic` | `validateThemeLevels()` (semantic + visual) | No — reported | | `contrast` | `validateThemeLevels()` | No — reported | | `accessibility` | `validateThemeLevels()` (CVD diagnostics) | No — reported | | `measured` | `measureThemeContrast()` — the canonical ratio measurement | No — reported | ### Why only one layer decides the exit code `required` is the contract that shipped first, and it is what existing pipelines already branch on. The deeper layers are stricter: they flag, for example, an `input` token that sits below the UI contrast floor, or a `card` and `popover` that are not visually distinguishable. Turning those into failures by default would make themes that pass today start failing — a breaking change to a tool people run in CI. So they are **reported** here, and *gating* on them belongs to `themvora audit`. ## Output On success, the summary line is followed by the layer breakdown: ``` ✓ Theme is valid: mint-light + mint-dark mint-light structure pass semantic pass contrast pass accessibility pass measured 16 pairs · text 12/12 · ui 4/4 ``` A theme that is structurally valid but has deeper problems says so without failing: ``` ✓ Theme is valid: forest-light + forest-dark forest-light structure pass semantic 1 issue(s) · `card` and `popover` are not distinguishable (ΔL 0.000 < 0.005) contrast 2 issue(s) · input/background is 1.40:1, below 3:1 · input/card is 1.45:1, below 3:1 accessibility pass measured 16 pairs · text 9/9 · ui 5/7 ``` On failure, every missing token is listed and the command exits `3`: ``` ✗ Theme is invalid: x - Missing token: `colors.background` - Missing token: `colors.foreground` (validation failed for 1 theme) ``` `--quiet` suppresses the success summary. It never suppresses errors. ## JSON output `--json` emits one document on stdout, with nothing else mixed in — diagnostics never contaminate a payload. ```bash themvora validate theme.json --json ``` ```json { "valid": true, "themes": [ { "name": "mint-light", "valid": true, "issues": [], "layers": [ { "layer": "structure", "issues": [] }, { "layer": "contrast", "issues": [] } ], "contrast": { "pairs": 16, "text": { "total": 12, "passing": 12 }, "ui": { "total": 4, "passing": 4 } } } ], "summary": { "themes": 2, "valid": 2, "invalid": 0 } } ``` The shape is stable: `valid` mirrors the exit code, `themes` is in file order, and `summary` is the aggregate. A failing run still emits the document *and* exits `3`. ## Exit codes | Code | Meaning | | ---- | ------- | | `0` | Theme is valid. | | `1` | File not found, unreadable, or not parseable as JSON or JSONC. | | `2` | No theme file supplied (invalid arguments). | | `3` | Validation failed (issues are listed). | Because failure is a real nonzero exit code, `validate` works in any build tool: ```bash themvora validate themes/ || exit 1 ``` ## Next Steps - [Inspect validation output](./inspect) - [Export as CSS or JSON](./export) - [CLI reference](./reference) ## Related - [Themvora Quick Start](../quickstart) - [Custom Themes](../../custom-themes) - [API Reference](../../api-reference) Next: [inspect](/cli/inspect).

title: Prerequisites
text: Prerequisites - Node.js 18+ - @themvora/cli installed (globally, locally, or via npx) - A Themvora project or JSON theme files to work with The CLI is a small, composable toolkit. The commands chain into real workflows you can run in a terminal or a pipeline — one for authoring a theme, and one for standing a project up on one.

title: The theme authoring loop
text: The theme authoring loop ```text 1. Generate ── seed · preset · brand → theme.json 2. Edit ── tweak tokens by hand 3. Validate ── `themvora validate themes/` 4. Inspect ── review what changed 5. Compare ── `themvora diff before.json after.json` 6. Audit ── gate on the quality scorecard 7. Commit ── git 8. CI validates ── on every push / PR 9. Ship ── merge, deploy 10. Migrate later ── when the schema changes ``` ```bash themvora generate --preset mint --output themes/mint.json themvora validate themes/ themvora inspect themes/mint-light.json themvora diff themes/mint.json themes/iris.json ``` ```text Git ─→ PR ─→ CI validate ─→ merge ```

title: The project setup loop
text: The project setup loop The other half of the CLI works on a *project* rather than a file. ```text init ──→ scaffold or integrate ↓ theme.config.ts ──→ the single theme declaration ↓ add ──→ extend the registry with another source ↓ doctor ──→ is the project still healthy? ``` ```bash themvora init my-app --framework react --preset mint themvora add brand apple --dir my-app themvora doctor my-app ``` `init` and `add` are idempotent: running either again changes nothing, and both refuse to rewrite a file they do not own. `doctor` is the check to run when something looks wrong.

title: Generate then validate
text: Generate then validate Always validate right after a generate or an edit. A theme can be complete yet fail contrast; catch it before it reaches an app. ```bash themvora generate --seed "#6366f1" --family indigo --output theme.json themvora validate theme.json || echo "fix before commit" ```

title: Light / dark pairs
text: Light / dark pairs `--mode both` (default) writes a pair. Many apps want only one mode; generate a single theme with `--mode light|dark` when you prefer.

title: Migrate legacy themes
text: Migrate legacy themes Schemas change. Keep `migrate` in your maintenance runbook: ```bash themvora migrate themes/legacy.json --output themes/current.json ``` `migrate` reports by default and writes nothing: use `--dry-run` to see what would change, `--output` to write elsewhere, or `--write` to migrate the file in place. There is no path that overwrites the input without `--write`. ```bash themvora migrate themes/legacy.json --dry-run themvora migrate themes/legacy.json --write ```

title: Export for another system
text: Export for another system `export` is where the CLI becomes a bridge: ```text Themvora theme ─→ export ─→ CSS variables / JSON map ``` ```bash themvora export theme.json --format css --output theme.css ``` The CSS variables apply with **no runtime** — Tailwind, shadcn/ui, daisyUI, and any hand-written stylesheet consume them directly.

title: The CLI + your framework
text: The CLI + your framework ```text THEMVORA │ Runtime CLI Documentation │ │ │ ┌────────┼───────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ themes registries projects │ │ │ │ │ generate list init │ validate completion add │ inspect doctor │ diff │ explain │ audit │ migrate │ export │ │ └────────────┼────────────────────── │ theme.json · theme.config.ts ``` A theme generated in the terminal is the same object a provider consumes: ```tsx import { ThemeProvider } from "@themvora/react"; const themes = [light, dark]; ```

title: Quick start
text: Quick start Attach the plugin to your runtime and a panel to your page: ```ts import { createThemeRuntime } from "@themvora/core"; import { createDevToolsPlugin, createDevToolsPanel } from "@themvora/devtools"; const runtime = createThemeRuntime({ plugins: [createDevToolsPlugin()], }); // Optional: mount the UI panel anywhere const panel = createDevToolsPanel( runtime.plugins.get("devtools-inspector") as any, ); document.body.appendChild(panel); ```

title: createDevToolsPlugin(options)
text: createDevToolsPlugin(options) A Themvora plugin that instantiates an inspector, binds it to the runtime and exposes it on `window.__THEMVORA_DEVTOOLS__` so extensions can find it. ```ts const plugin = createDevToolsPlugin({ maxEntries: 200, maxPerfEntries: 100 }); const runtime = createThemeRuntime({ plugins: [plugin] }); plugin.getInspector().getState(); // { // currentTheme: ThemeDefinition, // selection: { mode, family }, // history: [{ index, point: { theme, selection } }], // entries: [{ type, timestamp, label, data }], // performance: [{ duration, type, timestamp }], // cssVariables: { "--theme-color-primary": "#6366f1", ... }, // } ``` Internally it subscribes to `beforeThemeChange` / `afterThemeChange` to record perf entries and emits a `theme-change` event entry on every switch.

title: createDevToolsInspector(options)
text: createDevToolsInspector(options) The standalone recorder — use it directly if you are not going through the plugin. Records theme-change entries, lifecycle performance events and state snapshots, capped at `maxEntries` (default 200) and `maxPerfEntries` (default 100). ```ts const inspector = createDevToolsInspector(); // Read what has happened inspector.getEntries(); // [{ type: "theme-change", timestamp: 1712345678901, label: "Theme changed", data: {} }] inspector.getPerformance(); // [{ duration: 0, type: "afterThemeChange", timestamp: 1712345678901 }] // Jump through history inspector.jump(0); // restores snapshot at index 0 // Inspect live state inspector.getState(); inspector.getCSSVariables(); // Export inspector.exportState(); // JSON string of the full state inspector.exportCSS(); // { "--theme-color-primary": "#6366f1", ... } inspector.clearEntries(); inspector.clearPerformance(); inspector.destroy(); ```

title: createDevToolsPanel(inspector)
text: createDevToolsPanel(inspector) Renders a floating, framework-free panel (plain DOM, no dependencies) with five tabs: - **Inspector** — the current theme and selection as pretty-printed JSON - **Events** — chronological lifecycle event entries - **Perf** — `beforeThemeChange` / `afterThemeChange` timings as bars - **CSS Vars** — the flattened `--theme-*` variables of the active theme with color swatches - **History** — every snapshot with a one-click "Jump" to restore it Footer buttons clear events/perf and export the state to JSON or the CSS variables to a `.css` file. ```ts const panel = createDevToolsPanel(inspector); document.body.appendChild(panel); ```

title: Global hook
text: Global hook Every inspector registered via the plugin is added to a Set on `window.__THEMVORA_DEVTOOLS__`, so a browser extension or your own code can enumerate and inspect all live runtimes: ```ts declare global { interface Window { __THEMVORA_DEVTOOLS__?: Set<{ getState(): unknown; getEntries(): unknown[]; getPerformance(): unknown[]; }>; } } for (const inspector of window.__THEMVORA_DEVTOOLS__ ?? []) { console.log(inspector.getState()); } ```

title: Entry types
text: Entry types Every recorded entry has a `type`: | Type | Meaning | | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | `theme-change` | The active theme changed | | `mode-change` | The mode changed (light / dark / system) | | `family-change` | The family changed (e.g. `plum` → `mint`) | | `persist` | Selection was persisted to storage | | `restore` | A snapshot was restored (undo / redo / jump) | | `batch` | An atomic batched update ran |

title: React (@themvora/react)
text: React (@themvora/react) Provider and hooks for React, with scoped themes, transitions, and an optional build-time bootstrap. **Tags:** SPA · Vite · Context

title: Feature map
text: Feature map **Provider** - **ThemeProvider** — Creates a runtime, wires DOM + CSS-variable bindings, and provides it via context. Accepts every ThemeRuntimeOptions prop. - **Runtime injection** — Pass `runtime` to share an existing instance, or `initial` to seed the server-resolved selection for hydration. - **scheduled prop** — Switches between `lightTheme` and `darkTheme` at each visitor's local sunrise and sunset. Latitude/longitude are optional — the location comes from the browser timezone unless you pin `timeZone`. **Root bootstrap** - **createThemeRoot()** — Optional client-only root bootstrap that lets Themvora control the initial React root commit when synchronous first-commit behavior is required. - **Standard createRoot()** — Use the normal React root API when no special first-commit optimization is needed. **Hooks** - **useTheme()** — Returns `{ theme, mode, effectiveMode, family, setMode, setFamily, toggleTheme }`. - **useThemeValue() / useThemeTokens()** — The active theme definition, and the active theme tokens. - **useThemeMode() / useThemeFamily()** — Granular reads for the current mode and family. - **useEffectiveThemeMode()** — The mode actually applied — `light` or `dark`, never `system`. This is what a label or icon showing the current appearance must render: it follows a sunrise/sunset transition, while `useThemeMode()` keeps reporting what the visitor asked for. - **useSetThemeMode() / useSetThemeFamily()** — Granular setters — set mode or family independently. - **useToggleTheme()** — Toggle function for light/dark. - **useThemeRuntime()** — Access the full runtime: registry, history, lifecycle, plugins. - **useThemeHistory()** — `{ undo, redo, canUndo, canRedo, clear }`. - **useThemeBatch()** — Wrap `runtime.batch()` for atomic, coalesced updates. - **useThemeSnapshot() / useThemeRestore()** — Serialize and restore the full runtime state. - **useThemeTimeTravel()** — `{ history, jump }` — indexed navigation through time. - **useThemeLifecycle()** — Subscribe to typed lifecycle events (`beforeThemeChange`, `afterPersist`, ...). - **useThemePacks()** — Install a theme pack at runtime via `runtime.use()`. - **useThemeSchedule()** — Reactive sunrise/sunset controller: `enabled`, `active`, `status`, `sunrise`, `sunset`, `nextTransition` plus `enable()`/`disable()`/`set()`. Returns `null` when the provider has no `scheduled` option. **Components** - **ThemeScope** — Apply a specific theme to a subtree; emits scoped CSS vars plus Tailwind-compatible `--color-*` / `--radius-*` variables. - **ThemeModeButton** — One-click light → dark → system cycle button. - **ThemeInspector** — Floating dev panel: active theme, selection, flattened tokens, generated CSS variables. - **useScopedTheme(ref, themeName)** — Imperative scoping for any element ref. - **useThemePacks()** — Install a theme pack at runtime via `runtime.use()`. **Library adapters** - **createMuiAdapter() / createChakraAdapter()** — Maps Themvora semantic tokens into native generated themes while preserving the framework-neutral runtime contract. - **createAntdAdapter() / createMuiAdapter() / createChakraAdapter()** — Rebuilds the library theme from the active Themvora theme and exposes a reactive snapshot/subscribe bridge for React providers. - **MantineThemeProvider + createMantineTheme()** — Mantine's generated-theme bridge: `createMantineTheme(runtime)` rebuilds the native Mantine theme from Themvora tokens, and `MantineThemeProvider` forces the color scheme to match the active mode. - **CSS-variable adapters** — Shadcn, Bootstrap, DaisyUI, and Open Props adapters can be registered directly with the runtime; their factories do not require React. **Transition** - **transition prop** — Transitions are enabled by default (300ms, smooth). Pass `transition` to tune duration/easing/preset/properties, or `transition={{ enabled: false }}` to disable. - **runtime.store.set(theme, { suppressTransition: true })** — Per-update escape hatch: `runtime.store.set(theme, { suppressTransition: true })` skips the configured animation for a single switch. For custom animation orchestration, compose the core diff/plan/runner APIs.

title: Notes
text: Notes - **Zero-flash:** Included. `ThemeProvider` injects a blocking script into `<head>` before the first paint, so a returning visitor sees their saved theme immediately. For an SSR app, inline it yourself with `createThemeBootstrapScript()`. - **Starting mode:** `defaultTheme` chooses the starting theme. Add `initialMode="system"` to follow the visitor's OS on the first visit. - **Configuration:** Themes and the starting mode come from the provider props. That is the whole setup, with or without a build tool. If you do build with Vite, you can declare them once in `theme.config.ts` instead and let `themvoraVitePlugin()` derive the pre-paint bootstrap from the same file — the provider then takes no theme props. The plugin is optional either way.

title: Next.js (@themvora/next)
